That is, the mercy of God, Exalted is He, belongs to Him alone; none distributes it except Him by His will, distributing it as He wills, just as He distributed among them their livelihood and gave them material provision. If the Lord, glory be to Him, has distributed their provision in the lower realm, how do they wish to dispose of the higher? They said, as the Qur'an records on their tongues:

﴿O God, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ (al-Anfal: 32).

The correct reasoning would have been for them to say: "O God, if this is the truth from You, then guide us to it." But in their foolishness they asked for death instead of guidance. Their zealotry, then, was directed against the person of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Whoever among them declared his faith in God should have testified that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the Messenger of God.

The Blessed and Exalted says:

﴿Only he who believes in God and the Last Day...﴾ (at-Tawbah: 18).

This statement carries in its meaning faith in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because God says after it: ﴿and establishes the prayer﴾, and establishing the prayer is not valid from them unless they believe in the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is he who told us that they are five(2), he who taught us how to perform them and what to say in them, and he whom we bear witness to while we pray, in the call to prayer and in the tashahhud. Therefore, whenever we establish the prayer, we must be believers in the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Accordingly, His saying, ﴿and establishes the prayer﴾, necessarily implies faith in the Messenger of God (ﷺ). In this noble verse, the Glorified and Exalted made conditional belief in Him and in the Last Day, and establishing the prayer, within which is contained belief in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and then giving the zakat, and He asked us not to fear anyone other than Him. Khashyah is fear. The Glorified and Exalted said to His Messenger (ﷺ):

﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾ (al-Anfal: 58).

So there is fear of other things. We say: when the Truth says ﴿and fears none but God﴾, it means that in his religion he fears none but God; but there is no objection to the fear that makes you prepare for your enemy and guard against his aggression upon you. Observe the precision and greatness of the noble Qur'an: it combined in one verse belief in God and the Last Day, prayer and zakat, and there is no mention in it of belief in the Messenger, because it is a matter folded within the pillars of faith. Whoever does this enters the company of those whom the Truth, Glorified and Exalted, described in His saying:

﴿Then it is they who may be among the guided﴾ (at-Tawbah: 18).

One might say: how, after they have believed in all of this, do we say "may" ( 'asa)? So what is the ruling on one who has not believed?

We say: 'asa and la'alla are verbs of hope, and mentioning them means hope that what follows them will be realized. The degrees of hope differ according to whether it concerns oneself, others, or God. You say, for example: "Ask so-and-so, perhaps (la'alla) he will give you," which is one degree of hope; and you say: "Perhaps (la'alli) I will give you," which is closer to certainty than my hoping that another gives you.

So this is a higher stage in the response. And saying "perhaps God will give you" is a third and lofty degree of hope, because you hope in God and do not hope in any human being. God, Glorified and Exalted, is Generous and gives lavishly. But when God, Glorified and Exalted, speaks of Himself: "Perhaps I will give you," this is an expectation of giving.

So the stages of hope are: hope for others from others, hope from you for others, hope from God for someone else, and a statement from God in the form of hope. When God, Glorified and Exalted, says:

﴿Perhaps your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾ (al-Isra': 8),

we say: this is hope that is realized, because He, Glorified and Exalted, is Generous and loves to have mercy upon us, and nothing prevents Him from realizing that. So the hope has been realized. And His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Then it is they who may be among the guided﴾ (at-Tawbah: 18).

Guidance is either to a path that leads to an end, that is, God guides us to the method, and if we act by it we reach Paradise, because the method is the road to Paradise, as evidenced by God, Glorified and Exalted, saying of the disbelievers: ﴿and He will not guide them to any path (168) except the path of Hell﴾ (an-Nisa': 168-169). So guidance is sometimes to the method, so that we believe in it and act by it, and sometimes to a path that leads to a goal. Those whom God mentioned in this noble verse are all those who:

{believe in God and the Last Day, establish the prayer, give the zakat, and fear none but God} (at-Tawbah: 18). Since they have done so, this is the application of the method; and by that, they—God willing—must have Paradise as their end.

1 That this is not undermined by God, Mighty and Majestic, having related of the disbelievers of Quraysh that they said: (Has he made the gods into one God?) (Sad: 5), and that among them was one who "made for Us a comparison and forgot his own creation, saying: Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" (Ya-Sin: 78). This may be, for some of them, a cover for the truth of their rejection of the person of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), out of envy from themselves and arrogance.

2 On the authority of Anas (may God be pleased with him), who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of God, inform me of what prayer has been enjoined upon me. He said: "God has enjoined upon His servants five prayers..." The hadith. Recorded by Ahmad (3/267), al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (1/201), who graded it sound, and al-Daraqutni in his Sunan (1/229).

3 Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir (2/341): every 'asa in the Qur'an is binding (wajibah). Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "'Asa" from God is truth.

Al-Sha'rawi, in his commentary (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66), on surah 9, verse 19:

Then the Truthful, Glorified and Exalted says:

﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the way of Allah? They are not equal in the sight of Allah. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ (19)

This verse came as a response to the disbelievers of Makkah who were taken captive at the Battle of Badr. Among them was al-'Abbas, the uncle of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when some of the Companions spoke to him, calling him to Islam and to jihad in the way of Allah. He said: "We give drink to the pilgrims, we tend the House, we ransom the captives, and we maintain the Sacred House." Al-'Abbas said this while he had not yet embraced Islam. What al-'Abbas said is a summary of the opinion of the people of polytheism from Quraysh, who set these matters against faith in Allah and jihad in His way. The word of the Truth came to affirm that the scales are not balanced, so He said: ﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims..﴾ (19).

The word ﴿siqayah﴾ (giving of drink, watering) is used in three senses. It refers to the place where water gathers for people to drink from, which we call the sabil (public water fountain). It is also used of the vessel from which we drink water, which is raised to the mouth, such as the cup and the goblet, or it is called the "cup of the king" (sawa' al-malik). In the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him, the noble statement comes:

﴿Then when he had furnished them with their supplies, he put the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag.. (70)﴾ (Yusuf).

As for the third meaning, it is the craft itself. We say: this is tailoring (khiyatah), this is smithing (haddadah), and this is watering (siqayah), meaning that it is a work connected with giving water to people. So siqayah is either the wide place where water gathers, or the vessel we use for drinking, or the craft practised by the saqa (water-carrier).

And here the Truth, Blessed and Exalted, says:

﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day.﴾ (al-Tawbah: 19).

If you boast that you are the givers of drink to the pilgrims and the maintainers of the Sacred Mosque, and you set this against Islam, then that is by no means fit to be a counterpart to faith. The scale of belief in Allah and the Last Day is never equal to the scale of giving water to the pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque. Who determines this is Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, and He has absolute will as to whether He accepts the deed or does not accept it. The believer who strives in the way of Allah seeks his reward from Allah, whereas one who gives drink to the pilgrims and tends the House of Allah without acknowledging the oneness of Allah, like the polytheists before Islam, seeks his reward from those for whose sake he did the deed. And since He, the Glorified, is the Giver of reward, He, may He be exalted, makes clear to us that these two deeds are not equal in His sight, that is, neither of them equals the other in reward.

It is said(2) that our master, the Imam 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him and ennoble his face, passed by Talhah ibn Shaybah and al-'Abbas and found them boasting, that is, each of them was boasting over the other with the virtues in which he took pride, in order to establish that he was better and more excellent than the other. Boasting was a trait of the Arabs even in matters in which they had no merit, and which were bestowed upon them by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, such as appearance, lineage, and so on, because no one chooses his father and mother to boast of them; rather, all of that is a gift from Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.

The Arabs, for example, used to sit before a place full of water, boasting of which of them could dive into the water and keep his head under it for longer, that is, which of them had greater breath than the other, although this is a matter subject to the structure and makeup of the body created by Allah the Creator, and no one has a hand in it. Some have been given by Allah lungs stronger than others, and he is the one who can dive for a longer period. Yet this matter was among the aspects of boasting among the Arabs.

Talhah and al-'Abbas sat boasting, and Talhah ibn Shaybah said: "The key of the Ka'bah is in my hand, and if I wished to sleep inside it, I would sleep."

Al-'Abbas replied to him: "And I have the giving of drink to the pilgrims with me, and if I wished not to give drink to anyone, I would be able [to do so]." The Imam 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, passed by them while they were boasting, and when he heard their words he said: "I do not know what you are saying. I prayed six months before the people, and I am the owner of jihad." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the way of Allah? They are not equal in the sight of Allah.﴾ (al-Tawbah: 19). Al-'Abbas had hardly heard this verse before he said: "We are content, we are content." He said that because it was Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, who had judged, and in this statement is an indication that the boasting between al-'Abbas and Talhah was not in its proper place.

The phrase ﴿in the sight of Allah﴾ in the noble verse indicates that the standards with Allah differ from the standards of human beings, because standards commonly differ even among people: you have your standards and people have theirs. You may flatter yourself in your standards, and people may flatter you in theirs, or they may be harsh toward you. Every standard that is held by desire contains bias, because every person prefers himself, and every person tries to take everything. But the standards in which there is no desire, and in which there is nothing but absolute justice, are the standards of Allah; therefore, you find that they surpass everything, and there is no opportunity in them for criticism.

Then the Truth, Glorified and Exalted, concludes the noble verse with His saying: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ (al-Tawbah: 19).

This clause provides the solution to several problems that some people raise concerning guidance, and how it is from Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, and not from the servant, based on His saying:

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills.﴾ (al-Qasas: 56).

We say: yes, the will to guide is from Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, but He, the Glorified, has made clear to us those whom His guidance does not include, so He said: ﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ (al-Baqarah: 264).

He, the Glorified, also said: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ (al-Baqarah: 258).

And He, the Glorified, said: ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 108).

The Truth, Glorified and Exalted, has mentioned these realities in many verses of the Noble Qur'an. Some people say: guidance is from Allah; if Allah had guided me, I would not have killed, stolen or taken bribes. We say: this is a mistaken understanding. Let us return to the Noble Qur'an: the Truth, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿And Allah does not guide﴾, meaning He negates what would necessitate guidance for those who do wrong, or are defiantly disobedient, or disbelieve. For the Truth, Glorified and Exalted, does not guide one who has put forward disbelief, or put forward wrongdoing, or put forward defiant disobedience. It is as if the disbeliever, the wrongdoer, or the defiantly disobedient is the one who prevents guidance from himself. Had the person put forward faith, he would have entered into the guidance of Allah, the Exalted. So the person's exit from the will of Allah's guidance is a matter of his own action and by his choice. A person may choose the path of error and leave the path of guidance, and so Allah does not guide him, because He, the Glorified, guides only the one who believes in Him. If a person chooses the path of guidance, the Truth gives him more guidance, because he believed in Allah, chose the path of guidance, and received the method of Allah with contentment. And thus is the understanding of the saying of the Truth, Blessed and Exalted:

﴿So indeed, Allah leaves to stray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.﴾ (Fatir: 8).

Thus the Truth guides whoever listens to the Qur'an with the spirit of faith and whose certainty is settled that he has a Lord, and believes that he has a God. We have explained this in the matter of destiny and decree, and we said: those who read the Qur'an to understand the question of guidance must survey all the verses related to the subject. He, the Glorified and Exalted, has made clear that He does not guide the disbeliever; therefore He guides the believer. He made clear that He does not guide the wrongdoer; therefore He guides the just. He made clear that He, may He be exalted, does not guide the defiant disobeyer; therefore He guides the obedient. So let no one say: Allah has not willed to guide me, for this is a mistaken understanding of the meaning of guidance from Allah. He, the Glorified and Exalted, has explained to us whom He wills to guide and whom He wills to misguide, and He guides whoever has put forward the causes of guidance and surrendered the reins of his affairs to faith. Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, says:

﴿And Allah increases those who are guided in guidance, and the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in return.﴾ (Maryam: 76).

﴿And those who are guided, Allah increases them in guidance and gives them their piety.﴾ (Muhammad: 17).

Thus Allah has informed us in advance of who deserves His guidance and who does not enter into it, and you, by your choice, choose your path: either you believe, and so you enter into guidance, or you choose the path of disbelief and wrongdoing, God forbid, and so you refrain from guidance. If someone comes to dispute with you and says to you that Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, has said:

﴿Thus Allah leaves to stray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.﴾ (al-Muddaththir: 41).

You may say: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made clear whom He wills to be guided and whom He wills to be led astray. We have struck an example for this, and to Allah belongs the highest example. We said: guidance has come in the Noble Qur'an with two meanings. The first meaning is indication of the way, and this is guidance for all(3). Allah has indicated to believer and disbeliever the path of faith in His messengers and His books; that is, He has clarified for them what pleases Him, what angers Him, what necessitates His mercy and what necessitates His curse. So the first guidance came with the meaning of indication for all, that is, it is general guidance. Then there is a second guidance, specific to believers, which Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, has described in His saying:

﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety.﴾ (Muhammad: 17). That is: He helps them to His method; He makes obedience easy for them and makes sins difficult for them. When the believer complies with the method of Allah and obeys Him, the Mighty and Majestic opens his breast to that, makes obedience beloved to him, and so he increases in obedience. And when he begins to commit a sin, He makes it hateful to him and makes it heavy upon his soul until he leaves it(4).

We have struck an example for this with a man who drives his car toward a certain place. At a junction he finds a traffic policeman, who directs him to the road. This is general indication. When the man thanks the traffic policeman, the policeman increases the clarification for him: "Do not take this road, because it has hardships and difficulties; take that road, and you will arrive quickly and easily." This is an increase in indication, or an increase in guidance. But if the driver says to himself: "This is a traffic policeman who knows nothing," and ignores his thanks, the policeman leaves him to his own affairs.

Thus the Truth, Glorified and Exalted, has guided both believer and disbeliever to the path of faith, and whoever takes the path of faith, Allah, the Exalted, helps him in it; and whoever takes the path of disbelief, God forbid, Allah leaves him to struggle and go astray. Therefore we must always remember that guidance is of two kinds: guidance of indication for all people, and guidance of help for believers only. Concerning general indication, the Truth, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿And We showed him the two highways.﴾ (al-Balad: 10).

As for the guidance of help, it is that of which the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety.﴾ (Muhammad: 17).

What reveals to us that guidance is general is that the Truth, Glorified and Exalted, when He spoke of the people of Thamud, to whom Allah sent their brother Salih, said, Glorified is He:

﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them.﴾ (Fussilat: 17).

Had the guidance here meant that they became guided and followed the path of faith, He would not have said after it, Glorified is He:

﴿But they preferred blindness over guidance.﴾ (Fussilat: 17).

Thus ﴿We guided them﴾ in this noble verse means: We indicated to them the path of faith, but they chose the path of blindness and disbelief.

(1) Ibn Kathir says: "Ibn Abi Talhah said, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, in explanation of this verse": It was revealed concerning al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib when he was taken captive at Badr. He said: "If you preceded us in Islam, emigration and jihad, we used to maintain the Sacred Mosque, give drink to the pilgrims, and ransom the captives." Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: (Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims...) up to his saying: (And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people), meaning that all of that was in polytheism, and I do not accept what was done in polytheism. Tafsir Ibn Kathir (2/341).

(2) Mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (2/34) from the saying of Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and he attributed it to Ibn Jarir with its chain. In it is Ibn Lahi'ah; there is discussion concerning him.

(3) Of this guidance is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib in a long hadith: "That Allah should guide one man through you is better for you than having red camels." Recorded by al-Bukhari (2942) and Muslim (2406) in their Sahihs.

(4) This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you faith and has made it pleasing in your hearts, and has made hateful to you disbelief, defiance, and disobedience. Those are the rightly guided.﴾ (al-Hujurat: 7).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 20:

The Lord, glory be to Him, says after that:

﴿Those who believe, and emigrate, and strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank with Allah. And those are the triumphant.﴾ (20)

In Surah al-Anfal there is another classification, in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And those who believed and emigrated and strove in the way of Allah, and those who gave refuge and helped—those are the believers in truth. For them is forgiveness and a noble provision.﴾ (74) (al-Anfal)

In this noble verse of Surah al-Anfal the classification of the believers was made immediately after the hijrah. Then the hijrah ended, and all became equal, so the comprehensive classification came in the verse of at-Tawbah.

The Lord, glory be to Him, has made clear that these deeds were not accepted from the polytheists, whereas if the believers perform them, they have a rank with Allah. In this noble verse the Truth describes them as ﴿greater in rank﴾, and "greater" (a'zam) is the form of the comparative (af'al al-tafdil). It gives an excess beyond the original quality that is known, so it is said: "So-and-so is more knowledgeable than so-and-so." Thus the second person is knowledgeable, but the first person is more knowledgeable than him. It is said: "So-and-so is more generous than so-and-so," meaning the second described person is generous, and the first described person is more generous than him. Allah, glory be to Him, wanted to show us the triumph in His sight, so He said:

﴿Greater in rank with Allah, and those are the triumphant.﴾ (20) (at-Tawbah)

So these are the ones who obtain the greatest reward with Allah, the Exalted, namely the believers who emigrated and who strove with their wealth and their lives. Triumph is a judgment that leads to your obtaining what your soul loves. Then the Truth, clarifying what they gain, said:

﴿Those who believe, and emigrate, and strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank with Allah. And those are the triumphant.﴾ (20) (at-Tawbah: 20)

Since these are the triumphant, triumph occurs in two arenas. Those who work for matters specific to this world may triumph in them with a degree of bliss, but their bliss is in proportion to their capabilities; and it is not everlasting, because either it departs from them through the loss of the blessing, or they depart from it through death. Therefore it is incomplete bliss.

As for the one who believes, emigrates, strives and works for his Hereafter, he will triumph with a bliss not in proportion to his capabilities, but in proportion to the capabilities of Allah, and there is no comparison between the capabilities of Allah and the capabilities of His creation. Moreover, it is everlasting bliss that does not leave you so that it departs from you, nor do you leave it, because in Paradise you are an eternal one who does not die.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 21:

Then the Truth mentions after that His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him, and approval, and gardens wherein they will have lasting bliss.﴾

So this is the peak of success for the people whom God gives good tidings of in this verse: mercy from Him and lasting approval. Good tidings (bushra), as we know, is a kind of informing about something that will come in the future; that is, when you give someone good tidings, you tell him of something coming that will please him.

So the benefit of good tidings is that it entices a person to follow the path that achieves them. I say to you: "I give you the good news of success if you stay steady, study, and listen to the teachers," and my words encourage you to exert yourself until you achieve this good news. It is as if the good news makes you adopt the means that lead you to it.

For this reason we have said that causes and effects, cause and caused, condition and response, all must be understood in another way. For we used to learn that the condition is the cause of the response, as in your saying: "If you study, you will succeed." Accordingly, the condition is studying, and the cause of the response is success. But we say: No, the response is the cause of the condition, because you do not study except when success is imagined for you with all the joy it brings you. So the condition is the cause of the response's existing in reality, and the response is the cause of the condition's existing as a motive; that is, the motive for your studying is what success represents to you in material and moral value. Every person desires success, but success is not achieved by wishing alone, rather by the study that makes success a reality. The meaning is that you do not study except when success has been imagined for you with its merits and advantages, and your family rejoices in you, and you rejoice in yourself. Hence we say: the cause is that which first exists in the mind.

Another example: suppose you want to travel to Ta'if. Then Ta'if is the goal, and you have planned the means while the goal is in your mind. So the response exists as a motive, and the condition exists in reality. As for His saying, ﴿their Lord gives them good tidings﴾, that is, He informs them of the joyful end they will reach, so that they bear the hardship of the duties that the divine method commands them; for Paradise is surrounded by hardships(1), and because divine legislation is a restriction on the freedom of choice of the servant, and the believer is bound by God's commands in "do" and "do not do."

But the non-believer merely follows his desire in all his movements, does what his whims dictate, and obeys his impulses as he wishes. As for the believer, his freedom is only in what no legislation from God has addressed; as for what falls under the method, he is restricted in movement by what God has decreed. It is as if faith came to restrict, but if we compare the two recompenses, we find that the one who follows his desires in this world obtains a temporary pleasure, and his life in this world is limited; so he is the loser, because the one who restricts his movement by God's method gains tranquility in this world and lasting bliss that does not cease or end in the Hereafter(2). The example I always give is the student who does not go to school and does not study, but spends his time in play and amusement; he has given himself what it desires, but he has taken a limited enjoyment, and then afterward lives in misery for the rest of his life.

As for the one who restricted his life to study, he has prevented his soul's desires from play and amusement. The fruit is that he achieves for himself a comfortable and esteemed future for the rest of his life.

So each of the student who strives and the one who plays and amuses himself has taken a kind of enjoyment. But one of them took a very short enjoyment, then became one of life's beggars; while the second restricted himself for a number of years in order to enjoy a successful future.

Likewise you in this world: if you restrict yourself with the duties "do" and "do not do," the apparent matter is that you have restricted your freedom; but if you do that willingly, God gives you ease, tranquility, and enjoyment in the soul. This is why we find prayer, which the Muslim performs five times a day at least; this prayer, in its outward appearance, takes some of the time each day, but it gives psychological ease, and it gives a conviction that exceeds imagination if the person is humble in it and performs it in its proper manner. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "O Bilal, give us rest with the prayer"(3).

And the Prophet (ﷺ) said, in a hadith narrated to him by Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him): "And the coolness of my eye has been made in prayer"(4).

Because the duty moves from pleasure to rest. A person enjoys in it the manifestations of his Lord and His overflowing bounties, so his soul is at ease and calm. Look at the saying of the Truth, glorified and exalted: ﴿their Lord gives them good tidings﴾; you find the good tidings here coming from a Lord, Creator. The Lord is the Owner, the Manager who arranges your affairs, and He is trustworthy over you.

﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him and approval﴾ (At-Tawbah: 21).

Mercy and approval are attributes of God, may He be exalted, and they are essential attributes of God; and what relates to the servant regarding them is that He, glorified, grants them to whomever He wills.

Then the Mawla, glorified and exalted, continues His saying:

﴿And gardens wherein they will have lasting bliss﴾ (At-Tawbah: 21).

We find that this is an ascent and gradation in blessing: God, glorified and exalted, first gave them good tidings of mercy, which is essential in Him, then of a lasting blessing in life. Note that there is a difference between blessing (ni'ma) and the Bestower (mun'im). We give an example, and to God belongs the highest likeness: if a person invites you to his house at mealtime and then brings a dish containing apples, the apples in the dish must be enough for all those seated, so that each of them takes an apple. If the host takes an apple and gives it to one of those seated, this is a manifestation of special care from the host, and a distinction of his guest from the rest of the guests; this represents a higher degree of generosity and concern. It represents mercy and approval. As for the apples themselves, they are the blessing, and like them are the gardens.

Thus we see that there is a difference in honoring. Believers, as they rise in the degree of faith, live always with the blessing and the Bestower; when food comes they say, "In the name of God," and when they eat they say, "Praise be to God." But when they rise higher in faith, they live with the Bestower alone. This is why God boasts of His servants to the angels(5); He boasts of their worship and obedience, which they uphold in whatever state they are, even if the severest affliction befalls them and blessings are taken from them, and these are of the people of high rank. Hence, "the people most severely tested are the prophets, then the righteous, then the next best and the next best"(6); so that the Truth, glorified and exalted, may see who loves Him for His own sake even if a blessing is taken from him, and this is a lofty rank. Whoever worships God in order to enter Paradise, He gives it to him; but whoever worships Him, glorified, because He deserves to be worshipped, will ascend in Paradise to see the Face of God at all times; while others see Him in glimpses. Therefore the recompense in the Hereafter is according to the depth of the servant's faith. For this reason the Truth, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ (Al-Kahf: 110).

And one of the righteous said: "I do not associate anyone with You, not even Paradise, for Paradise is a 'someone' (a created thing)."

And here the Truth, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him﴾. A person may be shown mercy but not attain approval; so the Mawla, glorified and exalted, clarified that and added "approval" to "mercy." Therefore the Truth, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿of mercy from Him and approval﴾. Approval is that which is above bliss. After approval the Truth, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿and gardens wherein they will have lasting bliss﴾.

Someone may say: Is there a garden without bliss? And why was bliss mentioned? Paradise was created so that a person may enjoy it.

We say to such a speaker: pay attention and consider the meaning well. The One speaking is God, glorified and exalted. A person may have wide blessings but live amid many troubles, which prevent him from enjoying the blessing: such as an illness that fills him with pain, or an undutiful son who troubles his life, or a wife who fills life with distress and wretchedness. All of that may happen, and a person does not enjoy what he possesses of God's blessing, because troubles have surrounded him. Here the Truth, glorified and exalted, wants to draw our attention to the fact that the Paradise of the Hereafter has none of the troubles of this world; rather it is purity and enjoyment, in which the Truth, glorified and exalted, gives His servant what his soul desires and removes from him all troubles. A person may fear that such bliss will not endure; therefore God reassures the believing servant that it is ﴿lasting bliss﴾. Someone may look at "residence" (iqama) as a word that carries doubt, for residence may last a long time and then end; but God, Mighty and Majestic, willed to reassure the believer with a true promise, and promised the believers eternal abiding in Paradise. So He, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿Abiding therein forever. Indeed, with God is a great reward﴾ (At-Tawbah: 22).

1. From Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires." Related by Muslim in his Sahih (2822), Ahmad in his Musnad (3/284, 254, 153), and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2559), who said: hasan gharib from this route, sahih.
2. This is like the saying of God: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them according to the best of what they used to do﴾ (An-Nahl: 97). As for the one who turned away from God's method and refused it, the Qur'an said of him: ﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ (Ta-Ha: 124).
3. Related by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad (5/364) and Abu Dawud in his Sunan (4985) from a man of the Aslam tribe; Ahmad stated it, and the wording is his.
4. The hadith of Anas was related by Ahmad in his Musnad (3/285, 199, 128) and al-Nasa'i in his Sunan (7/61), and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (2/160), who said: sahih according to the conditions of Muslim, though they did not relate it; and al-Dhahabi agreed. The complete hadith is: "Women and perfume were made beloved to me of this world..."
5. Ibn Majah related in his Sunan (801) from Abdullah ibn Amr that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rejoice! This is your Lord who has opened a gate of the heavens, boasting of you to the angels: He says, 'Look at My servants who have completed an obligation while they are waiting for another.'" Ahmad also related it in his Musnad (2/196). Al-Busiri said in al-Zawa'id: this chain is sahih and its narrators are trustworthy.
6. Related by Ahmad (1/172), al-Tirmidhi (2398), and Ibn Majah (4023) from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. al-Tirmidhi said: hasan sahih.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 22:

This confirms the sense of security in the words of the True One, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿For them therein is lasting bliss﴾. The word ﴿for them﴾ gives this bliss a semblance of ownership. Therefore a person owns things in this world, but this ownership does not go beyond sitting down while servants carry out his orders, because enjoyment is either in your own hand, or you enjoy comfort that others bring to you. For example, when you want to eat, either you prepare the food for yourself, or someone else prepares it for you. No person, however much kingship he is given, can achieve everything he wants with his own hand; he must always turn to the help of others. But the believer in Paradise attains whatever he wishes the moment it crosses his mind. This differs from this world, because when you desire something in our world, you must either do it yourself or rely on someone else to carry it out for you, even if what you ask for is merely a cup of coffee, and you specify to its maker the form and type: whether you want it without sugar, with a little sugar, or with a lot of sugar. This is because each of us in this world lives with the means (asbab) of God. But the believer in Paradise lives with the One who causes (al-musabbib), who is God, the Capable, the Great.

When the Lord, glorified and exalted be He, says: ﴿Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him, and of approval and gardens﴾, we notice the matching of plural with plural, and as we have learned before, this requires distribution to individuals. If the teacher enters the classroom and says to his pupils: "Take out your pens," then it does not mean each pupil takes out all the pens, but rather each pupil takes out his own pen. And if we say: "Ride your cars," this does not mean that each one rides all the cars, but that each one rides his own car.

The word of the True One ﴿gardens﴾ does not mean that every believer enters all the gardens, but the meaning and intent is that each of them enters his own garden according to the deeds he has earned and the rank he has reached(1).

It is important to know that the owner of a high-ranking garden will not receive envy from the owner of a middling garden. The owner of the lowest garden will not envy one above him, and likewise the owner of a high-ranking garden will not boast over others. Each of them rejoices in the other's station, just as sometimes happens in this world when a person excels in his studies, and we may find one of lower standing rejoicing for him with a pure heart, and likewise the one who excels does not boast of his standing over those below him. If this is what happens in this world, how much more so in the Hereafter, where the True One, glorified and exalted be He, says:

﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, upon couches facing one another﴾ (al-Hijr: 47). That is, each of the people of Paradise rejoices in his own station, and rejoices in the station of the one above him, because he will receive of the overflowing goodness that is with the one of higher station when he comes to visit him. Regarding the word of the True One, glorified and exalted be He:

﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ (al-Rahman: 46), they have said: every person whose station is elevated in Paradise has a special garden for himself, and another garden which he generously gives to those below him, as if it were a guesthouse for those he loves. Thus in the Hereafter the people of Paradise rejoice in those above them, because they will receive good from them.

In this world, if a person wishes to receive the blessings of all creation, he must rejoice in the blessing in the possession of its owner, because when he rejoices in the blessing with its owner, it comes to him and he benefits from it. We must be certain that a blessing loves its owner more than the owner loves it, because it knows that God has sent it to him. Therefore the True One, blessed and exalted be He, says:

﴿It gives its produce every time by the permission of its Lord﴾ (Ibrahim: 25).

When you sow the seed of a tree, the tree gives you its fruits, and it is the one that gives you its yield. You are not the one who extracts it from it. Therefore we always say: sustenance knows your address very well, but you never know its place. You search for sustenance everywhere and may not find it. But what God has apportioned to you of sustenance, you will find it seeking you out and coming to you without fail.

The people of Paradise know neither spite nor envy nor resentment. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to his companions one day while they were sitting with him: "A man from the people of Paradise will now come upon you."

The man entered, and the companions recognized him. They wished to know what this companion did to deserve the Prophet's (ﷺ) good news of Paradise. They said to him: "We want to know what you do so that we may be with you." The man said: "I pray as you pray, fast as you fast, and give zakat as you give zakat. But I go to sleep with no resentment in my heart toward anyone." They went to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said to him: "The man said such and such." He (ﷺ) said: "Has Paradise been preferred over this world except by this?"(2)

So God, glorified and exalted be He, says of them:

﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾ (al-Hijr: 47).

1 On the authority of Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "It will be said to the companion of the Qur'an: Recite and ascend, and recite slowly as you used to recite in the world, for your station will be at the last verse you recite." Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (2/192), al-Tirmidhi (2914) who said: hasan sahih, and Abu Dawud in his Sunan (1464).

2 Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (3/166) and Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd (694), and al-Haythami in al-Majma' (8/79) attributed it to Ahmad and al-Bazzar in similar wording, and said: "The men of Ahmad are the men of the sahih." The phrase "Has Paradise been preferred over this world except by this?" is not in it. Abdullah ibn Amr followed him to observe his deeds, then said to him: "I have not seen you doing many deeds, so what has brought you to what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said?" He said: "It is nothing but what you have seen... except that I do not find in myself deceit toward any Muslim, and I do not envy anyone for a good that God has given him." Abdullah said: "This is what has brought you, and it is what we cannot bear."

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 9, verse 23:

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith. And whoever of you allies with them, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ (9:23)

The *walī* (ally, close protector) is the one who stands by you, accomplishes what you love, and whom you turn to in every matter, from whom you take counsel. He is also able to grant you protection when you flee to him, and he is always like a helper for that purpose, the near one who hears you. When you call for help, he helps you and supports you, and he is with you in all your affairs. Let us compare seeking the created and seeking the Creator. Allah, glorified and exalted, makes clear to us here: if you want the structure of Islam to be strong, without any flaw, then beware lest your allegiance be other than the allegiance of faith. It is above allegiance by lineage, by family standing, and anything else. If we compare seeking the created with seeking the Creator, what the Creator asks is above what the created asks, because if you anger the created in order to please the Creator, you are the winner. Allah casts into the hearts of everyone around you their approval of you, and it will be said of you that you are a person of principle and conscience. You would not want to anger Allah so that someone might be pleased with you. If you provoke Allah to please any created being, whoever he may be, you will find that Allah makes that created being become angry with you and despise you.(1) If you bear false witness for the benefit of a person, the one against whom you bore false witness will know about you that you are a false witness, and so he will not trust you. And if you happen to come to testify before him, he will not accept your testimony and will hold your words in contempt.

For this reason the wise have said: the false witness may raise your head over your opponent by his testimony, but you trample on his dignity with your foot, because he has fallen in your eyes.

Allegiance, then, is allegiance to Allah. If a close relative happens to want you to do what angers Allah, do not obey him, but do not be harsh with him, especially with the two parents, because Allah, glorified and exalted, says about them:

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, then do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness.﴾ (Surah Luqman: 15)

And here Allah, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith.﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah: 23)

So what binds everything together is either disbelief or faith. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave us the eternal example. Sayyidunā Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr (may Allah be pleased with him) was the most pampered of young men in Makkah, and his life in Makkah before his Islam was extremely luxurious. He used to strut about in luxurious garments.(2) When he migrated to Madinah, he lived in the harsh conditions of material poverty, to the extent that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him on the road covering his private parts with a sheepskin. The Prophet (ﷺ) drew the attention of the Companions to his condition and to how faith had affected Mus'ab, for he preferred faith over all the pleasures of this world. Mus'ab (may Allah be pleased with him) saw that his honor in belonging to Islam was greater than fine garments and luxurious living,(3) and the saying of the Blessed and Exalted Lord applied to him:

﴿Those who believed and emigrated and struggled in the way of Allah with their wealth and their selves are greater in rank with Allah, and it is those who are the attainers of success. Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him and approval and gardens for them wherein is lasting pleasure, abiding therein forever. Indeed, Allah has with Him a great reward.﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah: 20–22)

Sayyidunā Mus'ab and those with him gave us the great example in belonging to faith, and in striving in the way of Allah with wealth and self, and in how we make our choice align with the method of Allah, a method that restricts a person in those matters where he has a choice. A human being is compelled in some things and free to choose in others.

We know that obligation does not come in matters over which we are compelled. It comes only in matters where there is choice. So when we have a choice, let us take care to choose between alternatives within the framework of the method of Allah, the Exalted, and not go far outside this framework. The early Muslims used to sacrifice home, wealth and children, and emigrate in the way of Allah. They received all these difficult sacrifices with believing hearts and with severe patience and endurance, because they trusted the good tidings from Allah, glorified and exalted, that they would have Paradise, approval and lasting bliss, abiding therein, never leaving it nor it leaving them. Through this the structure of Islam was established.

After Allah explained to us the foundations of belonging to the religion and the reward of this belonging, He warned us against deviating in order to please a father, brothers or relatives. So He said:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith, and whoever of you allies with them, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ (Surah al-Tawbah: 23)

Allah wants us to know that allegiance to Allah is not surpassed by anything. So if we turn away from the truth in order to please relatives, or to keep wealth or a position, that is wronging oneself, because the reward of the truth and its bliss is greater. Let no one support falsehood, and let none of us make faith a servant to disbelievers who do not believe in Allah. Allah, the Exalted, illustrates this image by His saying:

﴿if they prefer disbelief over faith﴾

The word *istahabbū* means: they sought to love, and it is like *istakhraja*, meaning: sought to extract something. When we say *istajāba Allāh*, its meaning is: He answered.

So *istahabba* means: loved, but *istahabba* contains *iftiʿāl* (the form implying effort and deliberate doing), whereas *aḥabba* contains outward flow without *iftiʿāl*.

Allah's saying, blessed and exalted, ﴿if they prefer disbelief over faith﴾ shows that disbelief contradicts the innate faithful nature (*fiṭra*) of a human being, because by his nature a human being is a believer who loves faith. If he tries to love other than faith, he must force himself to do so and fabricate it, because he is not created for it and it is not his nature. For this reason the noble Qur'an says:

﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah?﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah: 28)

This questioning and amazement make clear to us that those who rely on logic, thought and reason find it hard to disbelieve in Allah. Why? Because the universe came into existence first, then the human being came into existence. So when we come to a universe in which we did not make anything, it is necessary to ask: who brought it into existence? It is natural for reason to seek the one who originated it, especially since there are things in the universe that human beings have no power to create, such as the sun, the earth, water, air, plants and animals. All of these represent the comprehensive provision that gathers the essentials of your life.

So it is natural, then, to ask: who created this universe? Especially since we search for whoever invented for us a simple invention, such as the electric lamp, and we study the history of its life and how it was discovered, merely because it added to our lives something we benefited from. How much more so for the One who created this universe? Allah, glorified and exalted, has spared us from the misguidance of confusion, and sent us a Messenger with mercy from Him, to alert us and tell us: this universe is the creation of Allah, the Mighty, the Great. Why then do we not believe the Messenger and follow the method that was sent down to us?

We have given an example, and to Allah belongs the highest example, of a person whose airplane crashed in the middle of the desert and who remained alive, but with no water or food. Then drowsiness overtook him, and he woke up to find food and drink and everything he needed beside him. Would he not, before eating, think about who brought all this? You, O human being, have come into this great universe, which has been prepared in an ideal way for your life, a preparation beyond human capacity. So it was necessary for you to think about who created this universe.

So faith is a natural necessity and also an intellectual necessity. If you turn away from faith, this requires forcing yourself, because you are departing from the logic of nature and reason in order to fulfil the desires of your self. And since you have followed your whims and submitted to the appetites of the self, this is a kind of artificial effort that afflicts your faculties with imbalance and your mind with derangement. Love of disbelief is neither emotional nor innate, nor does it harmonize with sound reason. Rather, it is a forced love. The one who does what is lawful lives with all his faculties in harmony, while the one who does what is unlawful lives with his faculties in disorder.(4) For example, when a man looks at his wife, he is looking at what is lawful to him, and he feels that his faculties are in harmony. But if he looks at another woman, he feels the disorder of his faculties. So behavior that accords with faith is sound behavior. Behavior that departs from the method of faith is what requires forcing, and this forcing opposes human dispositions. Whereas the consequences of faith, such as uprightness, require no forcing. The believer is upright, so he does not take bribes, does not steal, and does not enter by himself into the slippery places of desire or lust, and he lives a good life. If he opens his own cupboard and takes something from it, he takes what he wants calmly and with assurance. But the deviant is one who enters a room that is not his to take something from some cupboard, even if it is his sleeping father's cupboard. So you find him walking on the tips of his toes, stealthily, to open his father's cupboard.

So then: uprightness requires no forcing, but deviation is what requires forcing. For this reason Allah, glorified, said *istaḥabbū* and did not say *aḥabbū*, because love is a natural matter. For example, a person loves his son with natural emotional love, and emotional love cannot be regulated. You cannot say: I will love so-and-so and I will hate so-and-so, because emotion does not come in this way. So you love your son emotionally, even if he is failing in his studies. But you may love the son of your enemy intellectually if he is outstanding. So intellectual love is what can be regulated.

Likewise, you dislike bitter medicine with your emotions, but you love it with your intellect if it contains your cure. So you seek it out, pay money for it, and are careful to take it. We all know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None of you truly believes until I am dearer to him than himself."(5)

Sayyidunā 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) stopped at this and said: O Messenger of Allah, I love you more than my wealth and more than my children, but how can I love you more than myself? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) repeated the hadith, saying: "None of you truly believes until I am dearer to him than himself."

He (ﷺ) repeated it three times, and 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) understood that this was an obligation. Obligation comes only through intellectual love, which can be regulated. The believer may rise in his love for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until it becomes both intellectual and emotional. But intellectual love is the basis of obligation, while emotional love is not made an obligation. Allah, glorified and exalted, did not regulate the movements of emotions, because He, glorified and exalted, does not prevent emotions from being stirred in their natural ways. You love someone who does you a favor, and there is someone you love without knowing why. There is someone you hate without his having wronged or harmed you.(6) All of that is left to you. But Allah, glorified and exalted, forbade that this should lead to aggression against the truth, so He said, glorified and exalted:

﴿Let not hatred of a people prevent you from being just.﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah: 8)

That is: do not let the hatred of a people push you to deviate from the path of truth and wrong them. If you hate them, then hold to justice with them.

So Allah, glorified and exalted, did not forbid love or hatred, but He forbade us to wrong those we hate or to flatter those we love at the expense of truth and justice.

Sayyidunā 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) gives us a living image of this. Abu Maryam al-Hanafī killed Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, the brother of Sayyidunā 'Umar, at the Battle of Yamāmah, and then he embraced Islam. Whenever he passed by Sayyidunā 'Umar, he said to him: Turn your face away from me, for I do not love you. Abu Maryam al-Hanafī said to him: Does your not loving me prevent me from one of my rights?

He said: No. The man said: He weeps only over

1. From 'Ā'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever seeks the pleasure of Allah at the cost of the displeasure of people, Allah will be pleased with him and will make people pleased with him. And whoever seeks the pleasure of people at the cost of the displeasure of Allah, Allah will be displeased with him and will make people displeased with him." Narrated by Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ (2442), and narrated by al-Tirmidhī in his Sunan (2414), from a letter I sent to Mu'āwiyah.
2. *Yarfulu*: he struts in his walk and drags his garment.
3. From 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) looked at Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr approaching, wearing the hide (skin) of a ram, tied around him with a cord. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Look at this man whose heart Allah has illuminated. I saw him between two parents who nourished him with the finest food and drink, but the love of Allah and His Messenger drove him to what you see." Narrated by Abu Nu'aym in Ḥilyat al-Awliyā' (1/108). Al-'Irāqī said in his takhrīj of the hadiths of the Iḥyā' (4/295): its isnad (chain) is good.
4. From al-Nawwās ibn Sam'ān al-Anṣārī who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about righteousness and sin. He said: "Righteousness is good character, and sin is what troubles your breast and you dislike people finding out about it." Narrated by Muslim (2553), al-Tirmidhī (2389) who said: ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ (good, sound), and Aḥmad in his Musnad (4/182).
5. Narrated by al-Bukhārī in his Ṣaḥīḥ (6632) and Aḥmad in his Musnad (4/233). In the isnad of Aḥmad is Ibn Lahī'ah, but Ḥaywah followed him from Zahrah ibn Ma'bad. The rest of the hadith here is narrated in meaning.
6. From Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Souls are like armies drawn up; those that recognize each other become attached, and those that do not recognize each other differ." Narrated by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ (2638), Aḥmad in his Musnad (2/295, 527, 539), and Abu Dawud (3834).

Following this, Allah the Exalted wished to address them with a plain address, and so He said:

﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kinsfolk, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce you fear will slump, and the dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ (24)

The address here is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he may convey it to the believers. In this noble verse, Allah the Exalted has brought together the stages of kinship: first, the ties of lineage, of fathers, sons and brothers; then marriage, which is the means of increase; then family and clan; then the wealth we already possess; then the wealth we wish to gain; then the dwellings we are content with; and after that He mentioned commerce, which increases wealth. Allah the Exalted distinguished between the wealth in our possession and commerce, because commerce may bring us wealth beyond wealth, and a person does not obtain a dwelling except when he has a surplus of wealth. The Exalted reminds us here: if any of these things, which are the adornment of the worldly life, is dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in the way of Allah, ﴿then wait﴾, that is, await until the command of Allah comes to you, and then you will know the true value of this world and the value of what is with Allah of pleasure and bliss.

This noble verse has occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to emigrate from Makkah to Madinah, he commanded the Muslims to emigrate, and they left their wealth that they had acquired in Makkah, their commerce, their dwellings, their fathers, sons, brothers, spouses and clan who could protect them. They left all of this and emigrated to a new land.

But some of the Muslims inclined to the world and stayed beside their wealth, their wives and their children who were polytheists. A polytheist wife would cling to the feet of her Muslim husband who wished to emigrate, so that he would not leave her, and his heart would soften towards her. Others among them feared the loss of their wealth and the slump of their trade, which was between them and the polytheists, so this verse was revealed.(1)

Allah the Exalted wished to clarify the worth of the bond of faith and to train the believers in it. A Muslim's faith was not complete until he emigrated, cut off (yusarim)(2) his family and relatives and severed ties with them, and this was difficult for them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if we withdraw from those who oppose us in our religion, we shall cut off our fathers, sons, wives and relatives, and we fear for our wealth and commerce from ruin, and we fear that our dwellings will be destroyed, and thereby we shall be lost." So Allah the Exalted revealed this noble verse, as if it commanded them that the gain of faith is higher than any other gain. Then the Exalted revealed the noble verse:

﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kinsfolk, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce you fear will slump, and the dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ (al-Tawbah).

When this noble verse was revealed, the Companions took it seriously and emigrated, and they cut off their fathers and sons, to the extent that one of them would meet his father or son and not speak to him, nor let him into his house, nor host him in his home if he met him, nor spend on him, until the noble verse was revealed: ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, and accompany them in this world with kindness﴾ (Luqman: 15), that is: kindness towards them is restricted only to dealings and to spending on the one in need.

As for obedience to them in what angers Allah, it is forbidden. Some orientalists tried to attack the Qur'an, and some of them said: there is a contradiction between the verses of the Qur'an. The two verses we have mentioned: the first requires cutting off fathers and sons if they prefer disbelief to faith, and the second requires accompanying them with kindness or not severing ties, and a third verse says:

﴿You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day loving those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers or their kinsfolk﴾ (al-Mujadilah: 22). These people did not realise that there is a difference between affection and kindness. Affection is an act of the heart: you love with your heart and feel affection with your heart. But kindness is not an act of the heart, because you may do a kindness to a person you do not know, and you may do a kindness to your enemy when you find him in a predicament, yet you do not love him or feel affection for him.

Therefore, what is forbidden is that there be love and affection between you and those who oppose Allah and His Messenger; but kindness is not forbidden, because Allah wants the believing soul to acknowledge the favour of parenthood. If you find your father, who is not a believer, in a predicament, then do a kindness for him and help him, but you must not obey him in what angers Allah, because the Exalted wants to train the believing soul to honour the one who has a favour upon it. Father and mother are among the causes of our existence in life, so the command to accompany them with kindness in this world came, on condition that we do not accept from them their call to disbelief if they are people of disbelief, because your faith in Allah must be the strongest. And therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has three qualities will find the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anyone else; that he loves a person only for Allah's sake; and that he hates to return to disbelief after Allah has rescued him from it, just as he hates to be thrown into the Fire."(3)

This is so that the measure of love is not lineage or kinship, but nearness to Allah is the cause of love, and distance from Allah is the cause of hatred. The matter of faith overrides the matter of emotional attachment. At the Battle of Badr, our master Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while his son had not yet embraced Islam and was with the disbelievers. When Abu Bakr's son later became a Muslim and believed, he said to his father: "I saw you on the day of Badr and I turned my face away from you so that I would not kill you." Our master Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) replied: "Had I seen you, I would have killed you." This is consistent with faith, because the psychological weighing required that the son compare his father with an idol he worshipped, and his father's side outweighed; but Abu Bakr, when he saw his son, compared his Lord with his son, and his Lord's side outweighed.

If this is the case regarding kinship, and how faith overrides emotion, then why regarding wealth?

The Lord, the Exalted, continues: ﴿and wealth you have acquired﴾, that is, you took it with hardship. It derives from "al-qarf", which is the husk or peel. If you want to remove the husk from a grain of some plant, you may find some difficulty, because there is adhesion between the husk and the grain. The Truth here says: ﴿and wealth you have acquired﴾, that is, you took it with effort and hardship. This is different from inherited wealth, on which its owner did not toil, but inherited from another, and in that case its matter may be light for its owner. As for wealth a person earned by the sweat of his brow and by exertion, its owner is more eager to keep it than inherited wealth. It is said: "So-and-so iqtarafa such-and-such," meaning he exerted himself until he obtained it; and it is said: "He iqtarafa lying" and "iqtarafa theft," meaning he exerted effort to lie, or exerted effort to steal, that is, he carried out an act involving effort.

Then the Truth, the Exalted, says: ﴿So wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾. Here He, glorified be He, clarifies to them: await the command of Allah that will come, for He, the Exalted, does not guide a defiantly disobedient person who has departed from faith, nor does He guide those who made their love for worldly relationships above their love for Allah and so departed from the will of Allah's guidance. He does not guide them, just as He does not guide the wrongdoers or the disbelievers, because these are the ones who put forward wrongdoing, disbelief and defiance, and that was the reason Allah did not include them in the will of guidance to the help toward faith; as for the guidance of indication, He has already offered it to them.

Then the Truth, the Exalted, wished to send faith's tranquillity into the hearts of the believers, so He clarifies to them: if you seek strength through fathers, sons, clan, relatives and wealth, know that the strength of the believer comes from his Lord, and beware of looking to any protector other than Allah, for the protection of human beings is subject to change and alteration, since the human being is a created thing that turns between changing states. The rich among them may become poor, the healthy may become sick, and the strong may become weak; but lasting protection can only come from a Powerful, Dominant One who does not change. So if Allah is your protector, He is always capable, always dominant, always victorious, always existent, always the Helper. But if protection is from one person to another, changing circumstances in this world turn the friend into an enemy, the helper becomes weak and owns nothing, and the one who exists ceases to exist through death. Therefore, you must make your protection with Allah, glorified and exalted be He, for He is the Everlasting, the Abiding. For this reason the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, teaches His believing servant to be always watchful, alert and discerning, so He, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿And rely upon the Living who does not die﴾ (al-Furqan: 58), that is: do not rely upon one who might become dead tomorrow when you find him dead, but rely upon the Living, the ever-existent, the Mighty who cannot be subdued, the Strong who cannot be overcome. The Truth, the Exalted, alerts the believers: if you fear, when we isolate you from the society of disbelief because of its false glory of fathers, sons, brothers, relatives and wealth, know that Allah is the One who gives victory, and He is the Protector; but the disbelievers have no protector, for they take as protectors things that change, and changing things are not trustworthy. Therefore it is said: when a person reaches the summit, this is the end of perfection, for since he has reached the summit and everything in this world changes, he too must change. And the poet says:

When something is complete, its decline begins;
watch for its passing once it is said to be complete.

For every changing thing is a son of change and must descend downward. The Truth, the Exalted, clarifies to the believers that if He has commanded them to isolate themselves from the society of disbelief, thereby depriving them of strength and a helper, they are in greater protection, because then they are with Allah, and Allah is the Helper. This is not a theoretical statement, but a statement confirmed by the events you have witnessed.

(1) See Tafsir al-Qurtubi (4/3021), Dar al-Ghad edition, and Asbab al-Nuzul by Imam al-Suyuti (pp. 92–93).
(2) Yusarim ahlahu: he cuts them off with a complete severance.
(3) Agreed upon. Related by al-Bukhari (16) and Muslim (43) from Anas ibn Malik.
(4) Al-Kadd: hardship and fatigue in obtaining a thing.

Wa-subhanahu wa-ta'ala yaqulu ba'da dhalik:

﴿Indeed, Allah had given you victory on many battlefields, and on the Day of Hunayn, when your great number impressed you, but it availed you nothing, and the earth, for all its vastness, became too narrow for you, and then you turned back in retreat.﴾ (9:25)

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah had given you victory on many battlefields﴾ draws our attention to the fact that victory comes from Allah alone. The proof that victory comes from Allah is that He, glorified and exalted, gave victory to His Messenger and to those who were with him on many battlefields. ﴿Battlefields﴾ is the plural of "mawtin" (place), and a mawtin is a place in which one settles. All people settle on the earth, and every group of us claims a portion of the earth to be its homeland (watan). The watan is a specific place in which we live, within the general homeland which is the earth, because the earth is the home of all humanity; yet people are distributed over it, and each group lives in a region to which it returns in the evening and departs in the morning, and in which it dwells.

Allah, glorified be He, says here: ﴿Indeed, Allah had given you victory on many battlefields﴾. Since the discussion concerns victory, the meaning is: Allah, the Truth, glorified and exalted, gave you victory on the fields of war, that is, their sites, such as the Day of Badr, the Day of Hudaybiyyah, the Day of Banu al-Nadir, the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), and the Day of Makkah. All of these were sites of victory granted by Allah to the Muslims. But in this verse He singles out one day for mention after speaking generally of the many battlefields. Having spoken in summary of the numerous battles, He says: ﴿and on the Day of Hunayn, when your great number impressed you﴾. Thus, the great number of believers on the Day of Hunayn was a particular circumstance. As for the other battlefields, such as the Day of Badr, they were few in number; and on the Day of the Conquest of Makkah they were many, yet they were not impressed and did not become conceited because of it. Therefore, on the Day of Hunayn, abundance combined with self-admiration, and for this reason Hunayn has a distinction: it is a specific day following a general discussion.

﴿And on the Day of Hunayn, when your great number impressed you﴾: this "impressment" is a clause extending over the day itself. Hence "the Day of Hunayn" is not coordinated with ﴿many battlefields﴾ but is an independent sentence in itself, because abundance and admiration at abundance were not present in the other battlefields. This is a precision in linguistic expression that calls for linguistic investigation. The word ﴿battlefields﴾ is an adverb of place (ẓarf makan), and ﴿the Day of Hunayn﴾ is an adverb of time (ẓarf zaman). How, then, is it permissible to coordinate an adverb of time with an adverb of place?

We say: this is what the Arabs call "ihtibak" (interlacing of elements), because every event, such as "he ate," "he drank," "he struck," or "he mentioned," must have a time and must have a place. If you say, "I ate," we ask: when? In the morning, at noon, in the afternoon, or at night? And where? In the house, in the hotel, in the restaurant, or in the street.

Therefore, every statement must have an adverb of time and an adverb of place. If you observe this, you obtain absolute adverbiality: the adverbiality of the occurrence of the act and the adverbiality of its time. If you say, "I ate at three o'clock," without my asking where the eating took place, or if you say, "I ate at home," without my asking about the time of the eating, whether at noon, in the afternoon, or at night, the event lacks complete adverbiality.

It is well known that time and place share adverbiality but differ: place is a fixed adverb that does not change, while time is constantly changing. There is dawn, noon, afternoon, sunset, and night; time revolves, with past, present and future. Thus time and place share adverbiality, but time is a changing adverb, whereas place is a fixed adverb.

The verse here brings both together. ﴿The Day of Hunayn﴾ is both time and place for a great event, and the verse takes the adverb of place in ﴿many battlefields﴾ and the adverb of time in ﴿the Day of Hunayn﴾. If it is said that the adverb of time and that of place do not both appear in each, we reply: no, the adverb of place appears in one part and the adverb of time in another part, and this, as we have said, is what they call "ihtibak." The first has omitted what the second indicates, and the second has omitted what the first indicates. The meaning is: Allah gave you victory on the day of such-and-such battlefields. If you coordinate the Day of Hunayn with them, the meaning becomes "and battlefields of the Day of Hunayn," that is, both are brought together here. But Allah, glorified and exalted, willed that there be no repetition, so He brought one here and the other there. This appears clearly in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿There has already been a sign for you in the two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah, and another disbelieving﴾ (3:13).

Since the other is ﴿disbelieving﴾, the first must be "believing," but "believing" is omitted because "disbelieving" indicates it. And since the believing army fights in the way of Allah, the disbelieving army fights in the way of Shaytan. "Fights in the way of Shaytan" is omitted because "fights in the way of Allah" indicates it, so that there is no repetition. The believer who listens to the words of Allah must have depth of understanding and must be all ears, so that he knows and notices that from one clause something is omitted which the other indicates. Thus the adverb of time is present in one clause and the adverb of place in the other, and each indicates the other. An example of this: after this battle ended and the Muslims returned to Madinah exhausted, without taking off their war gear, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "None of you shall pray the afternoon prayer except in Banu Qurayzah."

So the Muslims set out, without resting, toward the land of Banu Qurayzah, who were the Jews living in Madinah, who had broken the covenant of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and allied with the disbelievers against the Muslims. While the Companions were on their way to Banu Qurayzah, the sun was about to set. Some Companions said: "The sun will set and we must pray the afternoon prayer," and they prayed. Another group of Companions said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked us not to pray the afternoon prayer except in Banu Qurayzah," and they did not pray until they arrived there.

We say: both groups reasoned, because prayer requires an adverb of time and an adverb of place. The one who looked to the adverb of time said, "The sun will set," and prayed; the one who looked to the adverb of place which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had specified did not pray. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved both groups and respected their ijtihad (independent reasoning) regarding the adverbiality of time and the adverbiality of place. On this, Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said on the Day of the Confederates: "None of you shall pray the afternoon prayer except in Banu Qurayzah." Some of them were overtaken by the afternoon prayer before reaching them, and some said: "Rather, we will pray; it was not meant of us that [we delay it]." This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not rebuke any one of them.

﴿And on the Day of Hunayn, when your great number impressed you, but it availed you nothing﴾. Ghina (sufficiency) is the absence of need for others. Hunayn(2) is a place in a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if, where the disbelievers gathered, who were distressed by the Muslims' conquest of Makkah, and they wished to carry out a counter-operation that would nullify the value of this victory. The tribes of Hawazin and Thaqif gathered, and they chose Malik ibn 'Awf to be their commander in this battle. Malik ibn 'Awf was able to assemble four thousand fighters, and a number of the confederate tribes around them joined them. Malik laid out his plan on the basis that the army would go out with the wealth of the participants, including money, cattle and camels, and that the women and children would go out with the army as well, so that each of them would defend his honor and property and would not flee from the battle, and would continue fighting with courage and vehemence, because he defends his women, his wealth and his children. Thus he put in place all the factors that would ensure victory for him, whereas the believers, when the battle begins, would fight in defence of the religion of Allah and its method.

The disbelievers gathered and descended into a valley called "Wadi Awtas." Among them was an old, blind man named "Duraid ibn al-Simmah," who was chief of the tribe of Jusham. When he arrived at the battle site, he asked: "In what land are we?" They said: "We are in Wadi Awtas." He smiled and said: "A rugged place (hazn) without stones (dhirs), and a level ground without soft sand," meaning that it is a suitable land, with no sharp stones that tire the one who walks upon it, nor soft ground in which the feet of those walking sink; "hazn" is roughness and harshness, and "dhirs" is fatigue during walking; and it is also not a flat sandy plain in which feet sink.

When the old man heard the crying of children and the bleating of sheep, he said: "I hear the crying of boys and the lowing of cattle." They said to him: "Malik ibn 'Awf has brought with him his families and all his wealth." He said: "As for the wealth, there is no harm in it; but as for the women and children, this is the reckless one" (i.e., one who does not understand war), "send him to me." They brought him to him. When he arrived, he said: "O Malik, what has moved you to this?" He said: "And what do you want?"
