So: al-lumazah is the frequency of finding fault in others, and it indicates the weakness of the one who does it; if he were not weak, he would say what he wants openly.

The Almighty says: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities.﴾ Al-lumz, as we have known, is the search for a fault, and here it is enclosed in a thing, which is the charities.

Some of the hypocrites used to backbite about the legislation of alms, and they would object that the wealthy man exhausts himself and toils to obtain money, and then the poor man takes the money without effort. So do they object to the legislation itself? Do they object to the amount of alms imposed on them and consider it large? Or do they object to Allah's urging people to give alms? Or do they object to the manner in which alms are disbursed to the poor, that some give a lot and some give little? They were objecting to all of these matters or some of them.

So, al-lumz is either in the legislation, or in the amount of alms, or in the manner of disbursement. The incident in which this noble verse was revealed concerned the disbursement of alms: Harqus ibn Zuhayr, who was the head of the Kharijites and the son of Dhu al-Khuwaysirah, stood up and said: "Be just, O Muhammad!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you! Who will be just if I am not just? You have failed and lost if I am not just." Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, permit me to deal with him; I will strike his neck." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Leave him, for he has companions, in comparison to whose prayer one of you would consider his own prayer insignificant, and whose fasting one of you would consider his own fasting insignificant. They recite the Qur'an but it does not pass their collarbones. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through the game. Then one looks at its blade and finds nothing on it; then one looks at its feathering (risaf) and finds nothing on it; then one looks at its shaft (nadi), which is its shaft, and finds nothing on it; then one looks at its fletching (qudhadh) and finds nothing on it. It has outstripped the dung and the blood. Their sign is a black man, one of whose arms is like a woman's breast, or like a lump of flesh that jiggles. They will come out at a time when people are divided."

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "I bear witness that I heard this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I bear witness that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) fought them, and I was with him. He ordered that the man (that is, the black man) be searched for, and he was found and brought, until I looked at him according to the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he gave."

The Almighty says, explaining the state of these people: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities. If they are given from them, they are satisfied; but if they are not given from them, at once they become angry.﴾ That is: these people, if they were given from the alms, were content and rejoicing, and if they were not given from it, their hearts were filled with anger, and they began with fault-finding. So the amount given to them from the alms was the basis of their fault-finding.

A similar thing happened at the battle of Hunayn. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) distributed the spoils among the Quraysh and the people of Makkah, and gave the Ansar nothing.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) did not include the Ansar in this distribution, some of them were displeased by that. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered them and said to them:

"Are you not pleased that people should return with the sheep and the camel, while you return with the Messenger of Allah? By Him in whose hand is my soul, the living of you is my living and the dying of you is my dying. If people were to take a path and the Ansar took a path, I would take the path of the Ansar." (3)

Here the Ansar wept, and they knew that they would return with something far greater than the spoils: they would return in the company of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) may give some of the alms to a man newly converted to Islam, in order to bind him to this religion; he may give for the reconciliation of hearts; and he may give to a poor man whose self-respect refuses to admit his need before people.

Therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had considerations in distributing alms and spoils, which perhaps no one noticed. It was obligatory upon the Muslims to accept the action of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because his conduct is the judgment, and we must accept it.

For example, at Hudaybiyyah, where a treaty took place between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the disbelievers of Quraysh that none of them would attack the other for a period of ten years (4), this peace stirred the anger of a number of believers, and they said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Shall we accept the humiliation in our religion?" That is: how do we give them these covenants when they are detrimental to us? So much so that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) became agitated and wanted to speak harshly, and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Are you not upon the truth, O Messenger of Allah?" Abu Bakr said to him: "Hold fast to his stirrup, O 'Umar" (that is, know your place). "Indeed he is the Messenger of Allah." (5) After a period of time passed, the Muslims came to know the wisdom behind the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, and what this treaty brought to Islam of spread and strength which led to the conquest of Makkah. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "No victory was greater for Islam than the victory of Hudaybiyyah." But the Muslims at that time had not grasped what lay between Muhammad and his Lord, because worshippers are always hasty, while Allah does not hasten as worshippers hasten, until affairs reach what He wills.

Allah the Almighty wished to calm the souls of the believers. And when they were about to reach Madinah returning after the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the Almighty's saying was revealed:

{They are those who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram, and the offering detained from reaching its place. And if not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and there would befall you because of them a sin without knowledge — [it was so] that Allah might admit to His mercy whom He wills. If they had been apart, We would have punished those who disbelieved among them with a painful punishment.} (25)

Thus Allah informed the believers of the reason for accepting the treaty of Hudaybiyyah and for not fighting the polytheists at that time and in that place. There were believers in Makkah concealing their faith, living in a society where those [disbelievers] could overpower these Muslims if they knew of their presence. Also, the Muslims who came with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not know these believers, so if battle broke out, a Muslim might kill a Muslim, because those who came from Madinah, if they entered into fighting with the people of Makkah, might kill some of their brothers in faith who were in Makkah, since they did not know them. And if the believers were in one area and the disbelievers in another, Allah would have punished the disbelievers at the hands of the believers with a painful punishment.

So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew from his Lord a secret which he did not announce except at its appointed time, despite the haste of those who were with him (ﷺ). Something similar happens in our lives: we may find a believer who calls upon Allah and his supplication is not answered. The believer should not grieve over this; rather he should know that in non-answering there may be a good he does not know, and that it is part of Allah's mercy that He did not answer this supplication, just as you prevent your young son from carrying a weapon out of fear that he may act rashly in some quarrel and kill someone, even though the weapon is with him for his protection, but this method of protection may carry harm and may lead to dire consequences.

When you call upon Allah and He does not answer your supplication, be certain that He, glory be to Him, is protecting you from yourself, because you do not know and Allah the Almighty knows. You may pray for something you deem good while Allah the Almighty knows it to be evil. So, not answering this supplication is itself the answer to it (6).

The Almighty says: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities. If they are given from them, they are satisfied; but if they are not given from them, at once they become angry.﴾ Sakhat (anger) is: dissatisfaction in the heart, which then extends to the tongue, just as Harqus ibn Zuhayr said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Be just, O Muhammad!" That is: he was angry in his heart first, then he offended with his tongue second.

When the Almighty presents to us the disease within the community of faith, He, may He be exalted, gives the remedy that protects the society from this disease. These people used to find fault with the legislation of alms, and although if they were given from it they were satisfied, and if they were not given they became angry, so their scales are unbalanced, and they are not scales of established truth, but scales of the desires of the self. The scales of truth do not follow or depend on the desires of the self; rather they are fixed scales in which a person acts justly even with his most bitter enemy (7).

But these people's emotions vary according to their interests: when they receive, they are pleased, and when they are denied, they are angered, because their measure is private interest, far removed from all justice.

And 'Umar went to Abu Bakr and said to him something similar, and Abu Bakr said to him: 'O man, he is truly the Messenger of Allah, and he does not disobey his Lord, and He is his helper, so hold fast to his stirrup, for by Allah he is upon the truth.'" (Fath al-Bari 5/332). That is: hold fast to his command and abandon opposition to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

They said: "Then we will increase [our supplications]." He said: "Allah is greater." And here the Exalted Lord brings the remedy, so He says, may His majesty be exalted:

﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them, and said, "Sufficient for us is Allah; Allah will give us of His bounty, and [so will] His Messenger. Indeed, we are toward Allah inclined."﴾ (9:59)

How can the Exalted Lord say ﴿what He had given them﴾ when they had taken nothing, and indeed they were angered because they had received nothing?

We say: Allah wants to draw their attention to the fact that He has a giving in bestowal and a giving in withholding. The giving of the Exalted Lord is to those who receive, and the withholding of the Exalted Lord is to some; yet all of that is a giving from the Exalted Lord, but people do not pay attention to it. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) withheld the spoils from the Ansar at Hunayn, they took the companionship of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is greater and more lofty than spoils. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them:

"The living is your living, and the dying is your dying. If the people were to take a valley and the Ansar a valley, I would take the valley of the Ansar."(1)

Thus they took what is greater, more important and more magnificent than spoils. So withholding may also be a form of giving.

The Exalted Lord says ﴿what Allah and His Messenger had given them﴾: He, the Mighty and Majestic, is the Legislator, and the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) is the conveyor and executor. So if they were content with the division of Allah, then contentment is an act of the heart, which they should have expressed with a verbal utterance, namely ﴿and said, "Sufficient for us is Allah"﴾. So contentment is the act of the heart, and expressing contentment is the act of the tongue. Since they had entrusted the matter to Allah, then Allah is the One who looks after, and in His giving there is good and in His withholding there is good. Therefore we find the good people among men, when they are overpowered in their affairs, saying: "Indeed, we have a Lord." That is: beware lest you think that when you withhold from me or take my right by wronging me, you will carry on with this act without punishment; for I have a Lord who is jealous for me, and He will compensate me with more than what you took, and will make what you have taken from me by force a vengeance upon you.

Therefore, what a believer must most care about is not the connection to the blessing but the connection to the Bestower. And in it is the fact that Allah is the One able to compensate for anything that is lost.

Then He makes the picture clearer for us, saying ﴿Allah will give us of His bounty﴾, i.e., He will compensate us for it with something better than it. And Allah's giving is always bounty, because He gives a person before he is able to worship Him; even while in his mother's womb he is unable to do anything. If, in this world, you have thought with the intellect that Allah created for you, and acted with the energy that Allah created for you, and on the earth that Allah created, then in your mother's womb you were not able to do anything at all. And when you come out and grow and become big, you live in a cosmos full of the blessings of Allah, in which you created nothing and produced no good. Rather, you came into a universe already complete in its blessings: you did not create the earth, nor did you make the sun. Indeed, a single one of Allah's blessings, namely rain, if it were to stop, everyone on earth would perish. We feel the effect of this when the seasons of drought come to any region of the world, and we see how everything perishes: the crops, the human being and the animal.

The Exalted Lord has created us in a world of change, so the one who is able today may become unable tomorrow, and the healthy today may become sick and ailing tomorrow, and the strong grow weak, so that we know that the power and strength we possess are not inherent qualities in us, but a gift from Allah, which He takes whenever He wills. We see the strong man who used to maul with his hand, harm others with it and humiliate people with it, and we see his hand struck, so that the orders no longer reach it from the brain and it becomes paralyzed. So: the ability of any human being is not inherent in him, but is from the bounty of Allah, the Exalted, and everything in the universe is from the bounty of Allah.

The Exalted Lord says:

﴿Allah will give us of His bounty, and [so will] His Messenger; indeed, we are toward Allah inclined.﴾ It is said: "raghiba fi kadha" means he desired it; "raghiba 'an kadha" means he abandoned this matter; and "raghiba ila kadha" means he set out on the road toward it. Here the Truth said ﴿indeed, we are toward Allah inclined﴾. And as long as we are inclined toward Allah, we ought not to separate the giving of this world from the giving of the Hereafter, for the world is not everything to you, so long as you are inclined toward Allah, who will give you boundless bliss in the Hereafter. Therefore, our desire for Allah should not make us angry over a bliss that has escaped us in this world, because there is boundless bliss awaiting us in the Hereafter.

1 A sound hadith, whose takhrij has been mentioned many times before.

Then Allah, exalted is He, wished after this to explain the channels of charity, so that those who desire the goods of this world might recognize these channels and come to know the reality of the matter, and so that they might determine whether they deserve charity or not. So He, majestic is His majesty, said:

﴿Alms are only for the poor and the needy, and those employed to collect them, and those whose hearts are to be reconciled, and for freeing slaves, and for those in debt, and for the cause of God, and for the wayfarer; an obligation from God. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ (9:60)

When you hear the word ﴿innama﴾ ("only"), understand that it signifies restriction (qasr). When you say, "Only Zayd is the man," you have restricted manhood to Zayd. If you say, "Only Hatim is the generous one," you have restricted generosity to Hatim. The words of the Exalted, ﴿Alms are only﴾, mean that charity is confined to these groups and does not go beyond them.

Who are these whom God, exalted is He, has confined charity to? And what is meant by "charity" (sadaqah)? Is it voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu') or zakat (obligatory alms)?

We say: since God, exalted is He, has specified its channels, it is zakat. Someone may ask: why did God not say "zakat" but said "sadaqah"?

We say: do you not see, in societies without faith, atheistic ones, that some people think of establishing social institutions to care for the poor? Human compassion for a fellow human is an instinct that God created in all of us. Therefore we must understand that zakat is a sadaqah, and if God had not legislated it, a person would still have to give it to his fellow human. The events of the universe all attest to the truth of God's description of zakat as sadaqah, because it comes as a voluntary act even from the non-believer and from one who is not bound by the legislation. The one who is able feels happiness as he gives to the one who is not able. It is an instinct God placed in His creation to lighten misery in the universe.

Here God says: ﴿Alms are only for the poor and the needy.﴾ The scholars have differed over this. Some said: the faqir is the one who has nothing, so he is destitute (mu'dam), and the miskin is the one who owns something but it does not suffice him. On this view the miskin is in a better state than the faqir, and they relied on a Qur'anic text, the words of the Exalted: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to needy people who worked on the sea...﴾ (18:79).

Since these needy people owned a boat, they had something they owned, and the return the boat brought them was not sufficient for them.

But other scholars said the opposite. They held that the miskin is one who owns nothing at all, and the faqir is one who has enough to get by (al-kafaf). On this view the faqir is in a better state than the miskin. I do not believe there is any benefit in entering this dispute, because God gave both of them: the faqir and the miskin. The word "faqir" means one whose back has been broken by life, i.e., the vertebrae (fiqar) of his spine, and his condition expresses that. The miskin is one whom poverty (maskanah) has stupefied.

Then comes: ﴿and those employed to collect them﴾, meaning those who gather the charity, take it from those who give it, and deposit it in the public treasury (bayt al-mal). We note here that ﴿those employed to collect them﴾ is stated in an unrestricted way. It does not specify whether the one who deserves charity is the one who collects it while being poor, or the one who collects it while not being in need. We say: collecting charity is a work. If we said that the one who is not in need and works at collecting charity should not be paid, then his work becomes a form of benevolence. And since work done as a favour is not performed with the same competence as work done for a wage, and also so that the community is not deprived of a clever, energetic collector of charity merely because he is not in need, we give him a wage, so that he will be accountable for his work. Accountability only comes when it is tied to a wage.

The one who collects charity works for the benefit of the state of faith. He gathers the charities and gives them to the ruler or governor who distributes them. In this there is benefit for the whole Muslim community, especially if the charity is distributed from the public treasury, so that no one exalts himself over another and no one is humiliated before another. In this there is a preservation of the dignity of the believers, because whoever takes from outside the public treasury will suffer the breaking of his lower hand.

And whoever gives to other than the public treasury may, in his giving, display a kind of arrogance of the upper hand. Likewise, the children of the poor man will not see their father going to a rich man to take charity and being struck with humiliation and brokenness. And the children of the rich man do not see this poor man coming to their father to take charity, so they do not become arrogant toward the children of the poor man.

So if the poor take charity from the public treasury, that is a safeguard for everyone's dignity. And if a dispute arises between a rich man and a poor man, the rich man will not say to the poor man: "I give you such and such," nor will the children of the rich man say to the children of the poor: "Were it not for our father, you would have died of hunger."

Therefore: by this system God intended to prevent the tyranny of the giver and also to prevent the humiliation of asking. Everyone goes to the public treasury to take or to give. When the poor man goes to take from the public treasury by the order of the governor, there is no shame, because those under his rule are answerable to him.

Then the Exalted turns to another category and says: ﴿and those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾. These are people whom Islam wished to win over, or at least to restrain their harm against the Muslims. In the early period of Islam the Muslims were weak and could not protect themselves. When God strengthened the state of the Muslims with power, might and standing, the caliph 'Umar ibn al-Khattab prevented giving the mu'allafah qulubuhum a share of zakat, because he did not see that the strength of Islam needed anyone other than those whose faith was sound. Therefore 'Umar ibn al-Khattab did not include them among the categories of zakat.(1)

The words of the Exalted, ﴿those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾, raise a question: can the heart be reconciled? We say: yes. Kindness reconciles the heart of a sound person, and likewise it reconciles the limbs of a person who is not sound, so he does not transgress against one who has been kind to him with his tongue or his hand.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿and for freeing slaves﴾ (fi al-riqab), meaning the slaves who were taken captive in a lawful war. The elimination of slavery (riqq) was among the goals of Islam, and therefore it made freeing slaves one of the channels of zakat. Some people claim that Islam brought slavery and approved it. We say: Islam did not bring slavery, because slavery existed before the Prophetic mission. Islam brought manumission (itq) to eliminate slavery, so it made freeing a neck an expiation for some sins.(2) It made freeing slaves one of the channels of zakat. The Qur'an was revealed at a time when the sources of slavery were numerous.

It was customary in those days that if a debtor was unable to pay what he owed, the creditor would take one of his sons as a slave for himself.

If someone committed a crime, the offender would obtain pardon from the injured party in exchange for giving him one of his sons as a slave. If something was stolen, the thief was not punished; instead he gave one of his sons as a slave to the one from whom the item was stolen. The strong would enslave the weak, seizing their women and children by force and selling them in the slave markets. Thus the sources of slavery in the world were numerous, and there was only one outlet: the will of the master, who might free or might not free as he chose.

Slavery existed in Europe, in Asia, in Africa, and it also existed in America. So there were many sources of slavery, and one outlet, the will of the master. Slavery was increasing, and Islam came while the world was drowning in slavery. Why?

Because slavery at that time resembled a basin into which many faucets pour, while it has only one drain. Islam did not treat the matter in one leap, like most of God's legislation. It treated it in stages, just as with the prohibition of wine, when the prohibition began by forbidding it at the time of prayer. The Exalted said: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying...﴾ (4:43). Then He prohibited it with a definitive prohibition.(3)

When Islam came to address the issue of slavery and to free the human being from servitude, it began by closing the sources of enslavement and making the only source a lawful war of faith waged by the ruler. As for all the other means and forms of slavery, such as enslaving someone as a punishment for a crime, or because he cannot repay a debt, or for other reasons, Islam closed them by prohibition. As for the outlet, it did not make it one outlet, the will of the master, but made it many outlets. Whoever commits a sin knows that God will not forgive him unless he frees a neck. Whoever swears an oath and wants to be released from it frees a neck. If he does none of these, and wants to do a good deed that increases his reward with God, he frees a neck.(4)

Concerning this, the Exalted says: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path. And what can make you know what is the steep path? It is the freeing of a neck.﴾ (90:11–13)

Thus Islam made many channels for eliminating slavery so that it would end within a few years, and then it established what actually ends slavery, even if it did not end it in form.

If any master had some insistence on keeping his slave, he must clothe him with what he wears and feed him with what he eats, and assist him with what is beyond his capacity.(5) Thus the difference between master and slave became effaced.

When some Islamic states abolished slavery by law, the slaves went to their masters and said: "Let us live with you as we were." They did this because their life with their masters had been good. Thus Islam abolished all the distinctions of slavery, and it became a formality that counts for nothing.

But some people ask: what about the words of the Exalted: ﴿and what your right hands possess﴾ (4:36)?

We say: understand from God. This ruling applies only when the enslaved woman was a participant in war, that is, she fought alongside the man and then fell into captivity. What applies to her is this: from what source would she live while in the land of her enemy? If she is left in society, that poses a danger to society and to her. Also, because this woman has feelings that will be stirred, Islam enjoined on the master that if he loves this slave-girl, he may enjoy her as a wife enjoys her husband, and if she bears a child she becomes a free wife and her children are free.(6) In this there is an elimination of slavery.

The Exalted speaks of another category of those entitled to zakat: ﴿and the debtors﴾ (al-gharimin). The gharim is one who has borrowed in what is not sinful and then cannot repay his debt. The creditor did not give him respite as God commanded in the words of the Exalted: ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease...﴾ (2:280), nor did he forgive him or waive his debt. In this case the public treasury pays off this debt. But why this legislation?

God willed to give the debtor who cannot find what to settle his debt with, so that people do not turn away from generosity and from lending to one who is going through hardship. Thus ease remains in society, and people's help for one another in the hour of hardship remains, so that no one refrains from giving to a person in hardship, because he knows that if he does not pay, the public treasury will settle it from zakat. Or: the gharim is one who wanted to reconcile two parties, such as two people disagreeing over a sum of money, so he takes on the task of ending the dispute and pays the sum himself, and then his situation worsens because he bore this money out of a zeal of faith. So we say to him: take from the public treasury, so that the settling of disputes and the spreading of goodwill among people become widespread. Thus the gharim is one who borrowed in what is not sinful and cannot pay the debt, or one who bears the cost of reconciling two parties, and he is entitled to this kind of money.

The Exalted says: ﴿and for the cause of God﴾. Most jurists say that it applies to jihad.(7) Because the one who sacrifices his wealth in jihad for the sake of God would not have sacrificed his wealth if he did not know that jihad is a gate by which he enters Paradise. When you sacrifice wealth or self in the cause of God, that is from the certainty of faith.

If you were not certain that if you were martyred you would enter Paradise, you would not have fought. And if you were not certain that if you spent your wealth in jihad for the cause of God you would enter Paradise, you would not have spent.

Islam aims at two things: a religion that is conveyed, and a method that is realized. The mujahid in the cause of God is an example for the rest of the believers. And the example in

Here the Truth (al-Haqq) shows a new picture of their conduct, so He says:

﴿And among them are those who abuse the Prophet and say, "He is an ear." Say, "An ear of good for you: he believes in Allah, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe. And those of you who abuse the Messenger of Allah—for them is a painful punishment."﴾ (61)

We know that harming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came after prophethood, and some of the disbelievers said what the Qur'an related of their words:

﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment.﴾ (32) (al-Anfal).

This is the supplication of one who has no intellect. Had they been reasonable, they would have said: "If this is the truth from You, O Lord, guide us to it or make us believe in it." But, from the excess of their spite and misguidance, they wished for punishment rather than believe in the truth. This reveals to us the flimsiness of the disbelievers' minds.

Here the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And among them are those who abuse the Prophet﴾. Those who abuse the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are the lords, the men of influence, who fear that the method of this Prophet will strip them of their power, their wealth, and what they have taken unjustly from the weak. The weak—as we know—were the first to enter the religion of Islam, because they sensed that this religion protects them from the tyranny of the wealthy, their exploitation and their power. The Truth willed to turn the fear of the weak into strength and security, and He, glory be to Him, willed to add to faith a number of the wealthy and men of the top rank, such as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and others, may Allah be pleased with them all, so that the powerful of Quraysh would not say what the people of Noah said to their Prophet: ﴿And we do not see you followed except by those who are the lowest of us...﴾ (27) (Hud).

Thus the abuse of him (ﷺ) was after the mission; but before the mission, in the view of all, he was: the trustworthy, the truthful, and the one entrusted.

It is astonishing that, after the revelation came down, they would entrust no one with things as they entrusted Muhammad (ﷺ). Though everything precious to the disbelievers and opponents, they went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that he might safeguard these precious things for them. This contradiction is explained only by their confidence in his (ﷺ) character. Despite that, they were in rage and fury, because the Qur'an had been sent down upon him. And the Truth is the One who said what was on their tongues: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of the two cities, a great one?"﴾ (31) (al-Zukhruf).

By this they acknowledged with their own tongues the greatness of the Qur'an, after they had acknowledged by their conduct the trustworthiness of Muhammad (ﷺ). But they objected to Allah's choice of him, and wished that this Qur'an had been sent down upon one of their great men. The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, responded to them: ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord? We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world...﴾ (32) (al-Zukhruf).

In this is a call for them to show proper manners toward Allah, glory be to Him. He did not appoint them to choose whom His mercy and message should be sent down upon; rather He Himself chooses. He is the One who distributed among the servants their livelihood in this world and in the Hereafter. If anyone has a blessing of wealth, rank, glory, or anything else, this is not from human capacities or from their own essence, but is a blessing from Allah. Here the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And among them are those who abuse the Prophet﴾. So: the abuse has its cause in that he (ﷺ) came with a call to good, and a messenger does not come with a call to good unless evil has spread throughout society. When evil spreads in society, there are those who profit from it; so when the Messenger of Allah brings good, the soldiers of evil hasten to harm the bearer of the message of good. Thus it is natural that the Prophet should have enemies.

And the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy—devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with ornamented speech as deception...﴾ (112) (al-An'am).

Indeed, every scholar who bears the message of Allah to convey it to the following generations—even if he has no enemies, that diminishes his share of the inheritance of prophethood. And to everyone who has enemies and guides people to the method of Allah, we say: do not be disturbed, and be at ease; for the fact that someone opposes you means that there is in you a trace of the marks of prophethood.

The hypocrites' harm to him (ﷺ) took several forms; among them their saying: ﴿And they say, "He is an ear."﴾

For a human being—as we know—there are many means: the ear is a means of perception, the eye is a means of perception, and all the limbs are means of perception. Every person has multiple faculties, among them perceptive faculties and psychological faculties. The perceptive faculties are those by which one perceives things, such as hearing, sight, smell and taste. As for the psychological faculties, these are the qualities by which people are described. For example: we call the spy an "eye," because he spies and conveys what he sees to others; we call the man who hears every piece of news an "ear"; and we call the thief who encroaches on another's property "long-handed," and so on.

So: every limb has a sense, and seeing, hearing, smelling, touching and tasting are all means of sensory perception from which intangible impressions are formed, which then become beliefs. These means of perception receive from the sensory world what it gives them of information, and store it to act upon afterward, and together they constitute what a person knows. For this reason we find the Truth, glory be to Him, bestowing favor upon His creatures, saying:

﴿And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing, sight and hearts, that you may be grateful.﴾ (78) (al-Nahl).

Gratitude is only for a blessing, so these means of perception—what you hear, what you see with your sight, or what you perceive with your heart—are among the blessings of Allah for which we must thank Him, because they gave us sensory knowledge after we knew nothing.

When a human being is called by the name of one of his limbs, know that this limb is the core of him. So the hypocrites' description of the Messenger, ﴿he is an ear﴾, was a reviling of the Messenger. One of them would say: "Beware lest this reach the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he exposes your hypocrisy and harms you"; for in their opinion Muhammad (ﷺ) believes everything. They wished to accuse him (ﷺ) that he does not scrutinize the word conveyed to him and believes everything said to him, as we say in colloquial speech, "So-and-so is an ear," meaning he gives his ear to everything said to him.

So Allah responds to them: ﴿Say, "An ear of good for you,"﴾ because he (ﷺ) listens to the method of the heavens and conveys it to guide the people of the earth; so he is the best of all people. Even if we take their claim that the Messenger (ﷺ) believes them if they lie to him, this is good for them, because he (ﷺ) does not harm them; and he (ﷺ) is ﴿an ear of good﴾ because he hears only from Allah through revelation. For this reason we said: the wisdom of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) being unlettered is that he did not learn from any equal to him; his knowledge was from Allah. If illiteracy is a deficiency in us, it is complete perfection in the case of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he took only from his Creator; and he is an ear of good, for he is the ear that listened to the last transmission sent down from the heaven for the guidance of the earth.

If the hypocrites said "he is an ear," He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Say, "An ear of good for you,"﴾ which is good whose benefit returns to all mankind, but not in the sense in which they blame him for it. He may hear your offenses, then hear your excuses, so he does not harm you and pardons you.

Since this is the conduct of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), why do you harm him and burden him?

In language there is what they call "answering according to the premise" (al-qawl bil-mūjib). If someone says something to you, you agree and say to him: "Yes, but it may take on another meaning." If a person keeps adding favors to another and says to him, "I have burdened you," the other replies, "You have burdened my shoulder with your hands," meaning your favors to me are many. If someone says to you, "I have extended myself over you" (i.e., imposed), his friend replies, "No, you have shown favor to me," meaning: you gave me the blessing of making me happy by your company. So he agreed with what he said, but answered him with the opposite of what he said.

They blamed the Messenger for being "an ear," as if his ear controlled all his conduct, so that whatever he heard affected him, and if he heard something that troubled him, his position would swing from one extreme to the other. They tried to claim against him that he believes everything he hears and does not take precautions regarding the one who conveys to him; they said he (ﷺ) is "an ear," and the Truth, glory be to Him, replied, "An ear of good." Naturally, the Truth's words did not agree with what they said, because "ear" in their sense is not the "ear" that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, affirmed.

Some superficial people may say: the hypocrites called the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "an ear," meaning by it that he hears and believes everything said to him, and has no wisdom of scrutiny and choice. But let us attend to what the Truth has said: ﴿An ear of good for you﴾; for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hears only from Allah, and what he hears from Allah he obeys and applies; and what he hears from people he presents to the method of Allah; if it agrees with the method he executes it, and if it contradicts the method he rejects it. So he is an ear for good, who hears only from Allah, and nothing from his message comes but good to whoever follows him.

But why did the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, not say "an ear of good for the believers," and instead said ﴿an ear of good for you﴾? Because the goodness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) encompassed everyone, extending beyond the believers to the hypocrites and the disbelievers. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not expose a hypocrite unless Allah exposed the hypocrite through a Qur'an sent down from heaven.

For example, the hypocrites would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), offering excuses for not fighting in the way of Allah, and asking permission to stay behind; and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would grant them permission. And when the hypocrites came to the noble Messenger and swore falsely to him, he would believe them, or more probably he would not expose their lie before the people.

So the goodness in him (ﷺ) encompassed the hypocrites, because his noble character refused to expose them before people. As for the disbelievers, the goodness also encompassed them, because his call to them to Islam and his insistence upon this call (ﷺ) led a number of disbelievers to submit and believe, and abundant good reached them through their guidance to the religion of truth.

So the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, ﴿Say, "An ear of good for you,"﴾ means: for all mankind.

Thus the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, distinguished between what they intended and what Allah, majestic in His majesty, intended. They intended to describe the Messenger as an "ear" of mere listening; Allah says: it is an ear of good. This is what they call in language—as we have said—"answering according to the premise" (al-qawl al-mūjib): that you agree with your opponent in what he said, but you turn what he said from evil to good.

An example also is what the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, says, relating the words on the tongues of the hypocrites when they said:

﴿If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel therefrom the meaner...﴾ (8) (al-Munafiqun).

They meant that they themselves were the mightier, and the meaner were the believers. The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, agreed with them on what they said: yes, the mightier will expel the meaner therefrom. But He wished to show them who is the mighty and who is the humble, so He said: ﴿And to Allah belongs might, and to His Messenger and to the believers...﴾ (8) (al-Munafiqun). So it is as if the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, confirms to them that the mightier will expel the meaner, but they reckon themselves to be the mighty; so He tells them: ﴿And to Allah belongs might, and to His Messenger and to the believers.﴾ This is what they call "answering according to the premise": that you agree with the speaker, who intends to direct his words toward evil, and you turn the meaning of the speech and direct it toward good. What is meant here is that you increase the humiliation of the addressee, for you make him believe that you agree with him, so his face lights up and he feels happy; then afterward you diminish what he said, so he is struck with complete humiliation, just as a prisoner who feels intense thirst and insists on asking for a cup of water is told by the guard, "I will bring you a cup of water," and indeed he brings the cup.

1 Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (4/3117): "This verse was revealed concerning Itab ibn Qushayr, who said: 'Muhammad is only an ear that accepts whatever is said to him.' He is Nabtal ibn al-Harith." Ibn Ishaq said so.
2 The two cities here are Mecca and al-Ta'if. The scholars have differed in identifying the great man intended. From Mecca: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira or 'Utba ibn Rabi'a. From al-Ta'if: 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud or 'Umayr ibn 'Abd Yalil. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (4/127): "The apparent meaning is that they meant a great man from either of the two towns."
3 Al-kahil: what lies between a person's shoulders.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 62:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) presents one of the forms of the hypocrites, and He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you; but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾ (9:62)

It is remarkable that Surat al-Tawbah contains the greatest number of occurrences of the word "yahlifun" (they swear). The root "yahlif" appears only once in Surat al-Ma'idah, once in Surat al-Nisa', three times in Surat al-Mujadilah, whereas in Surat al-Tawbah it comes seven times, and in Surat al-Qalam the form "hallaf" appears. So much so that Surat al-Tawbah was named "Surat Yahlif" (the Surah of Swearing)(1), because it contains the greatest number of ﴿yahlifun﴾ in the Noble Qur'an.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾. In this there is the insistence of the hypocrites on swearing, falsely, and this clarifies their stupidity and their lack of perception. And also the Truth says:

﴿They will swear by Allah to you when you return to them, that you may leave them alone...﴾ (9:95) (al-Tawbah).

The Truth, glory be to Him, using the letter "sin" (sa-) means that they have not yet sworn, but they will swear after a period, that is, in the future. That is: the noble verse was revealed and they had not yet sworn; rather, they would swear after the revelation of the noble verse. Had they possessed even a grain of intelligence, they would not have sworn, and would have said: the Qur'an said "we will swear," but we did not swear. But despite the revelation of the verse, they came confirming the Qur'an, affirming faith, and swore.

The word "halafa" means the oath or the swearing. When we examine the Qur'an we find that "hilf" (swearing) is applied only to a false oath, whereas "qasam" (oath) is applied to both a true oath and a false oath. For example, when we read in Surat al-Ma'idah:

﴿That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn...﴾ (5:89) (al-Ma'idah).

Since there is an expiation for the oath, the swearing must be false, because what necessitates expiation is lying. If we then survey every "hilf" in the Qur'an, we find that it intends the false oath, and therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, said:

﴿And do not obey every habitual swearer, contemptible﴾ (68:10) (al-Qalam). So "hilf" here is meant as false swearing. But when the Truth, glory be to Him, says "aqsamu" (they swore), the oath may be true, and it may be false.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿They swear by Allah to you in order to please you﴾. That is: the aim of their false swearing is to please the believers, so that they feel secure with the hypocrites and do not expect evil from them. Then the Truth, glory be to Him, presents the reality: ﴿while Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. So they swear in order that you be pleased with them. As for the true believer, he swears only to please Allah, because a person may deceive people and may escape the justice of the earth, but you do not deceive Allah and never escape His justice.

Among the duties of faith is that a person keeps Allah in mind in every dealing with people, seeks His pleasure, and fears His anger; that is the true believer.

Here we note that the Truth, glory be to Him, said: ﴿while Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, and the linguistic analogy according to human speech would have been: "while Allah and His Messenger have more right that you should please them both." But the Truth willed to express it as ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, because the pleasure of Allah and the pleasure of His Messenger are one pleasure, since the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, does not bring the Qur'an from himself, but it is revelation from Allah. And pleasing the Messenger is following the path in which is the pleasure of Allah. Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are actually pledging allegiance to Allah...﴾ (3:10) (Al 'Imran). Hmm, verse reference as given: (3:31) (Al 'Imran)? [see note]

And He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you...﴾ (3:31) (Al 'Imran).

And He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah...﴾ (4:80) (al-Nisa').

So there is no obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger separately, nor pleasure of Allah and pleasure of the Messenger separately, because the pleasure from both is one pleasure.

Therefore the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him, ﴿while Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ is evidence of the unity of the pleasure from Allah and from His Messenger: whatever pleases Allah pleases the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and whatever angers Allah angers the Messenger.

Or: the Truth, glory be to Him, wants us to show proper manners toward His Essence, that when two matters are joined, for Allah and for His Messenger, we do not make anyone equal with Allah, but we make it for Him, glory be to Him, who is One. Therefore, when a man committed a sin, and they said to him, "Declare your repentance before the Messenger of Allah," the man said: "I repent to Allah and I do not repent to Muhammad." The Messenger of Allah said to him: "Put him on good (what is right)"(3). Look at the greatness of the Noble Messenger, who praises a man who says in his presence: "I do not repent to Muhammad; I repent only to Allah."

The saying of the Truth, glory be to Him: ﴿if they are believers﴾ means: if their faith is real, and not hypocrisy.

Therefore we do not seek pleasure from the creatures of Allah, but we seek it from Allah. The pleasure of Allah, glory be to Him, and the pleasure of the One who conveys from Him, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, are one pleasure; therefore the pronoun is singular in ﴿while Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, and He did not say "that they should please them both."(4)

(1) This surah has many names: Bara'ah, al-Tawbah, al-Fadihah, and al-Hafirah, because it dug out (hafarat) the hearts of the hypocrites. Hudhayfah said: it is the surah of punishment. Ibn 'Umar said: we used to call it al-Mushaqqishah. Al-Harith ibn Yazid said: it was called al-Muba'thirah, and it is said to be called al-Masawwirah, and it is said to be called al-Buhuth, because it searches into the secrets of the hypocrites. See: al-Burhan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an by al-Zarkashi (1/269).

(2) This came in a hadith agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh) from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah, and whoever disobeys me has disobeyed Allah." Related by al-Bukhari (7137) and Muslim (1830).

(3) From al-Aswad ibn Sari' that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was brought a captive and he said: "O Allah, I repent to You and I do not repent to Muhammad." The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "He has recognized the truth for its people." Related by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad (3/435). Al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (10/199): "In its chain is Muhammad ibn Mus'ab, whom one party considered reliable and others weak, and the rest of its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih." Al-Hafiz al-'Iraqi weakened the chain of this hadith in his takhrij of al-Ihya' (1/220).

(4) The linguists have many explanations for the singular pronoun here. Al-Qurtubi mentions three explanations and then said: "It was said that Allah, glory be to Him, made His pleasure in the pleasure of His Messenger. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah...﴾ (4:80). Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, whenever he passed by this verse, would stop and say: 'A letter, and what a letter! It was entrusted to him, so he commands us only with good.'" See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi (4/3119).

Then the Truth says, after that: ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein. That is the great disgrace.﴾ (63)

When you hear ﴿Do they not﴾, understand that this is a rebuke (istinkar), as if the means of knowledge had already come to them and it was obligatory that they know. If you say to a person, "Did you not know that such-and-such event occurred?", the meaning is that this event has been announced to him several times, and yet he did not know it. This is a rebuke for that person's failure to acquire knowledge.

Here, the Truth rebukes the hypocrites for not knowing a matter that Allah announced time and again, a matter they should have known and that should never have left their minds. We have said before that the interrogative carries a negation, and the hamza is the hamza of interrogation. It did not come to negate; and when the hamza of interrogation enters upon a negation, it becomes a rebuke. If you say to a person, "Did I not honor you?", it is as if you honored him many times while he denies it.

Allah's saying ﴿Do they not know﴾ is the establishment of proof (iqamat al-hujjah) that the ruling has reached them, because it is possible that they might say, "The ruling has not reached us," so the Truth clarifies: rather, the ruling has reached you, and I have informed you of it several times.

﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah﴾. What is the meaning of yuhadid (opposes)? We find in the countryside that people place iron markers that separate one plot of land from the adjacent one, as a sign of the thing that separates one right from another, and they call it a hadd (boundary). Those who oppose Allah are those who place Allah on one side and themselves on another side; by this they do not live in Allah's company, nor enjoy the blessing of faith in Him, nor apply His method. Rather, they make a boundary between themselves and what Allah has commanded.

When the scholars wished to explain this verse, they said: yuhadid means: yu'adi (opposes/is hostile), and they said: it means yushaqqiq (splits off), that is, he places himself in one side while Allah, His Messenger and His religion are on another side. Or: he wages war against the religion of Allah, so he is in one direction and the religion of Allah is in another direction.(1) There is a connection between the word "harb" (war) and the word "hadd" (edge): the edge of a sword is its cutting part that separates anything into two parts. So it is as if the one who opposes (yuhadid) is one who wars against the method of Allah and His Messenger. He not only disbelieves in Allah, but he also bears arms to make the creatures of Allah disbelieve as well.

The Truth, glorified and exalted, wants the believers to always be on the side of faith, and not to set up a boundary between themselves and belief in Him. The legal rulings are called hudud (limits), meaning that every ruling has been established to define a limit of the limits of Allah, by which rights and commands are preserved.

The method of Allah is either commands or prohibitions, for the whole method of religion lies in "do" and "do not do." The Truth, glorified and exalted, sets a penalty for whoever transgresses His limits, so He says:

﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them...﴾ (187) (al-Baqarah)

And He says:

﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them...﴾ (229) (al-Baqarah)

Some people ask: what is the difference between the two expressions ﴿do not transgress them﴾ (ta'tadu-ha) and ﴿do not approach them﴾ (taqrabu-ha)?

We say: if there are commands, do not exceed the command; and if there are prohibitions, do not draw near to what is forbidden.

We notice that when the Truth, glorified and exalted, forbade Adam and Eve from eating from the forbidden tree, He did not say: "Do not eat from the tree," but He said: ﴿So eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree...﴾ (19) (al-A'raf).

Thus He permitted eating from all the fruits of Paradise, but commanded ﴿and do not approach this tree﴾, because approaching this tree is an incitement to disobedience: its sight may please them, its scent may entice them, and its color may tempt them. But when they do not draw near to all these enticements, they protect themselves from disobedience.

When the Truth, glorified and exalted, spoke about wine, He said:

﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous sacrifices, and divining arrows are an abomination of Satan's work, so avoid it...﴾ (90) (al-Ma'idah)

The Truth did not say "do not drink wine," but commanded avoiding wine, that is: do not approach any place where there is wine,(2) because a person's presence in a place where there is wine may suggest to him consuming it, and among those sitting there may be someone who tries to entice the one who does not drink to take even a sip. Therefore, the Truth, glorified be He, wishes to protect the believing soul from being enticed into disobedience and falling into it.

He, glorified be He, says in the etiquette of i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque): ﴿And do not have intimate relations with them while you are staying in the mosques. These are the limits of Allah...﴾ (187) (al-Baqarah).

What is forbidden here is intimate relations (mubashara); that is, if a wife is present with her husband in the mosque, there is no sin in this matter unless the husband touches her.(3) Then the Truth, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾, and He did not say "so do not do them," but said: ﴿so do not approach them...﴾ (187) (al-Baqarah).

So, what Allah, glorified and exalted, has forbidden, the Muslim is required not to approach it; that is, do not put yourself and the thing Allah forbade in the same place, but you must keep away from the place, because disobedience has enticements, and as long as you are far from the enticements, you protect yourself; but if you approach them, you may fall into them.

As for commands, the Truth, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿so do not transgress them﴾. For example, if a dispute arises between the spouses and all attempts at reconciliation fail, the Truth, glorified be He, says:

﴿And if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon either of them concerning that by which she ransoms herself. These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them...﴾ (229) (al-Baqarah).

So, in commands the Truth says: ﴿so do not transgress them﴾, and in prohibitions He, glorified be He, says: ﴿so do not approach them﴾.

Here, in the verse about which we are reflecting, the Truth, glorified and exalted, warns those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, saying: ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein. That is the great disgrace.﴾ The warning here is expressed through an image: it clarifies to them that what awaits them is not merely physical punishment, but a punishment of disgrace and humiliation. For example, some people endure and bear pain before their enemy so that he will not gloat over them; so the punishment which Allah promises them in the Hereafter is not only painful, but contains disgrace and humiliation. Disgrace is manifested in that the arrogant one in this world comes to the Hereafter and is humiliated before all creation, and it suffices as disgrace that he be in the Fire. And the believers whom he scorned in this world live in the bliss of Paradise, and that is a regret after which there is no regret.

(1) Ibn Kathir gathered all these meanings in his commentary on the verse, saying: "That is, he opposed Him, fought Him, and contradicted Him, and was on one boundary while Allah and His Messenger were on another boundary." See Tafsir Ibn Kathir (2/366).

(2) It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has cursed wine, its drinker, its server, its seller, its buyer, its presser, the one for whom it is pressed, its carrier, and the one to whom it is carried." Related by Ahmad in his Musnad (2/97), Abu Dawud in his Sunan (3674), al-Hakim in his Mustadrak as a witness, and he said: "and they did not narrate it," and al-Tabarani in al-Saghir (1/266).

(3) "The matter agreed upon among the scholars is that the one in seclusion (mu'takif) is forbidden women as long as he is in seclusion in his mosque; and if he goes to his home for a necessity that he cannot avoid, it is not permissible for him to stay there beyond the time needed to finish that necessity, such as relieving himself or eating; nor may he kiss his wife, nor embrace her, nor occupy himself with anything other than his seclusion, nor visit a sick person, but he may inquire about him while passing on his way." See Tafsir Ibn Kathir (1/224).

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, exposes the hypocrites, saying:

﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock on! Indeed, Allah will bring forth what you fear."﴾ (9:64)

Al-hadhar (caution) means preparing oneself to ward off a danger or harm that is expected. For example, one says to someone traveling a road fraught with dangers: "Take your caution as you walk this road." Here the traveler may take a companion with him, or carry a weapon with which to defend himself should he meet a gang of highwaymen. So, caution is preparation to ward off an expected danger or harm.

But if the surah is being sent down from Allah to His Messenger, how can they be wary of and prepare for the descent of this surah?

We say: this is said in mockery of them, because they showed faith and concealed disbelief, and because earlier verses had been revealed exposing what they hid in their souls. They are therefore always fearful that a new verse will be revealed that exposes them before the Muslims.

Allah, glorified and exalted, wants them to know that He knows what is in their souls, and He frightens them that verses will descend that uncover them; they fear that what is in their bellies of disbelief, which they conceal, will come out. The unseen (al-ghayb), as we know, is veiled by time and place. The unseen of time is veiled by the past or by the future. If there was an event that has passed and you did not witness it, it is unseen to you unless you learn of it from history books. Likewise, if there is an event that will come in the future, it has not yet occurred, and so it is veiled by the future. As for the veil of place, it is the veil of the present. For example: if we are now in Cairo, we do not know what is happening in Alexandria. Allah, glorified and exalted, has torn away all these veils in the Noble Qur'an. Allah, glorified be He, tore away the veil of the past in many examples which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed of, such as His saying:

﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Moses the command, nor were you among the witnesses.﴾ (28:44)

And He also says:

﴿Nor were you a dweller among the people of Madyan, reciting to them Our verses, but We were sending [the message].﴾ (28:45)

So it is as though Allah, glorified and exalted, revealed to His Messenger from the veils of the past time what no one had known, confirming His saying:

﴿These are among the news of the unseen which We reveal to you; you did not know them, neither you nor your people, before this. So be patient; indeed, the best outcome is for the righteous.﴾ (11:49)

Allah, glorified and exalted, also revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers the veil of the future time, saying:

﴿The foolish among the people will say, "What has turned them away from their qiblah...?"﴾ (2:142)

These foolish ones heard the verse before they questioned the changing of the qiblah(1), yet despite that they questioned the changing of the prayer direction. Also, among the examples of the unveiling of the future, the Truth said:

﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs.﴾ (54:45)

This verse was revealed while the Muslims were suffering severe torment from the disbelievers, so much so that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "What multitude is this?"(2)

When the Battle of Badr took place, ʿUmar said: "You have spoken the truth, O my Lord: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs.﴾"

Likewise, Allah, glorified and exalted, unveiled the veil of the future when He said:

﴿The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but they, after their defeat, will overcome within a few years. To Allah belongs the command before and after. And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.﴾ (30:2–5)

That is, Allah, blessed and exalted, gave the outcome of the battle between the Romans and the Persians many years before it took place, and specified the victorious side, which was the Romans. Likewise, the Almighty informed His Messenger of what happens in the depths of the self and what turns in the breasts of creatures. When the veil of the self is torn away, it is as though He is making clear to every person: your inner secret is exposed before Allah. An example of this is the saying of the Truth:

﴿And they say to themselves, "Why does Allah not punish us for what we say...?"﴾ (58:8)

They said within themselves, and had they not said it, they would have contested what Muhammad (ﷺ) informed them of regarding what they had said within themselves, and declared it a lie. But they did not deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what he conveyed from Allah. This also shows us that the hypocrites were in a state of wariness, and that their assumption was that the Messenger of Allah was truthful.

The example here is the Truth's saying:

﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down about them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock on! Indeed, Allah will bring forth what you fear."﴾ (9:64)

Some of them even mocked, saying: "There is no need for us to speak, lest a Qur'an be revealed about us." So the Truth instructs His Messenger to answer them: ﴿Say, "Mock on! Indeed, Allah will bring forth what you fear."﴾ (9:64)

What you, O hypocrites, fear will be exposed by Allah to His Messenger and to the believers.

1 Al-Zarkashi said: "The sin (sīn) here indicates continuation, because that was revealed only after their saying 'What has turned them away,' so the sīn came to signal continuation, not futurity," see al-Burhan fi ʿUlum al-Qur'an (4/280).
2 Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir, attributing it to Ibn Abi Hatim (4/266), from ʿIkrimah who said: When the verse ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs (45)﴾ was revealed, ʿUmar said: "What multitude will be routed? What multitude is sought?" ʿUmar said: "When the day of Badr came, I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) standing firm in his armor, saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs.﴾ Then I understood its interpretation on that day."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 65:

Then Allah says:

﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say, "We were only engaging in idle talk and play." Say, "Is it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾

And if you, O Messenger of Allah, were to ask them whether they had belittled or disparaged Islam in their gatherings, they would say: "If this has indeed happened, it was merely idle talk and play, the talk of gatherings which has no worth"(1).

Al-khawd (immersion, plunging into something) means that you throw yourself into a matter, like one who wades into water or into mud. The word was applied to every kind of plunging, and then it was restricted to plunging into falsehood. That is to say, the matter was not serious; it was merely amusement and play.

Allah says to His Messenger: ﴿Say, "Is it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ Meaning: if they say to you, "This is mere talk for amusement and play," then play is something with no benefit except killing time. Say: "Is it not that you have nothing but mockery of the verses of Allah, His Messenger, and the rulings of Islam, by which you kill time? So is this matter idle talk and play?"

(1) This is because a man from the hypocrites, at the Battle of Tabuk, said: "I have never seen the like of these reciters of ours; they are the most gluttonous of stomachs, the most lying of tongues, and the most cowardly at the encounter," meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions. Awf ibn Malik said: "You lie, but you are a hypocrite; I will certainly inform the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Awf went to inform him, but found that the Qur'an had already preceded him. That man then came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as he had set off and mounted his she-camel, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we were only engaging in idle talk and play, speaking the talk of travelers to shorten the fatigue of the journey." See: Asbab al-Nuzul (Reasons for Revelation) by al-Wahidi, p. 144.

Then Allah gives them the judgment:

﴿Do not make excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group, because they were criminals.﴾ (9:66)

Had the hypocrites ever possessed faith and then fallen into disbelief? No. But His saying, ﴿you have disbelieved﴾, means: you hypocrites have exposed yourselves, for you used to proclaim faith only, and then the truth made clear that your faith was a matter of the tongue, not a faith of the heart and conscience.

Then the Truthful, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿If We pardon a group among you, We will punish another group, because they were criminals.﴾ Look at the mercy of Allah, and how, may He be exalted, He did not shut the door of repentance before them, after He had uncovered what was in their souls. Here the Truth declares to him that the group that repents sincerely, and that did not take part in this plunging into falsehood, Allah will forgive. As for those who remained upon their hypocrisy and criminality (ijram, "criminality", is cutting off; one says "jarrama al-thamarah," meaning he cut the fruit, and it is called ijram because it cuts off the truth from falsehood), that is, those who cut off their reality from faith by their hearts and conduct, Allah the Truthful will punish them.

Then the Almighty returns to the legal rulings (al-ahkam al-taklifiyya). Ordinarily, the rulings of God are all phrased in the masculine, and there are only a few verses in which the feminine is addressed explicitly, such as His saying:

﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule another people; perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule other women; perhaps they may be better than them...﴾ (49:11) (al-Hujurat).

And His saying:

﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female...﴾ (97) (al-Nahl).

As for the remaining rulings, they are directed at the masculine, and females are included in them, because the feminine is subsumed under the masculine in address. However, it was necessary here to mention the hypocritical men and the hypocritical women separately, each on its own, because men have their gatherings and women have their gatherings, and each of them has deeds and speech that differ from the other. Therefore it was necessary to state the hypocritical women explicitly.

As for the saying of the Truth, the Almighty: ﴿They are of one another﴾, meaning: none of the hypocrites, men or women, is distinguished from the other in baseness, ugliness and disgrace. God specifies their traits in His saying: ﴿They enjoin what is wrong and forbid what is right, and they withhold their hands﴾. So if people do something good, they forbid them from it; rather, they encourage them to do wrong, and they do not spend in the way of God when they are asked to spend.

Then the Truth, the Almighty says: ﴿They forgot God, so He forgot them﴾. Does the Almighty forget by nature? No. What is meant is that they neglected God's requirements and obligations, so God neglected them, meaning He abandoned them. Whoever distances himself from God, God increases him in distance, in confirmation of His saying: ﴿In their hearts is a disease, so God increased them in disease...﴾ (2:10) (al-Baqara).

Then the Almighty gives the judgment: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾. The word "munafiq" (hypocrite), as we know, is derived from "nafaqa' al-yarbu'" (the escape-hole of the jerboa), an animal resembling a mouse that lives in the desert and digs for itself a tunnel in the ground with two openings. If a hunter lies in wait at one of them, it exits through the other. Thus you see that the hypocrite has two faces. And "fusuq" (defiant disobedience) means going out of the path of obedience, and it is derived from "fasaqat al-rutab," meaning the peel separated from the fruit. The peel, as we know, is created to protect the fruit, so when it separates from it, the fruit is spoiled. And when a person commits fusuq, he goes out of obedience to God.

Then Allah brings about what He has prepared for the hypocrites, saying:

﴿Allah has promised the hypocrites, men and women, and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, to abide therein. It is sufficient for them. Allah has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾ (9:68)

Promise (wa'd) is used for good, and warning (wa'id) for evil. It is said: "awada" (he threatened) regarding evil. Sometimes the word "wa'ada" is used instead of "awada", so that the listener, upon hearing it, expects good; but when the punishment comes, it is all the more painful to the soul. This is a form of mockery toward the hypocrites and the disbelievers, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass that scalds the faces...﴾ (18:29) (al-Kahf).

It is as if Allah gave them a promise that if they call for relief, relief will come to them; then He turns it against them and makes it boiling water that scalds their faces—we seek refuge in Allah. We also note that the Truthful, glorified is He, has placed the hypocrites before the disbelievers, and this is confirmed by the saying of the Truthful, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire, and you will not find for them a helper﴾ (4:145).

Here the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrites, men and women, and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, to abide therein. It is sufficient for them. Allah has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾

Thus we see that the hypocrites' place is the lowest depth of the Fire, and the disbelievers' place is the higher depth. A questioner may ask: how is that so?

We say: the disbeliever, by his disbelief, has given us immunity; since he declares his disbelief, we always take our precaution against him, so he does not inflict limited harm upon us. As for the hypocrite, he has feigned faith, so we granted him security, and he can inflict upon us dreadful evil, because by virtue of the safety he has obtained from us, he knows our secrets and our points of weakness, and his stab may be fatal.

The hidden enemy—as we know—is worse than the apparent enemy, because we are on guard against the apparent enemy, but we do not take precaution against the hidden enemy; he knows what is in my soul, knows all my movements, and can betray me at any time without my being aware of that betrayal.

Therefore, if a people wish to plot against Islam without embracing it, their plot fails, because they, in their disbelief, will find immunity among the Muslims from listening to them. But if they resort to trickery and enter Islam from within the Muslims themselves, they recruit a number of weak in faith to attack this religion, and the stabs of these Muslims by name are the deadly and the effective ones.

Here we note that the saying of the Truthful, glorified is He: ﴿the fire of Hell, to abide therein﴾, and the Truthful did not mention abiding in the Fire with the word "forever" except three times only in the Noble Qur'an. In His saying: ﴿except the path of Hell, to abide therein forever; and that is ever easy for Allah﴾ (4:169) (al-Nisa').

And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever; they will find no protector or helper﴾ (33:64–65) (al-Ahzab).

And the saying of the Majestic, whose majesty is great: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, indeed, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ (72:23) (al-Jinn).

But He mentioned abiding in Paradise forever many times(1).

We say: Paradise is the glad tidings of bliss for the believers. The Truthful, glorified is He, wishes to reassure His creation with the bliss awaiting them; but as for the Fire, it is a place of punishment, and the mercy of Allah—He being the Creator, Merciful to His servants—refuses to mention abiding in the Fire followed by the word "forever" except in three verses, lest the disbelievers think that by His saying ﴿abiding therein﴾ without mention of eternity, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, means a temporary abiding in the Fire; so He reminds them that it is an everlasting abiding. At the same time, His mercy, glorified and exalted is He, refuses that this be in every verse where the Fire is mentioned, so that the path of repentance and mercy is opened to every disobedient one, perhaps he will repent and return to Allah.

The Truthful says: ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein is groaning and wailing, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the Effector of what He intends. And as for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills—a gift uninterrupted﴾ (11:106–108) (Hud).

Debate arose among the orientalists: how does the Truthful say about the Fire and Paradise "abiding therein forever"? Then in these verses He comes with an exception, saying ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and the exception applies to both the believer and the disbeliever?

We say: those who raise this objection have not understood the Qur'an or its method. Those who will enter the Fire are of two kinds: one kind believed but disobeyed and committed evil deeds, so he is punished in the Fire according to the measure of his evil deeds, then Allah brings him out of the Fire into Paradise because he is a believer; and another kind is a disbeliever or a hypocrite—both enter the Fire, but the first of them, the believer, is punished according to his evil deeds, while the second remains abiding therein because he disbelieved or was a hypocrite.

Thus, the disobedient believer does not abide forever in the Fire, and therefore the Truthful said: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, because he will not remain in the Fire except for the measure of his evil deeds; it is as if his abiding there from the beginning is temporary, and he does not remain abiding therein, for the will of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, overtakes him, and he comes out of the Fire into Paradise.

As for the disbeliever and the hypocrite, they are abiding in the Fire and do not come out of it. So there is one who enters the Fire without his abiding there being eternal, and this is the disobedient believer; and there is one who enters the Fire and abides there forever, and this is the disbeliever or the hypocrite.

As for Paradise, there is one who will enter it abiding forever, that is, from the end of the reckoning without end. This is the believer whose good deeds outweighed his evil deeds, and the Truth admitted him to Paradise. But there is one who will enter Paradise, yet his abiding there is incomplete—this is the disobedient believer, because he will enter the Fire first to be recompensed for his disobediences.

Thus, the abiding of the disobedient believer in the Fire is incomplete, because he will not remain there forever. Likewise he lacks the eternal abiding in Paradise immediately upon the end of the moment of reckoning, because he will not enter it directly after the reckoning, but will first enter the Fire according to the measure of his disobediences. So the saying of the Truthful: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ applies to the disobedient believers who will take their share of punishment first according to their evil deeds, and then afterward enter Paradise(2).
