Likewise, weeping may be artificial, like the mourning woman who sits among the family of the deceased and weeps, and may even put some glycerine drops in her eyes to fake tears. All of this is artificiality. As for genuine laughter and weeping, they are two matters of innate nature which Allah, glorified and exalted, alone possesses.

The saying of the Truth, glorified and exalted, ﴿So let them laugh little and weep much﴾ came after His saying ﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their staying behind, contrary to the Messenger of Allah﴾. That is, they rejoiced when they remained in Madinah while the believers went out to fight in jihad. They sat in the gardens of Madinah, rejoicing in comfort and happiness, laughing, because they believed they had won by not taking part in jihad. But this laughter is for a short period. After it will come weeping and regret for a long, everlasting period, when they enter Jahannam, and Allah forbid.

We notice that the Truth, glorified and exalted, said ﴿So let them laugh little and weep much﴾ and did not say, "They will laugh little and they will weep much." Why?

We say: when an action is attributed to a created being who lives in the world of contingencies, and who has choice in a number of his actions, it is possible that it happens, or it may not happen. But when the Truth, glorified and exalted, says ﴿So let them laugh﴾, that is, He commands laughter, and then He comes to weeping and says ﴿and let them weep﴾, that is, weep, then the command to laugh and weep is a voluntary command from Allah, glorified and exalted, in which obedience is possible and disobedience is possible?

If that is so, will the hypocrites obey a voluntary command of Allah? We say: that is not a voluntary matter, because the Truth, glorified and exalted, alone places in the human soul the reaction of laughter or the reaction of weeping at events. As we have explained, a person cannot produce laughter or weeping by his own will.

When the Truth, glorified and exalted, says ﴿So let them laugh little﴾, its meaning is that the reaction of laughter is a decree of the All-Knowing which must occur. And when the Truth, glorified and exalted, says ﴿and let them weep much﴾, they must weep, because the reaction of weeping has been decreed upon them by Allah. As people say: whoever laughs last laughs much, and likewise whoever weeps last weeps much.

Thus all matters are determined by their conclusion. A person may suffer an event that pleases him, then an hour of misery comes that erases all that joy, and the reverse is also true. If these hypocrites laughed a little in this world, then the lifespan of each of them in this world is short, for even if he lived in this world laughing all his life, how much would he laugh? Forty? Fifty years?

Each of us has a limited term in this world. If you compare the event to the world in its absolute sense, it is little. If you compare it to your lifespan in this world, it is the least of the little. Then comes the Hereafter with its long, endless eternity, and the weeping of the hypocrite there will be long, very long.

Therefore every person must attach to disobedience its punishment, and to obedience its reward, because a person may commit disobedience in order to satisfy the desires of his soul, and at the moment of committing disobedience he does not bring the punishment for it to mind. Had he called the punishment to mind, he would have refrained from disobedience. If a thief, at the moment of his theft, recalled that he might be caught, be tried, and have his hand cut off, and if he were certain of this, he would never steal. But he commits theft because he believes he will escape punishment. No thief plans a theft with the thought that he will be caught; rather, he is certain that he will steal and escape.

For this reason the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: { The fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer, and the thief does not steal while he is a believer. }(٢)

Because at the moment he commits fornication, if he imagined or were certain that he would be cast into the Fire as the price of what he did, he would never proceed to fornication. Likewise the drinker of wine cannot put the cup to his mouth if he imagines the Fire in which he will be tormented. But heedlessness of faith occurs at the moment of committing disobedience, because faith requires that you call the punishment to mind at the moment you proceed to disobedience, and that you know with certainty that everything you do you will be held accountable for in the Hereafter, and there will be a recompense.

So if you rejoice in what faith forbids, you must weep in the Hereafter. If you rejoice, for example, in abandoning prayer or zakat, believing that you have profited in this world, you must regret it, and grief will befall you in the Hereafter. And if you enjoy unlawful wealth, you must be punished with it in the Hereafter. The Truth, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed (29). And when they passed by them, they would exchange winks (30). And when they returned to their people, they returned jesting (31).﴾ (al-Mutaffifin)

Thus Allah gives us several images of the mockery to which the believers are subjected in this world. The first of these images is the laughter of the hypocrites and disbelievers at the believers, such as when one of them says to a believer who performs prayer: "Take us on your wings in the Hereafter." Then comes winking and sneering. Then the hypocrite returns to his family and begins to mock the obedient and says:

"I did such-and-such to a religious man." He mocked him, and he could not respond. He feels pleasure as he tells the story, rejoicing in what he has done. He forgets that he has committed three crimes: the crime of the act, the crime of rejoicing in the act, and the crime of reporting the act. Had he mocked the believer and then regretted it, perhaps his punishment would have been light. But since he rejoiced in it, his punishment is greater. And when he returns to his family, recounting what happened, proud and joyful, his punishment is a third.

Yet they did not stop there; they even accused the believers of misguidance, in confirmation of His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are misguided (32)." But they had not been sent as watchers over them (33).﴾ (al-Mutaffifin)

That is, they added to all of this by accusing the believers of misguidance. This is what they did in this world, and it is perishing, and its lifespan is short. Then, in the Hereafter, Allah, glorified and exalted, brings the counterpart, saying:

﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers (34), upon couches, observing (35). Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do? (36)﴾ (al-Mutaffifin)

Just as the disbelievers laughed at the believers in this world, the believers will laugh at the disbelievers in the Hereafter. The believers will sit on couches in Paradise, looking at the disbelievers as they are tormented in the Fire. That is, Allah repays them in kind, with the difference between their limited abilities and His, glorified be He, which have no limits.

The Truth, glorified and exalted, did not say "they will laugh" as a declarative statement that may or may not happen; rather, He brought it emphatically. His saying here regarding the hypocrites, ﴿So let them laugh﴾, means that laughter must occur, because this statement comes from Allah, glorified and exalted. The saying of the Truth, glorified and exalted, ﴿So let them laugh little and weep much, as recompense for what they used to earn﴾ gives us the reason or cause why their laughter will be little and their weeping will be much: this is the recompense for what they did in this world. They rejoiced at fleeing from jihad and were glad for the comfort in Madinah, so they must meet their recompense for this deed in the Hereafter, just as the believers will be rewarded for going out to jihad in the heat.

Thus the Truth, glorified and exalted, did not wrong them; rather, He gave them the recompense for what they did, as He said: ﴿as recompense for what they used to earn﴾. The word ﴿earn﴾ here has a point that we must explain. It could have been said "as recompense for what they used to do" or "as recompense for what they used to perform." Why did the Truth use ﴿earn﴾ (yaksibun), and what is the difference between it and "yaf'alun" and "ya'malun"?

We know that each bodily organ of a human has a field of action: the ear hears, the eye sees, the hand grasps, the foot walks, the nose smells, and the fingertips touch. Thus each organ has a function. If the function is speech by the tongue, we call it saying (qawl). If it is one of the functions of the other organs apart from the tongue, we call it deed (fi'l). The tongue alone takes saying, and all the organs take deed. Saying and deed together we call action ('amal).

When the Truth, glorified and exalted, says "yaf'alun" (they do), it is in contrast to "yaqulun" (they say), because a person may say with his tongue and not do with his organs. The noble verse clarifies this: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? (2) Greatly hateful is it in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do (3).﴾ (al-Saff). But when saying and deed are united, there is action. Everything that is not consistent logically with the values of the method involves artificiality. Earning (kasb) is an action, and acquisition (iktisab) is the artificial pursuit of earning, because earning is a natural action, while acquisition is artificial earning. Allah, glorified be He, says: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has acquired...﴾ (al-Baqarah: 286). Because acquisition through what is unlawful involves artificiality that exhausts the soul and does not make it harmonious with its organs. A man with his wife at home is at rest in all his organs and fears nothing. But with another man's wife his organs become agitated, so he closes the windows and turns off the lights, and if the doorbell rings, he is struck with panic and terror, because the faculties of his soul are not harmonious with the act.

But if the soul has become accustomed to sin, as one who has become accustomed to crime, then forbidden things no longer agitate it. In this case the process of acquisition turns into earning, the soul becomes accustomed to disobedience and sin, and its recompense before Allah becomes painful and its punishment great.

The Truth, glorified and exalted, says in this verse: ﴿as recompense for what they used to earn (kasabu)﴾, whereas the expected phrasing would have been "as recompense for what they used to acquire (iktasabu)", because this process involves sin and disobedience, so it must involve artificiality. But the Truth, glorified and exalted, draws our attention to the fact that these hypocrites had become accustomed to disobedience and lived in disbelief, so the process became easy for them and required no artificiality on their part.

Consider the Truth's saying: ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as recompense for what they committed, as a deterrent from Allah... (38)﴾ (al-Ma'idah). Stealing is not a natural matter, which is why the thief does it secretly, plans for it, and contrives it. Therefore it would have been logical to say "iktasabu" (they acquired). But Allah willed that we know that stealing has become in the blood of these people, and from how much they committed it, it has become for them an automatic, easy process. The legislation set a threshold for it, which is a quarter dinar, for example.(٣) Whoever steals below this threshold is not subjected to the hadd (the prescribed penalty) of cutting off the hand. Why? Because a quarter dinar at that time was enough for the subsistence of a family of average size for one day. So if anyone steals an amount sufficient for a family's subsistence for one day, it may be said that he did it because his family had nothing to eat. But if he takes more than necessity, he has taken more than he needs, and the theft is complete, and the hadd is applied to him.(٤)

Yet we know that the function of the human intellect is to choose

١ There is a difference between infi'al (reaction) and iftial (artificiality), because infi'al is innate nature and iftial is contrivance. The reaction that appears on a person's face, whether joy, sadness or interest in something, is an innate matter that Allah has created in him in response to external stimuli. Iftial, however, is the fabrication of a reaction, such as affecting joy in a situation that does not call for it..
٢ Agreed upon. Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (2475) and Muslim in his Sahih (57)..
٣ On the authority of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to cut off the hand of a thief for a quarter dinar or more." Narrated by Muslim (1684), Ahmad (6/36), and al-Tirmidhi (1440), who said: "Hasan sahih."..
٤ Theft is of two kinds: one kind that requires ta'zir (discretionary punishment), and one kind that requires hadd (the prescribed punishment). The kind that requires ta'zir is that in which the conditions for applying the hadd are not met, such as stealing fruit from a tree. The kind that requires the hadd is that in which three conditions are met:
1. Taking the property of another that is not less than a quarter dinar.
2. That this property is in a protected place (hirz), such as a treasury, a house, or a mosque.
3. That the theft is committed in the manner of concealment and secrecy. By this, one who plunders, embezzles, or betrays (i.e., the minimum value, nisab) is not considered a thief for whom the hand must be cut off. If the crime of theft is established with all these conditions, the right hand of the thief is cut off at the wrist joint. If he steals a second time, his leg is cut off. For the details of how this hadd is carried out, see Fiqh al-Sunnah by Sheikh Sayyid Sabiq (2/461-476)..

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 83:

The Exalted Almighty comes to show us His judgment in this world upon these hypocrites who rejoiced at staying behind from jihad in the way of Allah, so He says:

﴿So if Allah returns you to a faction of them and they ask your permission to go out, then say: "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me. Indeed, you were satisfied with sitting [at home] the first time, so sit [now] with those who remain behind."﴾

Allah the Exalted explains to His Messenger (ﷺ): when the campaign ends and you return to Madina, there is a ruling you must apply to these hypocrites who stayed behind and rejoiced at not fighting.

As for His saying ﴿fa-idha raja'aka﴾ (then if He returns you), the word "raja'a" (returned) is a verb, and every verb must have a subject (fa'il) and an object (maf'ul). You cannot say, "Muhammad struck," and then stop, because you must state who was struck. Nor can you say, "Muhammad plucked," but rather you must say what he plucked. Thus we need an object upon which the action falls. However, there are verbs that do not need an object, such as when you say, "So-and-so sat." The verb that needs an object is called fi'l muta'addi (transitive verb), and the verb that does not is called fi'l lazim (intransitive verb). So there is a transitive verb and an intransitive verb. Here in this noble verse the Exalted says: ﴿fa-in raja'aka Allah﴾ (then if Allah returns you), where the Exalted is the subject, and the kaf in ﴿raja'aka﴾ is the object. But because it is a pronoun attached to the verb, the object precedes the subject. So: ﴿fa-in raja'aka Allah﴾, "raja'a" is a transitive verb, its subject is the word Allah, and its object is the pronoun referring to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: Allah returns you, O Muhammad.

However, there is a verse in the Qur'an that says: ﴿And when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved...﴾ (150) (al-A'raf). In the verse we are discussing, ﴿fa-in raja'aka Allah﴾, the subject is Allah, whereas in His saying ﴿wa-lamma raja'a Musa﴾ we find that Musa is the subject and there is no object. So "raja'a" can be an intransitive verb (lazim)(1), as when you say, "Muhammad returned from the campaign." It can also be transitive, as in His saying ﴿fa-in raja'aka Allah﴾, meaning: O Muhammad, from the raid. So "raja'a" is used both intransitively and transitively. But in the story of our master Musa (peace be upon him): when his mother cast him into the sea, the family of Pharaoh picked him up, and his sister walked following him; then Allah forbade him the wet-nurses so that he would be returned to his mother to ease her sorrow. The Exalted says:

﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to someone who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve...﴾ (40) (Ta-Ha).

What is the difference between the three verses? And why was the verb "raja'a" used both intransitively and transitively?

We say: in the saying of the Exalted, ﴿wa-lamma raja'a Musa ila qawmihi﴾ (when Musa returned to his people), it was from Musa's own self that the return came, meaning it was a voluntary decision by Musa. As for His saying ﴿fa-raja'naka ila ummik﴾ (so We returned you to your mother), Musa at this stage was a nursing infant who could not return by himself, so Allah had to arrange a way for his return, that is, someone to carry him and bring him back. As for His saying ﴿fa-idha raja'aka Allah ila ta'ifa minhum﴾, it could have been said, "wa-idha raja'a ila ta'ifa minhum" (and when he returns to a group of them), as was said about Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿wa-lamma raja'a Musa﴾. But the Truth used ﴿raja'aka﴾ to indicate that the reins of Muhammad (ﷺ) in doing and abandoning are not in his own hand.

It is as if the Exalted is clarifying: beware of attributing events to the human nature of Muhammad (ﷺ), for when Muhammad goes to a place, it is Allah who sent him there, and if he returns from a place, he does not return except when Allah returns him from there. Likewise, the Hijra of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Madina was by the permission of Allah; before Allah permitted him to emigrate, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by his human nature, could not have emigrated. So the Exalted wants us always to know that the going and returning of Muhammad (ﷺ) from any place is not by the human nature of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but by the will of the Exalted.

But why did the Exalted say ﴿fa-in raja'aka Allah ila ta'ifa minhum﴾ when He could have said "fa-in raja'aka Allah ilayhim" (if Allah returns you to them) or "fa-idha raja'aka Allah ila al-Madina" (when Allah returns you to Madina)? We say: the Exalted here intends to speak about the group in which the violation occurred. There were those who remained in Madina against their will, who had nothing to spend, or whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had no means to carry. Likewise the sick and the elderly who could not fight. These had good Islam, and Allah and His Messenger accepted their excuses. But the Exalted here speaks of the group who stayed behind from jihad while they were able, who refrained from going out, while they possessed wealth, weapons, and all the means of jihad. This is the group that rejoiced at staying behind from fighting. As for the other groups, their eyes overflowed with tears from grief at not participating in jihad.

So the Truth here means the faction of hypocrites who persisted in their hypocrisy. Whoever of them repented before the revelation of this verse, his repentance was accepted, and whoever of them died before the revelation of this verse, his reckoning is with Allah. There remained the faction of hypocrites who rejoiced and laughed when they stayed behind in Madina, and Allah's punishment for them was that their names were wiped from the register of those who strive in the way of Allah, and they were deprived of the great reward of jihad.

The Exalted says: ﴿So if He returns you to a faction of them, and they ask your permission to go out﴾. How did they ask permission at first to stay behind and tricked [the Prophet] into it, and how do they now ask your permission to go out? We say: when they saw the believers returning with the spoils, a grief entered their hearts, because they were people of this world. Then they asked to go out so as to obtain the booty and worldly gains. But the Exalted asked His Messenger (peace be upon him) not to permit them to fight with the Muslims, so He said: ﴿Say: "You will never go out with me, ever"﴾, meaning that your names have been struck from the register of the fighters and the warriors. And why did the Exalted decide not to give them the honor of jihad and the reward of going out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? The Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, you were satisfied with sitting [at home] the first time﴾.

But the Truth also says here: ﴿they ask your permission to go out﴾, and this only happens in campaigns. So what is their position if an attack is made on Madina? The Exalted shows His Messenger (peace be upon him) that He does not accept fighting from them even in this case, so He asked His Messenger (peace be upon him) to inform them of this and say to them: ﴿And you will never fight an enemy with me.﴾ Thus the matter is settled: they are not permitted to go out in campaigns, nor to fight the enemy if they attack Madina, because they have been completely dropped from the register of the fighters, and there is no jihad for them inside Madina or outside it, as long as they have rejoiced at staying behind and refused to take part in jihad while they were able. Therefore the Truth ruled that they remain with those who stay behind.

What is the meaning of khalifin (those who stay behind)? The root is kha', lam, fa', from which come khalf, khilaf, khulouf, and so on. "Khalifin" may mean that they stayed behind from going out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or that they opposed the Messenger by refusing to go out, or that they are khulouf (spoiled). The Prophet (ﷺ) said, in a hadith about fasting: "The odor of the mouth of the fasting person is better with Allah on the Day of Resurrection than the scent of musk."(2)

Khulouf is a change of smell, and change of smell indicates the corruption of a thing, as if they had become corrupt. "Mukhalifin" means corrupt, because they opposed the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it means they stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The punishment of these ones who stayed behind is not limited to having their names struck from the records of the fighters; there is another penalty, shown by the saying of the Exalted:

﴿And do not pray over any of them who dies, ever, nor stand at his grave. Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger and died while they were defiantly disobedient.﴾ (84)

(1) The transitive verb is the one that by itself takes one, two, or three objects without needing a preposition or anything else. The intransitive is the one that does not take an object by itself, but takes it with the help of a preposition. There is a type in which both can apply, such as shakara and nasaha. The verb raja'a mentioned in the verse belongs to this last type.
(2) Agreed upon. Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (1904) and Muslim in his Sahih (163), from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him).

The prayer of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) over a deceased person is a mercy for him and a forgiveness of his sins, because praying over the dead means asking mercy and forgiveness for him, and asking God to join him with the righteous. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said these words and made this supplication, then the supplication of the Messenger of God is answered by God. Thus God, glory be to Him, deprived them of a mercy that a person is in the greatest need of when he passes from the life of this world to the life of the barzakh (1).

The saying of the Truth to His Messenger: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾ means a prohibition against an act whose time has not yet come. And His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Nor stand at his grave﴾ means: do not go to his grave and ask mercy for him. But the Truth, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾, even though the prohibition concerns the future, that is, whoever dies after the revelation of these verses. So why did the Truth not say "yamut" or "yamutu" and use the past tense verb ﴿died﴾? We say: because death is a determined process that is decreed and measured by God. The appointed time of death is written and known to God, and it is not something God decides in the future. In other words, the time of death is not fixed a night or two before it happens; rather, the appointed time has already been set and the matter is settled.

As for the saying of the Truth: ﴿And do not pray over any of them﴾, it indicates that this command is not specific to a particular cause, but is a general ruling. The cause of the ruling is like the verse that was revealed concerning the hypocrite Abdullah ibn Ubayy. When Abdullah ibn Ubayy fell ill with his final illness, his son Abdullah came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and asked him to give him his shirt to shroud his father in, and he gave it to him. Then he asked him to pray over him, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) rose to pray over him and to ask forgiveness for him (2).

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out of courtesy to his son Abdullah ibn Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who had become Muslim and whose Islam was good.

When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood beside Abdullah ibn Ubayy, he said to him: "Your love for the Jews has destroyed you" (3), because Ibn Ubayy used to flatter the Jews and support them, and his hypocrisy in Islam was a flattery of the Jews; he would show disbelief before the Jews and show faith before the Muslims. Here Ibn Ubayy said: "O Messenger of God, I only sent for you so that you would ask forgiveness for me, and I did not send for you so that you would rebuke me."

So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked forgiveness for him, and here the noble verse was revealed:

﴿Whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them — even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, God will not forgive them...﴾ (80) (al-Tawbah).

Abdullah ibn Ubayy had asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to give him his garment so that he could be shrouded in it, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent to his house the upper garment. He (ﷺ) used to wear two garments: one next to his body and one over it. When the upper garment reached Ibn Ubayy, he said: "I want the garment that touched the body of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Look at the leader of the hypocrites, who in his life was filled with arrogance toward the believers; here he is making all these requests at the moment of his death. So what did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) do? He sent him the shirt that had touched his noble body. All of this was to please his son Abdullah ibn Abdullah ibn Ubayy.

Some of the believers did not accept this act and did not feel at ease with it. When Ibn Ubayy died, Abdullah came and asked the Messenger of God to pray over him. When the Prophet was about to pray over him, Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, stood between the Messenger and the qiblah (4). Here the Truth, glory be to Him, settled the matter and the noble verse was revealed: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had wanted to pray over Ibn Ubayy, because he was the Messenger of God, a mercy to the worlds. But Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, stood between him and the qiblah so that he would not pray, and so the Truth revealed His saying: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾. They said: that is among the matters in which the revelation agreed with Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him.

Among the matters in which the revelation agreed with Ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, is the change of the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Sacred House of God. Umar used to hope for it, and he would say to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "O Messenger of God, if only you would take the Station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer" (5).

Among these matters also is his opinion regarding the captives of Badr, that it was obligatory to kill them, while the opinion of Abu Bakr was that the captives should teach the Muslims reading and writing, or that ransom should be taken from them. So the noble verse was revealed: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives until he inflicts a massacre upon the earth. You desire the commodities of this world, but God desires the Hereafter﴾ (67) (al-Anfal).

Some people ask: how does Umar correct the Messenger of God (ﷺ)? We say: because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would not remain forever among his community; therefore he wanted to give them the good example that when he (ﷺ) held a good opinion, revelation would come down to him. Some orientalists say: you always say "Umar did such-and-such", so why do you not say "Muhammad did such-and-such"? We say: when Muhammad acts, he is the Messenger of God; but when someone other than the Messenger acts, it is evidence that the Islamic innate nature may see something that agrees with what God desires.

After the saying of the Truth ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾ was revealed, the ruling became general that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) should not pray over the hypocrites. But whoever among the people wishes to pray, let him pray. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to honor every Muslim by praying over him. When this verse was revealed, he refrained from praying over the hypocrites.

Likewise, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) refrained from praying over a deceased person who was in debt. He would ask the family of the deceased: "Is he in debt?" If they said yes, he would ask: "Did he leave anything to settle it?" If they said no, he would say: "Pray over your companion" (6), and he himself would refrain from praying.

But what was the sin of the one in debt that he should be deprived of the Messenger of God's prayer over him? The answer is found in his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever takes the wealth of people intending to repay it, God will repay it on his behalf; and whoever takes it intending to destroy it, God will destroy him" (7).

So if this indebted deceased had intended to settle his debt, God would have helped him to settle it. But if he left behind what would cover this debt, such as real estate, land, or money in banks, then he is not considered indebted.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says here: ﴿Nor stand at his grave﴾, and we know that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to go to the grave of Hamzah, may God be pleased with him, and stand at the graves of the believers, saying: "Peace be upon you, abode of a believing people" (8). The Truth prevented him from doing this for the graves of the hypocrites (9). God gives us the reason for this when He says: ﴿They disbelieved in God and His Messenger, and they died while they were defiantly disobedient﴾. We have understood how they disbelieved in God and His Messenger, but what about His saying: ﴿and they died while they were defiantly disobedient﴾? Did they die while outside the path? Yes, exactly as we say: "the date fasiqat" (the date has separated from its skin). For the unripe date, in its ripening, becomes red or yellow and its skin clings to it; when it becomes ripe, the skin separates from the date so that you can easily remove it. Likewise, the method of God for the believer must cling to him like the red skin of the unripe date; and if it separates from him, like the skin of the ripe date, he is afflicted with corruption.

But here we ask: is disbelief not a greater rank than fisq (defiant disobedience)? Because we know that there is no sin beyond disbelief. So how does the Truth, glory be to Him, say: ﴿and they died while they were defiantly disobedient﴾ when they disbelieved, and disbelief is the greatest of sins?

We say: disbelief is not having faith in God and His Messenger and not entering Islam, but fisq is not adhering to any values at all. Religion has established in souls, in general, known values that even those who disbelieve follow. For example, when they wanted to build the Ka'bah before Islam, they said: "We want to build it with lawful money, into which no money of prostitution enters" (10). In the past they used to bring prostitutes and set up banners for them, and take from their earnings. Islam had not yet come, but there were values from the methods of heaven that had come before Islam, and Islam came in agreement with some of them.

So the saying of the Truth: ﴿they disbelieved in God and His Messenger﴾ means they were not Muslims, and ﴿and they died while they were defiantly disobedient﴾ means they did not adhere to any values.

1. The life of the barzakh is the life between death and resurrection, as in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 100). And barzakh in the speech of the Arabs means a barrier between two things. Among its uses is the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who released the two seas, one sweet and palatable and one salty and bitter, and placed between them a barrier and prohibiting partition﴾ (al-Furqan: 53).
2. Its takhrij was previously mentioned in the commentary on the verse: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them...﴾ (al-Tawbah: 80).
3. Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir (2/379) as a mursal narration from Qatadah. Ibn Hajar cited it in al-Fath (8/33) and attributed it to Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari from Qatadah. Ibn Hajar said: this is mursal but its narrators are trustworthy, and it is supported by what al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn Abbas with similar wording.
4. Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4671), Ahmad in his Musnad (1/16), al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (3097), and al-Nasa'i (4/67). Al-Tirmidhi said: a hasan sahih gharib hadith.
5. Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4483) from Anas, in which the agreement of revelation with Umar in three matters is mentioned: the change of the qiblah, the veiling of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the admonition of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ).
6. Agreed upon. Narrated by al-Bukhari (2298) and Muslim (1619) from Abu Hurairah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would be brought a man who had died owing a debt, and he would ask: "Did he leave anything to settle it?" If it was reported that he had left enough to pay it, he would pray over him; otherwise he would say to the Muslims: "Pray over your companion."
7. Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (2387), Ahmad in his Musnad (2/361, 417), and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (2411) from Abu Hurairah.
8. Narrated by Muslim (249), Ahmad in his Musnad (2/375), Ibn Majah (4306), and al-Nasa'i (1/94) from Abu Hurairah.
9. Among what is reported regarding the occasion of revelation of His saying: ﴿Nor stand at his grave﴾ (al-Tawbah: 84): when Abdullah ibn Ubayy died, his son came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, you will not go to him, for we have not ceased to be disgraced by this." So the Prophet (ﷺ) came to him and found that he had already been placed in his grave. He said: "Would you not have done so before you put him in?" So he was taken out of his grave, and the Prophet spat on him with his saliva from his head to his feet, and clothed him in his shirt. Narrated by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad (3/371).
10. This is because when the Quraysh wanted to build the Ka'bah, Abu Lahab ibn Amr ibn Makhzum stood and took a stone from the Ka'bah, but it leapt from his hand until it returned to its place. He said: "O assembly of Quraysh, do not enter into its building from anything but good earnings; let no wages of prostitution enter it, nor any interest-based trade, nor the injustice of any person toward other people." See Ibn Hisham's al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (1/194).

Then the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, says:

﴿And do not let their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in the life of this world, and their souls will depart while they are disbelievers.﴾ (9:85). We know that the Truth stated in an earlier verse:

﴿So let not their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in the life of this world, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers.﴾ (9:55) (al-Tawbah). When a Qur'anic text agrees with another text, we say that the specific manner of expression and the requirements of the circumstances differ. Whoever considers the particularities and the requirements of the circumstances will know that this is an establishing (ta'sis) and not a repetition. Two verses may carry one general meaning, yet each verse touches on a particular aspect of the giving. Let us take an example from His saying, the Truth:

﴿And do not kill your children out of poverty. We provide for you and for them...﴾ (6:151) (al-An'am).

And His saying, exalted be He:

﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you...﴾ (17:31) (al-Isra').

Some Orientalists have claimed that there is repetition in the Qur'an. This is incorrect, because they look at the general sense of the verse and do not look at the particular aspect of the provision. The particular aspect of provision in each verse fits the requirement of each situation. In His saying, exalted be He, about the provision of children, they did not pay attention to the beginnings of the two verses but to the endings of the two verses, and that is from their ignorance of the faculty of expression in Arabic eloquence (al-bayan al-'arabi).

We may ask these Orientalists who raise such claims: do you see that one of the two verses is less eloquent than the other? You will find no answer from them, because they do not know the precision of Arabic eloquence. We say to them: if you look at the ending of each verse and its beginning, you will find that the ending of the verse requires its beginning, otherwise the meaning would not be sound. Allah, exalted be He, did not say in the two verses, "And do not kill your children out of poverty," but He said, "out of poverty," and He said, "for fear of poverty." And He did not say in the two verses, "We provide for you and for them," but He said, "We provide for you and for them," and He said, "We provide for them and for you."

So the beginnings of the two verses differ. The first verse: "And do not kill your children out of poverty." Al-Imlaq is poverty, as if poverty already exists. And His saying, exalted be He: "And do not kill your children for fear of poverty," as if poverty does not yet exist, but a person may fear that poverty will come with the arrival of children.

So the first verse addresses people who are actually poor, and the second verse addresses those who are not poor but fear that poverty will come if they are blessed with children. The poor person, as we know, is occupied first with his own provision before he is occupied with the provision of his children. Therefore the Truth, exalted be He, reassures him that his children will not take anything from his provision, so He says: "We provide for you and for them," meaning: be reassured, O poor man, about your provision, for your children will take nothing from it, because the Truth, exalted be He, provides for you first and provides for your children too.

As for the non-poor person who fears that a child will come bringing poverty with him, he may be preoccupied with the thought that the newborn will come and turn his wealth into poverty. The Truth, exalted be He, addresses him with His saying: "We provide for them and for you," meaning: their provision comes from Allah before your provision, so do not fear poverty and kill your children, for the Truth, exalted be He, will provide for them, and poverty will not befall you because of the children. Thus we see that the meanings of the two verses are entirely different, and there is no repetition.

Likewise, in the verse we are discussing, some people say: this verse has appeared in the same surah. We say to them: yes, but this one has a meaning and the other has a different meaning. Where is the difference between the two verses, so that we know that they are not repeated? The first verse says:

﴿So let not their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in the life of this world, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers.﴾ (9:55) (al-Tawbah). The second verse that we are discussing says:

﴿And do not let their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in the world, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers.﴾ (9:85) (al-Tawbah). The first difference we find is at the beginning of the two verses: in the first verse, "So let not...," and in the second, "And let not..."

In the first verse, the saying of the Truth, exalted be He, comes with the fa' (so), and the fa' implies sequence. So this is ordered upon what precedes it, which is His saying, exalted be He:

﴿And nothing prevents their contributions from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they do not come to prayer except while lazy, and they do not spend except while they are unwilling.﴾ (9:54) (al-Tawbah).

It is as if these are the grounds of their disbelief: they do not pray except hypocritically, and they do not spend wealth in the way of Allah except while they dislike that.

The enjoyment of wealth is that you spend it on what you love. If you love food, you buy it, and if you love a garment, you purchase it.(2) In this case you are happy while spending your wealth. But these people spend wealth while they are unwilling.

When the believer spends his wealth in charity or zakat, he does so out of faith that Allah, exalted be He, will give him many times over the reward in this world and the Hereafter.

Thus when the believer spends his wealth in zakat, he is joyful, because he has worked for his worldly life and for his Hereafter.

As for the hypocrite who conceals disbelief in his heart, he does not believe in the Hereafter and does not know the blessing in provision. It is as if he spent his wealth without obtaining anything, that is, in his view the matter is a loss of wealth and nothing else. If a person spends while unwilling, then the wealth he has is humiliation and toil, because he obtained the wealth after labor and hardship, and then he spends it while he does not believe in the Hereafter or in recompense.

The Truth, exalted be He, wants to draw our attention to the fact that His provision to these people is a cause of their misery and humiliation in this world. He makes them gather wealth through labor and toil, and then they spend it without reward, that is, they lose it. One of them goes out to war hypocritically, so he spends on his weapon and his mount,(3) and gets no reward. He raises his children, and then war comes, so they go out hypocritically to fight, and they die without martyrdom if they are hypocrites like their fathers. Thus we find that all the wealth of the hypocrite who displays Islam while he is a disbeliever becomes a source of regret for him.

Therefore, O believer, beware lest their wealth impress you, for it is humiliation and anguish for them in this world, since they spend it hypocritically. If they refrain from spending and from jihad while they display Islam, it is as if they have declared that they are hypocrites. Thus their spending under compulsion is a humiliation for them, and if you do not spend, this is a matter that exposes them. It is as if wealth and children are a punishment for them, and this is a matter that does not call for admiration, but rather calls for pity for them.

And do not think that when you removed them from the register of the warriors and the fighters, after they went out with you and then did not fight an enemy with you, that their wealth is a substitute for going out. Therefore do not be impressed by it, for it is punishment, disgrace, and humiliation for them.

But in the first verse, the Truth, exalted be He, says: "So let not their wealth or their children impress you." Why? Because among them is one who has wealth in which he takes pride, and among them is one who has many children who are his support, and among them is one who has both wealth and children.

Thus they differ in their conditions, and therefore the phrase came: "their wealth or their children," so that the meanings would all be expressed and would include the one who has only wealth, the one who has only children, and the one who has both wealth and children.

As for the second verse that we are discussing:

﴿And do not let their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in the world, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers.﴾

So the Truth, exalted be He, has given them wealth and children for punishment. But someone may say: since the Truth wants to punish them with wealth and children, are wealth and children the cause of punishment? And do actions of Allah have a cause? Do not the Muslims say that the actions of Allah have no cause? We say: they have said something similar in His saying, the Truth:

﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me.﴾ (51:56) (al-Dhariyat). They did not consider that the purpose of creation does not return to Allah, but rather it returns to the created being, because in worship there is benefit and advantage for the created being. So the reason for creation is worship, and this reason does not return to the Creator, and no least benefit returns to Allah. Nothing adds to His dominion, and nothing diminishes it. Or it is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah). The meaning of "lam of consequence" is that you do something and the outcome comes contrary to what you intended, in confirmation of His saying, the Truth:

﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become for them an enemy and a grief...﴾ (28:8) (al-Qasas).

Did the family of Pharaoh pick up Moses so that he would become an enemy and a grief to them? Or did they pick him up so that he would be a delight for the eye?(4) They picked him up so that he would be a protector and a helper for them, and yet it was at his hands that their end came. Had Pharaoh known the unseen, he would not have picked up Moses but would have killed him. The Truth willed that He conceal the unseen from him, so that he himself would raise the one who would bring an end to his kingdom, just as you enroll your son in school and he fails, and you spend on him and he graduates. Did you enroll him in school in order that he should fail? Of course not.

Likewise the saying of the Truth, exalted be He: "to punish them." Allah wants us to understand that punishment is not the reason for their gathering of wealth; rather, the reason for that is their love of wealth and enjoyment. Likewise children are not intended to be a cause of their parents' punishment; rather, they want children as a support for themselves. But the Truth, exalted be He, willed to punish them with wealth and children in this world. The hypocrite gathers wealth from lawful and unlawful sources. Then after that, either the wealth leaves him through some calamity that strikes him, or he leaves the wealth through death, or the wealth becomes a punishment for him, so he lives with the fear of God's displeasure, poverty, and the loss of blessing. Likewise, he raises his children and toils in raising them, and then after that either they leave him through death, or they grow up corrupt, and they become a source of punishment for him.

Thus the saying of the Truth, exalted be He: "So let not their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in the life of this world, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers," is a statement from the Truth, exalted be He, to the believers. For these hypocrites, Allah may give them wealth and children, but these are not good for them; rather they are a punishment for them, because by concealing disbelief and displaying faith they impose upon themselves obligations that take a portion of their wealth and children, and then these become a punishment for them, because they have lost everything and gained nothing. There is no reward for them on the death of their sons if they are killed, nor the reward of zakat and charity for what they spend out of show and hypocrisy.

As for the second verse: "And do not let their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in the world, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers," it is a judgment on those whom Allah gives the blessings of this world while they disbelieve in Him, and this blessing becomes a punishment for them. They live in fear of losing wealth or losing a child, and therefore they suffer punishment. Out of their fear of death and of leaving the blessings behind, they are tormented. They do not want to die, because they do not believe in the Hereafter, and wealth and children become a source of regret for them. For the believer, if a child dies, he knows that the loss of the child fills a gap against the fire and leads him to the mercy of Allah, and he has a reward for that. If the child was young, it is a treasure for him in the Hereafter, and if the child was grown, he remembers the saying of the Truth:

﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith, We will join their descendants with them...﴾ (52:21) (al-Tur). In this there is consolation for the loss of a child. But the hypocrite lives in fear and regret, and in this is punishment. He, exalted be He, draws our attention to the fact that the wealth of the disbeliever is always a source of regret for him, and He says:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert from the way of Allah. They will spend it, and then it will become for them a source of regret, and then they will be overcome. And those who disbelieve will be gathered into Hell.﴾ (8:36) (al-Anfal). That is: Allah, exalted be He, punishes the one who spends for the purpose of obstructing His religion by letting him spend, and then He grants victory to His religion, so that this becomes a regret in his soul when he sees the wealth he spent has produced the opposite result, namely the victory and spread of the religion.

And the saying of the Truth, exalted be He: "and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers." This is the greatest regret. When the disbeliever dies and finds no provision for himself in the Hereafter except the fire, because he died without certainty of Paradise and without certainty that he had sent forward anything, he is cast into the fire, regretful over what he left behind in the world.

(1) Zahaqat nafsuh: it departed and he died. Zahaqa al-batil: it vanished and became null, so it is zahiq and zahuq. Allah said, "and their souls depart," meaning: they go out, so they die.

(2) Ibta'a: bought, purchased.

(3) Al-rahilah: every camel capable of the hardships of travel or of jihad.

(4) Qurrat 'ayn: a source of joy, delight, and happiness of heart.

Then the Almighty gives us another picture of the hypocrites in His saying:

﴿When a surah is revealed, saying, "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," those of wealth among them ask your leave and say, "Leave us to be with those who sit at home."﴾ (9:86)

Thus Allah willed to expose the hypocrites, those who had grown accustomed to enjoying the very rights of the believers merely by declaring Islam, while their hearts concealed disbelief and plotting against the Muslims. His saying, ﴿When a surah is revealed, saying, "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger"﴾, is an address to the hypocrites that exposes the falsity of their faith. Therefore He says, ﴿Believe﴾, meaning: make your hearts sincere with your tongues, for Allah wants faith of the heart and the tongue, so that conduct accords with belief. His saying, ﴿and strive alongside His Messenger﴾, means: march forth for jihad with the Messenger of Allah. This is the practical expression of faith. Do not rejoice at your staying behind from fighting in the cause of Allah; it is a great honour with a great reward. Refraining from jihad is a forfeiture of a great good, for Allah gives abundant reward to whoever strives in genuine jihad.

And the Almighty says: ﴿those of wealth among them ask your leave﴾. The verb "ista'dhana" (ask leave) is of the form "istaf'ala", which comes for seeking, as when you say "istafhama" meaning he sought to be understood, and "ista'lama" meaning he sought to know. So His saying, ﴿ask your leave﴾, means they sought permission. Because they feign faith while concealing disbelief, you find them, at the moment of the call to jihad, not standing with the believers at all, though it was incumbent upon them to be among the fighters, and to find in that an opportunity to declare their repentance and return to the truth, so that their jihad would atone for the hypocrisy that preceded it. But they did not do this; rather they asked permission to remain seated.

And who was it that asked permission?

They are "ulu al-tawl" (those of wealth/ability). "Ulu" means possessors of strength and capability. "Al-tawl" is from "taala al-shay'", meaning to try to reach something; if your hand does not reach it, one says the thing is "beyond your reach" (lam tatulhu), meaning it was not within the grasp of your hand.

So ﴿ulu al-tawl﴾ means those who possess the means of jihad: soundness of body free from illness, the presence of strength, not suffering the weakness of old age, and having reached manhood, not being a small child, for an elderly man is weak and cannot fight, and likewise a small child does not possess the endurance for war. Also, there is the sick person whose illness may hinder him from movement.

Thus, ulu al-tawl are those who possess every requirement of war, bodily strength and arms, who have not reached the age of decrepitude, and who are neither small children nor sick.

So when a verse enjoining jihad is revealed, those who seek your leave are not people with excuses, for they are exempted; rather the request for leave comes from the hypocrites who possess all the conditions for fighting, and they ask to remain seated and not go out to fight. They say what Allah informs us of: ﴿and say, "Leave us to be with those who sit at home."﴾ The opposite of "qa'id" (one who sits) is "qa'im" (one who stands). Standing, as we know, is the prelude to movement: when a person wants to walk, he first rises from his place, then begins walking and motion. From standing the word "qawm" (people) is derived, meaning a group standing over its affairs. "Qawm" denotes men, while women do not enter into "qawm", in confirmation of the saying of the Almighty:

﴿O you who believe, let not a people ridicule another people, perhaps they are better than them, nor women ridicule other women, perhaps they are better than them...﴾ (49:11)

So: standing is opposed by sitting, and "qawm" is opposed by women. Sitting is the prelude to stillness: when a person sits, there is a prelude to a period of stillness. The sitting of the hypocrites, their staying behind, and their asking leave to remain with the women, the infirm, the sick and the children, is a belittling of their status.

For this reason the Almighty says of them:

﴿They were content to be with those who stay behind, and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.﴾ (9:87)

Note: "Qawm": a group of men with no women among them; the word qawm is used to include the whole community, men and women, such as "the people of Noah" and "the people of Abraham." Ibn Manzur said in Lisan al-Arab (under the root q-w-m): "Women may sometimes be included in it by way of following, since the people of every prophet are men and women, and qawm is treated as masculine and feminine. The names of collective nouns that have no singular of their own form, when they refer to humans, may be masculine or feminine. Allah says: ﴿And your people denied it﴾ (6:66), using the masculine, and He says: ﴿The people of Noah denied﴾ (26:105), using the feminine."

The word ﴿الخوالف﴾ is not the plural of "خالف" (khālif), but the plural of "خالفة" (khālifa), because "خالف" is not pluralized on the pattern "فواعل" (fawāʿil); it is "خالفة" that takes the pattern "فواعل" (fawāʿil).[1] They had accepted for themselves that the ruling applied to women should apply to them.

That is why they ﴿لا يفقهون﴾ (do not understand): they accepted for themselves a description that does not befit men, and they rejoiced in this description without noticing the humiliation in it, for they flee from fighting just as women flee. The hypocrite, as we know, has two faculties: a verbal faculty and a cardiac faculty. The hypocrite's speech is a declaration of faith, while his heart is filled with disbelief; in this state, his faculties conflict.

Allah, glory be to Him, makes clear to them: We will deal with you in this world according to the outward of your speech, and we will deal with you in the Hereafter according to the inward of your hearts. We will seal these hearts, so no disbelief will come out of them and no faith will enter them. For this reason, the Truthful, glory be to Him, says here: ﴿طبع(٢) على قلوبهم﴾ (He has sealed upon their hearts).

The Truthful, glory be to Him, has said: ﴿ختم(٣) الله على قلوبهم.... ( ٧ )﴾ (Al-Baqarah) ("Allah has sealed their hearts..." [2:7])

And He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿وطبع الله على قلوبهم... ( ٩٣ )﴾ (At-Tawbah) ("And Allah has sealed their hearts..." [9:93])

As long as the disbeliever is pleased with the disbelief of his heart, the Truthful, glory be to Him, seals his heart so that the disbelief within it does not come out, and what is outside it of faith does not enter it, just as you seal a thing with red wax; what is inside remains as it is, and what is outside remains as it is. Allah seals upon his heart, preventing the disbelief within it from coming out, and preventing the faith outside it from entering.

The Truthful, glory be to Him and exalted, says: ﴿فهم لا يفقهون﴾ (so they do not understand). Fiqh is understanding; that is, they do not understand what they have been deprived of, namely the reward and bliss of the Hereafter, because they rejoiced at staying behind from jihad while they thought this was good for them, when in fact it was evil for them.

[1] The pattern "فاعل" as an adjective for a rational male is not pluralized as "فواعل" except in a few examples that the earlier scholars regarded as anomalous exceptions to the rule, such as (فارس، فوارس) – (هالك، هوالك) – (ناكس، نواكس). Contemporary scholars have extended these to more than thirty examples, although they have said that the better course is to adhere to the rule, which is: "The form فاعل is not pluralized as فواعل when it is an adjective for a rational male." See on this question Al-Nahw al-Wafi by ʿAbbas Hasan (4/653–655), and Ibn Manzur's discussion in the entry (فرس) of Lisan al-ʿArab.
[2] The sealing (ṭabʿ) is never undone; the one whose heart is sealed is not receptive and not accepted.
[3] The sealing (khatm) may be undone, may have a known duration, and may be accepted with sincere repentance.

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, wishes to place tranquillity into the hearts of the believers, and asks them not to be distressed, because these people capable of fighting have stayed behind, though they are men of means who possess wealth and children. The Truth removes the effect of that from the hearts of the believers, so He, glorified is He, says:

﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their selves. And those, for them are the good things, and those are the successful.﴾

That is: beware of grieving over these hypocrites for their staying back from striving with you, and do not say: "We have lost in our fighting," because the Truth has no need of them nor of their striving. And glorified is He who says: ﴿And if they disbelieve in it, We have already entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it.﴾ (al-An'am: 89).

And He, glorified is He, says: ﴿But if they are arrogant, then those who are with your Lord glorify Him by night and by day, and they do not tire.﴾ (Fussilat: 38).

Likewise the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Here you are, being called to spend in the way of Allah, but among you are those who are miserly. And whoever is miserly is only miserly against himself. And Allah is the Rich, and you are the poor. And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, then they will not be like you.﴾ (Muhammad: 38).

And also we find His saying, the Truth: ﴿O you who have believed, whoever of you reverts from his religion - Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him...﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 54).

So, the staying back of some people of strength, wealth and standing from striving should not spread fear or grief among the believers, because Allah is with them, and because for them are the good things, that is: for them is everything that is called good.(1) ﴿And those, for them are the good things, and those are the successful.﴾ The mufliḥ (successful one): he is the one who wins, who is saved, who benefits from the fruit of his work. Its root is falaḥa al-ard, meaning he split it (ploughed it), because cultivation requires that the land be ploughed first, and this is the task of the human being so that the crop may come forth. And the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿Have you considered what you plough? Is it you who grow it, or are We the growers?﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 63-64).

When we plough the land we loosen it, and instead of being hard, not admitting air and not penetrated by the rays of the sun, after ploughing it becomes receptive to air; the land acquires the air necessary for the growth of plant roots, because if you put the seed in ploughed land, the crop does not sprout, due to the lack of air from which the roots breathe. But if the land is ploughed, you cause the rays of the sun to penetrate what is beneath the surface, and the stored water evaporates so that air enters in its place, and so the roots of the plant are able to grow. So, every work that leads to a good result we call falaḥ (farming/success). It is derived from a sensory matter that we see every day, which is agriculture (falaḥah).

When the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, wishes to clarify for us a non-physical matter, He presents to us an image from what we see before us, so that we can bring the meaning close to minds, especially in the unseen matters that we do not see. So when He, glorified is He, wishes to bring them closer to our minds, He strikes for us parables from sensory matters. And when a person ploughs the land, splits it and sows seed in it, it gives him abundant produce. Likewise, every work that leads to a good result we call falaḥ.

And when the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, speaks to us, He gives us an example from what we see every day, to bring close to our minds the reward of charity (ṣadaqah) and zakah (2), and His multiplying the reward for us, so He says:

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears; in every ear is a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills...﴾ (al-Baqarah: 261).

If a grain, when you put it in the earth, produces seven hundred grains, and if the earth, which is created by Allah, has given you seven hundred-fold for one thing, how much will the Creator of the earth give? And how much will He multiply?

It is a sensory image of the reward for charity and zakah. And when you cultivate the land, you do not say: "I have diminished my stock by a kayla (3) of wheat or an irdabb (4) of wheat," because you know that you take from what you have a portion of wheat to sow in the land. Rather, do not look at the irdabb you took from the stock you have, but look at what will come to you from this irdabb at harvest time. Likewise zakah: beware of looking at what will decrease from your wealth when you pay zakah, but look at how much Allah will multiply this wealth for you.

The Truth has struck an example with a sensory thing known to all, and from an image of what we see before us, so that we understand what awaits us. If the land - and it is the primary source of sustenance (5) - receives a single grain in which it gives you seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains, and if the land created by Allah compensates you for what you placed in it with seven hundred-fold, how much will the Creator of the land give you?

So, He, glorified is He, is able to multiply for whom He wills without reckoning. Therefore the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, gives good news to the believers in His saying:

﴿And those, for them are the good things, and those are the successful.﴾ This is the reward of the believers in this world, but there is another reward in the Hereafter. In this the Truth, glorified is He, gives us good news in His saying:

﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement.﴾ (89).

1 al-Khayrat: plural of khayr. The meaning: for them are the benefits of both abodes. Although al-Hasan said: "al-khayrat are the beautiful women," and his evidence is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿In them are good, beautiful ones﴾ (al-Rahman: 70). See Tafsir al-Qurtubi (4/3149).
2 al-Sadaqah: what is taken out of wealth as an act of drawing near to Allah, the Exalted: ﴿If you disclose your charities, how excellent they are﴾ (al-Baqarah: 271). Tasaddaqa: gave charity: ﴿And that you give charity is better for you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 280), with one of the two tas' removed. Assaddaqa: gave charity; saddaqahu: believed his speech. And al-Saddaqah (with a shadda): the dowry and mahr of a woman, which does not indicate charity of desire. The root ṣ-d-q in general: truthfulness with Allah, friendship with people, and friendship with the self. As for zakah, it is what is obligatory by a specified measure and threshold (niṣāb).
3 al-Kaylah: a vessel used to measure grains, its present measure being eight qadah. Plural: kaylat.
4 al-Irdabb: a measure containing twenty-four ṣāʿ, or six wibāt. Plural: arādib.
5 al-Iqtiyat: sustenance and provision.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 9, verse 89:

We have already come to know, from earlier passages, the reports about the Gardens and the rivers, and here the Truth clarifies for us the good in which the believers will abide forever.

And why did Allah, glorified and exalted be He, call the reward of the Hereafter ﴿the great triumph﴾?

That is because there is a difference between good and success in this world, and the triumph in the Hereafter. The world is limited by your lifespan, and you enjoy in it according to the extent of your means. Therefore, in it there is a limited success, which is not called a great triumph. As for the Hereafter, its blessing does not leave you, for the blessing is everlasting and you are everlasting. At the same time, this blessing is not by your own capabilities but by the capabilities of your Creator, glorified and exalted be He. It does not require from you any fatigue, work, or striving; rather, a thing comes to you merely as soon as it occurs to your mind. This does not happen except in the Hereafter and in the Garden, and this is the great triumph, because it is everlasting and without end.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 90:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿And those who had excuses among the Bedouins came seeking permission, and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back. Those of them who disbelieved will be afflicted with a painful punishment.﴾

The discussion here concerns the hypocrites who lived around Madinah and were called "al-A'rab" (the Bedouins). The preceding verses spoke of the hypocrites of Madinah, of whom the Truth said: ﴿And among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy...﴾ (al-Tawbah, 101).

Here the discussion turns to the hypocrites who dwelt in the desert regions around Madinah, namely the Bedouins.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿al-mu'adhdhirun﴾. There are two forms, "mu'adhdhirun" and "mu'taadhirun," and al-mu'adhdhirun are the same as al-mu'taadhirun. The plural of al-mu'taadhir is mu'taadhirun, with a fatha above the ta'. But when the fatha is placed above the 'ain, the letter after it is sukun-ed, and when the letter after the 'ain is sukun-ed, this means that there is an ifti'al (the reflexive infix form, i.e. a form that implies deliberate effort).

So al-mu'adhdhirun or al-mu'taadhirun are those who want to hold back from fighting with contrived excuses, and they wanted to sit and remain still and did not move to fight, and they did so without any genuine excuse. It is said: "al-mu'adhdhirun," "al-mu'adhdhir," and "a'dhara," meaning: he removed his excuse, like "a'jama al-kitab," meaning: he removed its obscurity. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who had excuses among the Bedouins came seeking permission, and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back.﴾ They lied to the Messenger in faith itself, because they did not even burden themselves with the mere act of offering an excuse, and they held back; had they been truthful in faith, they would have been ashamed to hold back from fighting, or they would have asked Allah's permission to stay behind.

Then the Truth says: ﴿Those of them who disbelieved will be afflicted with a painful punishment.﴾ Kufr, as we know, is the concealing of faith, and the hypocrites among the Bedouins displayed faith while their hearts were filled with disbelief. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts..."﴾ (al-Hujurat, 14), meaning that they performed the outward matters of Islam while faith had not entered their hearts.

The Truth informs us of the recompense awaiting these Bedouin laggards, saying: ﴿Those of them who disbelieved will be afflicted with a painful punishment.﴾ We have already learned that the punishment in the Qur'an is described either as painful (alim), or as humiliating (muhin), or as great (azim), or as enduring (muqim).

1 Nifaq (hypocrisy): that a person shows something contrary to what he conceals. In early Islam the term "munafiq" was applied to one who displayed Islam and concealed disbelief. Nifaq is the verbal noun of nafaqa. "Maradu 'ala al-nifaq": they became accustomed to it and trained in it, as if it had become a craft for them.
2 Al-mu'adhdhir: one who offers an excuse and has a genuine excuse. Al-mu'taadhir: the same. Al-mu'adhdhir: one who offers an excuse while having no excuse, but fabricates and invents it.

Al-Sha'rawi, Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66), on surah 9, verse 91:

The Truth (al-Haqq), glorified is He, willed to grant a concession (rukhsa) to those who are unable to fight and who have an excuse for remaining behind, so He said:

﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, if they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is no cause (sabil) against the good-doers. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

We know that the weak (da'if) is one who cannot work, not because of sickness but because of his old age, or he is a young child who cannot fight. Likewise, the Truth excuses the sick from fighting; they are those who have been afflicted with a sudden infirmity that makes them unable to fight. Likewise, Allah excused those who find nothing to spend, because due to their extreme poverty they cannot afford a mount to carry them or equipment with which to fight.

And spending (infaq), as we know, is that you are able to provide for yourself in the going, the staying, and the return during the period of war. Every mujahid was required to prepare the requirements of war.

So Allah, glorified is He, lifted blame from those who find nothing to spend, and assigned them another duty that serves the jihad, so He, glorified and exalted, said:

﴿If they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾, meaning: they advise and encourage those who are able to fight, to rouse them to battle, then they stand in aid of the families of the mujahidin (1), and they confront the rumours and lies that the hypocrites spread in Medina, aiming to undermine the morale of the Muslims; so they respond to them to silence the tongues of evil.

Then the Truth says: ﴿There is no cause against the good-doers, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ The sabil is the path, and its meaning is: there is upon them no sin, no reproach, no rebuke, or harshness. None of this finds a way (sabil) against the good-doers. The Truth did not say "there is no path (sabil) against the good-doers" in the sense that the path passes by them without ending in blame to them; for there is a difference between passing by them and reaching them. Passing by is an ordinary matter and not the goal; therefore the Truth clarifies that there is no way to them or to their reproach, because they fulfilled everything that jihad required of them, but they did not go to the battlefield for reasons beyond their will, and they did everything that faith requires.

As for the case where the mujahid has something to spend but does not possess a mount to ride, he should go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and ask him for a mount. If the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) says to him: ﴿I cannot find anything to carry you upon﴾, then this is permission to stay behind. On this the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Nor [is there blame] upon those who came to you to be provided with mounts, and you said, "I cannot find anything to carry you upon"; they turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears of grief that they could not find anything to spend.﴾

1. On the authority of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever equips a warrior in the way of Allah has indeed fought, and whoever takes care of a warrior's family with good has indeed fought." Agreed upon. Narrated by al-Bukhari (2843) and Muslim (1895). Al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: "This reward is attained by everyone who takes care of their family with good, such as meeting their needs, spending on them, or helping them with their affairs."

Therefore, those excused from jihad are: the weak, the sick, and the one who cannot find sustenance and cannot find a mount. He asks the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for one, and God says to him: ﴿I cannot find anything to carry you upon﴾. Whoever is in such a state grieves twice and does not rejoice. The first grief is due to the inability of the Muslims at that time to possess what would meet the expenses of those who fight, or to equip them with means of transport to the battlefield. The second grief is due to his not being present on the battlefield as a participant and a fighter, so there remains for him only a participation of capacity, a jihad that differs from jihad on the battlefield.

It is the jihad of protecting those who stay behind from the rumours of the hypocrites. For the hypocrites will not keep silent about fighting faith; rather, they will spread false reports to the families of the fighters. These are the ones we call in modern terminology the "Fifth Column," those who weaken the resolve and morale of the families of the fighters. Therefore, whoever sits out fighting because of a genuine excuse has another jihad: protecting the home front from the families of the fighters in the face of the war of rumours led by the hypocrites.

Thus we find jihad (ﷺ) to be one of the obligations of Islam, and fighting non-Muslims is for two matters. The first: when non-Muslims oppose the call to faith and stand in the way of the one calling, to silence him from calling to God. The second: that Muslims spread across the earth to make the word of God supreme, not by compulsion, for there is no compulsion in religion, and the sword that was carried in Islam was not carried to impose a religion, but to guarantee the freedom of choice for a person to choose the religion he wishes to adopt, not under compulsion. The liberation of a person's choice arises only by removing the obstacles that impose on him another religion; then the person encounters all religions and freely chooses the religion he approves.

Therefore, Islam was not imposed by the sword. Otherwise, who imposed Islam on those who embraced it earlier, when it was weak and could not protect those who entered it?!

Since jihad is an obligation in this sense, every Muslim is charged to strive: either as an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) if the believers are overpowered by something hateful, or as a collective obligation (fard kifayah), so that if some undertake it, it falls from the rest. God excused from jihad only these groups: the weak due to old age or youth, the sick who have ailments, and those who cannot find what to spend, and they are of two kinds: one who cannot find what to spend on himself, and one who cannot find what to spend on the war, that is, cannot find the implements of fighting or the mount he would ride.

God, glorified be He, lifted the burden from these, and assigned them to a faith-based duty that serves jihad: by being in aid of the families of the mujahidin, and by suppressing the rumour-mongers who seek to undermine the morale of the Muslims, and by answering them and silencing evil tongues. This applies to those who cannot find what to spend on themselves during jihad of food, weapons, and other things (3).

As for the one who has the means to spend but cannot find the vehicle that would carry him to the battlefield, he must go to the ruler to ask for a mount. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the leader of jihad during his lifetime, so if he tells someone, "I have nothing to carry you upon to the place of battle," this is permission to stay behind; but it is not enough to lift the burden from him. Rather, he must express with his conscience his emotion in love of jihad and his grief at not being among those who strive.

For this reason the Truth said: ﴿They turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears of grief that they could not find what to spend﴾. The phrase "their eyes overflow" clarifies what is in the hearts of these believers. Overflowing is always for tears, and tears are water around the eye; grief stirs it so it falls. If grief intensifies and the tears run out and the eye freezes from weeping, another fluid is taken, and it is said: "He wept blood."

God, glorified and exalted be He, wished to show us the intensity of the believers' grief at being deprived of jihad. He did not say, "their tears flowed," nor "they wept blood instead of tears," but He said: ﴿and their eyes overflow﴾, as if the eye has no water and no blood, and nothing remains but for the eye to overflow onto the cheek. That is a display of the intensity of grief in the heart. This mujahid is not to be blamed or faulted, because he did what was within his power and capacity, and expressed through it the burning of his feelings at not being among the people of jihad.
