1 Al-Qurtubi said: "It is narrated that the verse was revealed concerning 'Irbad ibn Sariyah. It was also said: it was revealed concerning 'A'idh ibn 'Amr. It was said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Muqarrin—and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes—and they were seven brothers, all of whom accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ)." There are many other opinions which al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir (4/3153).
2 Jihad becomes an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) when aggression occurs and the land is occupied by the enemy, and it becomes a collective obligation (fard kifayah) when aggression occurs without the land being occupied. Likewise, for spreading the call of God, jihad is by persuasion and proof, because Islam does not know the sword except at aggression and the occurrence of injustice upon Muslims from others.
3 That is, through religious information and curbing false rumours.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 93:

﴿Indeed, the blame is only upon those who ask your permission while they are rich. They are content to be with those who stay behind (al-khawalif), and Allah has sealed over their hearts, so they do not know.﴾ (9:93)

There, the Exalted said: ﴿There is no blame upon the good-doers﴾, those who had their excuses for staying behind from jihad, but who were good-doers in this staying behind. So the Exalted said: ﴿when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾. So, upon whom is the blame?

Here comes the answer of the Truthful, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the blame is only upon those who ask your permission while they are rich﴾. That is: the path of sin, reproach, censure and rebuke leads only to these rich ones who sit back from fighting. We know that "rich" (ghani), when stated without qualification, refers to wealth in money. But when "rich" is used in its specific sense, its meaning is what the text indicates. The one who does not find what he can spend is excused. So whoever finds what he can spend is rich in his food. The weak is excused, so the strong is rich in his strength. The sick is excused, so the healthy is rich in his health. And whoever does not find a means to transport himself to a place is excused, so whoever possesses ease is rich in his ease. On this basis, the word "rich" is not restricted to money alone; rather, look at who meets the conditions of jihad. So blame, rebuke, censure and sin fall upon the rich in these respects, who asked to sit back from jihad.

One might ask: And why do they ask permission while they are rich?

We say: Because they are hypocrites, and their hypocrisy has placed them in a position of humiliation, until the Exalted Truth said of them: ﴿They are content to be with those who stay behind (al-khawalif)﴾. Whoever is content for his position to be with those who stay behind has the characteristic of baseness of soul and lowness of aspiration. They were content to be treated as women are treated, and al-khawalif, as we know, came in stages. They said:

﴿Leave us to be with those who sit back (al-qa'idin)﴾ (9:86).

We said before that qu'ud (sitting) is the opposite of qiyam (standing), and standing is a quality of manhood, because the man is the qawwam (protector and maintainer) of his family. Sitting belongs to women. Al-khawalif is not the plural of khalif, but the plural of khalifa, and it is used only for women. Likewise the word al-qawa'id, as He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the women past child-bearing...﴾ (24:60). That is: they accepted for themselves baseness and meanness, so they abandoned the duties of men and were content to be with women in order to flee from fighting. The poet says:

"I do not know, and I do not think I know, whether the people of Hisn are men or women."

That is: "the people" (qawm) in contrast with "women" (nisa').

Then the Exalted Truth informs us of their punishment, saying: ﴿And Allah has sealed over their hearts, so they do not know﴾.

In the preceding verse He says: ﴿And He has sealed over their hearts, so they do not understand...﴾ (9:87).

What is the difference between the two texts?

When you see a verb of obligation in the passive voice, such as His saying: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you while it is hateful to you...﴾ (2:216).

And His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you...﴾ (2:183).

Someone might say: It should have been said "Allah has prescribed fighting" and "Allah has prescribed fasting", because it has become a binding duty, so it would have been better to say "Allah prescribed", meaning that the one who imposes it is Allah. Although the Exalted Truth is the one who imposes obligations, yet all obligations come in the passive form, such as His saying: ﴿Retaliation has been prescribed for you concerning the murdered: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female...﴾ (2:178).

And His saying: ﴿It has been prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, that he make bequest to parents and relatives...﴾ (2:180).

The reason for this is that Allah, the Exalted, does not impose any faith-based obligations upon a disbeliever. He does not impose any ruling of faith except upon the one who believes and submits to Him. Therefore, when He addresses obligation, He says: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you...﴾ (2:183).

From this we know that He has not prescribed any duty or task upon one who has not believed, and a person enters faith by his own choice. When he enters faith, Allah prescribes upon him. So faith is the entry point to the obligation. Since you have believed, you have become a party to what the Exalted Truth has imposed upon you, for if you had not believed, no obligations would be upon you. Thus you are the one who bound yourself to the command of Allah, because you believed in Him as God, Creator and Worshipped One. And by your faith, Allah imposed upon you, so you are a party to every obligation upon you. Although it is He, the Exalted, who imposed, He loved that you, by your faith, entered the sphere of obligation, so He put the verb in the passive.

When we come to His saying: ﴿He has sealed over their hearts﴾, we find that the Truth draws our attention here to the fact that the hypocrites are the ones who brought this sealing upon their own hearts, because they placed disbelief in their hearts, then began speaking with their tongues about faith, trying to deceive the believers and deceiving Allah. So Allah, the Exalted, wanted to make clear to them: since you have chosen hypocrisy and disbelief in your hearts, We will seal these hearts and close them, so that disbelief does not leave them and faith does not enter them.

So the Exalted, then, is the one who sealed over their hearts, but after they had filled their hearts with disbelief and acted hypocritically. They are the ones who caused this sealing for themselves, after they had begun with disbelief. So the Exalted Truth sealed their hearts with the sickness that was in them. Had they not begun with disbelief, Allah would not have sealed their hearts; for this reason the verb came in the passive, as they share in it.

As for the verse under discussion, the Exalted says: ﴿And Allah has sealed over their hearts, so they do not know﴾. When sealing is attributed to Allah, it is the strongest sealing upon hearts. It comes from Allah, the Exalted, as a final judgment from Allah by which He has decreed against them, so that not even a small measure of hypocrisy leaves their hearts, nor does an atom of disbelief depart from their hearts, nor does an atom of faith seep into their hearts, because they do not know the measure of true faith. A person may not understand something, that is, not comprehend it, yet another may understand it and he may know it from him. Therefore, the negation of understanding (fiqh) does not negate knowledge ('ilm); but when knowledge is negated, it negates understanding from the self and negates understanding from others. That is why, when it is said ﴿they do not understand﴾, it means they do not understand by themselves, but they may learn. So the negation of knowledge is attributed to the sealing of Allah upon their hearts, whereas the negation of understanding is attributed in a general way to the passive verb.

So when the Exalted Truth negated understanding from them by the passive verb, He made clear that in their hypocrisy they do not understand; yet He did not negate the possibility that they might come to know from others in the future. But when the Truth said ﴿so they do not know﴾, He has also negated knowledge from them by their own selves, and likewise negated their capacity to know from others, and this is stronger in effect; thus the sealing upon their hearts is stronger, because they rejected knowledge from themselves and rejected it from others.

That is why we find ﴿do not understand﴾ in one place and ﴿do not know﴾ in another, and each fits the place where it was said.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 94:

Then He, glorified is He, says:

﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say: "Make no excuses; we will not believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news. And Allah will see your deeds, and [so will] His Messenger. Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do."﴾

The meaning of "ya'tadhiru" (makes an excuse) is: he presents an excuse for something that removes him from blame or reproach. It is said: "I'tadhara fulan" (so-and-so made an excuse), meaning he did something that might be considered blameworthy, so he wants to offer an excuse for it.

The Truth says here: ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them﴾, and in an earlier verse, addressing the Prophet ﷺ, He says: ﴿So if Allah returns you to a group of them...﴾ (9:83).

Thus we observe that when He, glorified is He, attributed the return to the Companions and the fighters, He said: ﴿you return﴾, and when He attributed it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, He said: ﴿Allah returns you﴾. This shows us that the reins of Muhammad ﷺ are in the hand of his Lord alone, but the reins of his followers are in their own choice.

Here the Truth says: ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them﴾, and following it comes the clear response to the hypocrites' attempt at excuses: ﴿Say: "Make no excuses."﴾ This is a decisive answer. When a person makes an excuse to you, you may listen to his excuse, but you do not accept it. Merely listening to the excuse means there is a possibility that it will be accepted or rejected. But when you refuse to hear the excuse, it means there is no basis for the apology.

Allah, the Exalted, says to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Say: "Make no excuses; we will not believe you"﴾. It is as if, when the hypocrites approached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers, prepared to make their excuses, before they could speak the excuse, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, made clear to them: "Do not make excuses," and rejected the mere presentation of their excuse. Then he surprised them with the ruling in His saying: ﴿we will not believe you﴾. The root "amana" revolves around several meanings. We say "amana" meaning he believed and accepted as true, as in our saying: "We believed in Allah." It is said "amana bi al-shay'" meaning he affirmed it as true, and "amana bi kadha" meaning he affirmed what was said. The Truth is the one who says: ﴿But Moses was not believed (yu'min)...﴾ (10:83). And the brothers of Joseph said to their father: ﴿You will not believe us even if we were truthful﴾ (12:17), meaning: you will not accept us as truthful. When "amana" takes the preposition "bi," its meaning is belief (i'tiqad), and when it takes "li," its meaning is affirmation (tasdiq), and when it takes neither "bi" nor "li," its meaning is granting security (i'ta' al-aman), as in His saying: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House, who fed them after hunger and made them safe from fear﴾ (106:3-4).

"Amina" and "amina" also come in the sense of entrusting (i'timan), as in the words of Ya'qub, the Truth, the Exalted: ﴿Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted you with his brother before?﴾ (12:64).

So: "amana" when it takes "bi" its meaning is faithful belief; when it takes "li" its meaning is affirmation; and when it takes the object directly, it is granting security, safety and reassurance; and when it takes the object also, the meaning is the ability to discharge trusts, in confirmation of the Truth's saying: ﴿Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you constantly stand over him﴾ (3:75).

In the verse we are discussing, the Truth, the Exalted, says: ﴿Say: "Make no excuses; we will not believe you"﴾, meaning: we will not affirm you as truthful. The hypocrites came to make excuses with false pretexts, but the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused even to hear the excuse, and declared to them: "We will not believe you." Had the hypocrites possessed a grain of intelligence, they would have understood that the Lord of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, had informed him of everything, even what is in their hearts before they uttered it. And had they possessed a grain of discernment, they would have turned back from their hypocrisy and entered into faith. But they did not grasp the lesson, so the Truth, the Exalted, made the matter clear in His saying: ﴿Allah has already informed us of your news﴾. It is as if the matter were not a shrewd deduction, but a revelation from Allah.

Then the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, says: ﴿And Allah will see your deeds, and [so will] His Messenger﴾.

What is the deed that Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger will see, after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had rejected their excuse and informed them that Allah had told him of the lies hidden in their breasts? He, glorified is He, the Knower of all hidden things, has willed not to close before them the door of return to Him. After that, they should have restrained themselves and been certain that the Lord of Muhammad ﷺ does not conceal from Him even their intentions. Since you have come to know the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ in all that he has conveyed to you, it has become incumbent upon you, then, to return and leave the circle of hypocrisy to enter the fold of faith; and let the world then see your deeds having changed from hypocrisy to faith. But if you persist in what you are in, that means you have not benefited from the miraculous event in which Allah informed His Messenger of your lie.

Thus: Allah has opened the door of repentance before you out of His mercy, so seize this opportunity, for He will see your deeds in the future, and upon that vision He will arrange your recompense for what proceeds from you.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾.

Since He, glorified is He, is the Knower of the unseen, He is all the more knowing of the witnessed. The unseen, as we know, is what is absent from you so that you know nothing of it; but if it is absent from you and not absent from others, it is a relative unseen, because there are veils that prevent you from knowing. For example: if something is stolen from you, you do not know the thief, but the thief himself knows, and whoever shares with him knows. And whoever hid the stolen goods knows. And whoever bought the stolen goods knows.

Thus it is unseen to you, but not unseen to others. As for the absolute unseen, it is what is absent from you and from others. Some people resort to charlatans who claim to read thoughts, calling them hypnotists. The hypnotist asks anyone to take out the money in his pocket and count it, then tells him its amount. If you want to expose his tricks: put your hand in your pocket, take out an amount of money whose quantity you do not know yourself, and ask him about this amount, and he will not know. Why? Because you have moved the matter from a relative unseen, which another may know, to an absolute unseen.

Thus the absolute unseen (al-ghayb al-mutlaq) is what is absent from you and from others, and it is also what has no antecedents that lead you to it. For example, if you give your son a geometry exercise to solve, the solution is unseen to him at the moment he reads the problem; then he uses premises and theorems until he arrives at the solution. So there are things that have antecedents leading to results, and these are not unseen. Therefore no one says of the one who discovered electricity, or the one who discovered the splitting of the atom, that they knew the unseen. There were antecedents in the cosmos that led them to uncover some laws that were already present, but we did not know them.

In some exercises you find someone who sets the problem to be solved and places the final result beside it, because he does not aim to know the result, but aims to teach the student how to arrive at the correct method of solution.

Therefore, if you want to solve something in geometry, for example, you must have data that leads you to the solution; such as being asked to prove that two lines are parallel, and in this case each pair of corresponding angles must be equal and each pair of alternate angles must be equal. Thus you have taken premises or data that led you to the result. Likewise with proving that the sides or angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, which is proved by the equality of angles. In such a case, would one say that you were guided to the unseen? Or that you used premises that led you to results?

And when you prove the validity of a direct theorem, you say: "This equals that according to theorem number nine, for example," and "this corresponds to that according to the new theorem." If, in your proofs, you arrive at theorem number one, it is the theorem that has no premises, and it must be self-evident (badihi).

Thus we find that every science in this universe is built upon theories or self-evident premises, and then developed after the discovery of the secrets that Allah has deposited in His universe.(3) As for the Truth, the Exalted, He says of Himself: ﴿the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, meaning that He, glorified is He, knows the absolute unseen, for which there are no antecedents that lead us to it. Therefore we cannot know the absolute unseen, because it is not known to some and unknown to others, and it has no antecedents that lead us to it, for it is the unseen exclusively held by the Truth, mighty and majestic.

And we find the Truth, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen; He does not disclose His unseen to anyone (26) except to a messenger whom He has approved...(27)﴾ (72:26-27).

So He, glorified is He, is the Knower of the absolute unseen, which differs from the unseen that is concealed from some. And the Truth says, concerning the appointed times of disclosing secrets of the concealed unseen: ﴿And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills...﴾ (2:255).

When Allah wills to disclose some secrets of the unseen, He determines the time He wills for that. Everything in the universe has an appointed time of birth, such as electricity, the atom, reaching the moon, and the conquest of space; all these are things with appointed times of birth. Scientists search for them by using premises, but they do not reach the secret of the birth of any discovery except by the permission of Allah, when He draws their attention to that secret, either through scientific research or by its being found by chance.

Thus we find that human beings encompass knowledge of these secrets only after premises and by the permission of Allah.

Since the Truth, glorified is He, is the Knower of the unseen, He is all the more knowing of the witnessed.(4) One might suppose that if he sits in a secluded, hidden place and does what he wishes, Allah will not see him, because he may do what he wants without anyone seeing him. But that is not true, for the Truth, glorified is He, is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, so nothing in this universe is hidden from Him: the unseen is not absent from His knowledge, nor is the witnessed.

Since the Truth has said here: ﴿the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, there must follow it: ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, meaning: He informs you in advance of the recompense for what you will do of good or evil, so that no one may say: "He did not know," or "had I known that my act leads to evil, I would not have done it"; and so that every person may be a witness against himself, because Allah has informed him of the recompense, so the recompense is justice, not injustice.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Sufficient is yourself against you this day as a reckoner﴾ (17:14). So you are the one who passes judgment upon yourself.

1 Al-anba': important news. The Truth said: ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾ (6:67). "Anba'ahu bi al-shay'" and "nabba'ahu bihi": he informed him of it, and related to him its story.

2 Al-ghayb: a verbal noun, and it is used to designate what is absent and hidden. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen (3)﴾ (2:3). Al-ghayb is what is absent from the eyes, such as Paradise, Hell, the angels and the jinn; its plural is ghuyub. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen things (109)﴾ (5:109). This is the absolute unseen.
As for the relative unseen: it is what is absent from you but not absent from others; you may know it when its time of birth arrives.

3 These discoveries that became known through premises, theories and experiments are not called unseen, even though they were absent before one dealt with the premises or experiments. That is due to our ignorance in dealing with knowledge, and because the time of their emergence had not yet come; this is by the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

4 Al-shahada: a decisive report. The witness (al-shahid) is an active participle, and its plural is shuhud (like ra'ik and ruku', i.e., raki' and ruku'); the plural of the plural is shuhud or shuhud, the plural of shahid, like qa'id and qu'ud. Shahada in the sense of what is witnessed by the senses and the inner perceptions, leading to choice, is so with respect to man; as for Allah, glorified is He, He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He is ('Allam al-ghuyub), because He is its Creator, so He is most knowing of its unseen and its apparent aspects.

Then Allah says, after that:

﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may leave them alone. So leave them alone. Indeed, they are impure, and their refuge is Hell, as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾

The word ﴿they will swear﴾ carries a miraculous secret from Allah, because the particle "sīn" (سين, the prefix of future tense) here indicates that they had not yet sworn. That is, the verse was revealed, recited, and heard by the believers and the hypocrites before the hypocrites swore. The verses of the Qur'an are recited and read in prayer, and they do not change or alter until the Day of Resurrection.

Had the hypocrites had the capacity for reflection (tadabbur), they would not have come and sworn. They would have said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, in a Qur'an revealed to him: 'We will indeed come and swear,' yet we will not come and will not swear." But Allah is the One who speaks, the Creator, and the Doer. He willed that discernment be absent from their minds, just as He, glory be to Him, said earlier: ﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from their qiblah...?"﴾ (2:142) (al-Baqarah).

And they did say that after the verse was revealed.

The Exalted says here: ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them﴾. "Inqilāb" (انقلاب, return or turning from one state to another) means the return to Madinah, the abode of peace and security, after the battle. It is as if the departure to fight and the return to Madinah are the two ends. But why will the hypocrites swear by Allah to the believers? The Exalted says: ﴿that you may leave them alone﴾, meaning that you may leave off rebuking, blaming, and reprimanding them, because they did not strive with you.

Allah then says: ﴿So leave them alone﴾, meaning: give them what they seek of avoidance, but it is a different kind of avoidance. Do not blame them, do not rebuke them, and do not hold them to account for sin. Rather, turn away from them with an avoidance of contempt and humiliation, not an avoidance of forgiveness and pardon (1); this is recompense for what they did, because reproach and rebuke are themselves forms of recompense for disobedience, yet they may carry hope for the wrongdoer that he will return to what is right. For example, if your son does not go to school, you rebuke and reprimand him, and you do this because you hope his condition will improve. But if he continues in such a state, you neglect him, and neglect is evidence that you have lost hope of reforming him.

It is the same with the hypocrites. If reproach and humiliation would have made them awaken and return to the fold of faith, that would be evidence that there is hope for reform. But their condition will not be set right, and in this they differ from the believers. A believer, if he commits a sin, deserves reproach and rebuke from his brothers in faith, and this causes him pain. The believer is liable to be overcome by heedlessness and commit a sin, and when the sin occurs, the pain comes to him either from his own soul or through his believing brothers; he then awakens and feels guilt, and this sense of guilt leads him to repentance.

As for these hypocrites, reproach or psychological pain does not benefit them, because they will never return to the fold of faith. Therefore the command came: ﴿So leave them alone﴾, because they do not even deserve blame. Reproach is recompense for a sin from which the one who committed it might desist. But these have no hope in them, and the cause is given by the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, they are impure, and their refuge is Hell, as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ "Rijs" (رجس, impurity) is applied to multiple meanings. His saying ﴿Indeed, they are impure (rijs)﴾ means: they are wickedness in themselves. The scholars say: that is, there is in them corruption and filth. I say: rijs is filth itself, so we do not say "they are filthy" (qadhirūn), because if we said that, the meaning would imply that they are clean in their origin but filthy in their condition, and they are not like that. They are "filth" in their very essence, and nothing purifies them, because whatever emerges from filth becomes like it. They are wickedness that reproach or rebuke cannot cleanse. The term rijs is used here just as the Exalted says: ﴿The polytheists are only impure (najas)...﴾ (9:28) (al-Tawbah).

He did not say "najisūn" (نجسون, impure in condition) but that they themselves are impurity (najas).

Rijs is also applied to a physically filthy thing, such as carrion. The Exalted says: ﴿Say: I do not find within what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who would eat it unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine—for indeed it is impure (rijs)—or that which has been dedicated to other than Allah...﴾ (6:145) (al-An'am).

So carrion is physical filth, and likewise wine, of which the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are but defilement (rijs) from the work of Satan...﴾ (5:90) (al-Ma'idah).

Wine itself is rijs, meaning physical filth, and the Exalted joined to it gambling, idols, and divining arrows, which took the same ruling as wine. Thus we understand that wine is physical rijs, while idols, divining arrows, and gambling are moral rijs.

There is also rijz (رجز), which is applied to the whispering of Satan. The Exalted says: ﴿When He overcame you with drowsiness as a security from Him, and sent down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby and remove from you the defilement (rijz) of Satan...﴾ (8:11) (al-Anfal).

So rijs has related senses; its meaning here is disbelief, and the disbeliever is filth in his very essence, not a person who has been touched by filth.

The Exalted says: ﴿So turn away from them, for they are impure, and their refuge is Hell, as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ "Ma'wā" (مأوى, refuge) is the place that shelters you from an evil that reaches you; one says "āwā ilā kadhā" (he sought refuge in such-and-such), meaning he fled from an evil directed at him. If the refuge to which they turn is Hell, this means that they searched for an outlet and found no outlet except entering Hell, which is, by its nature, an evil destination.

Is that a fabrication against them, or recompense? The Exalted says: ﴿as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ We know that good deeds are described as "kasb" (كسب, earning), and evil deeds are described as "iktasaba" (اكتسب, acquiring), and the Exalted says: ﴿It has what it earned, and it bears what it acquired...﴾ (2:286) (al-Baqarah).

This is because doing the unlawful, which opposes the method of Allah, must be accompanied by contrivance, whereas doing the lawful is a natural matter that does not burden the soul, and the faculties do not struggle over it. But some people who do evil deeds become so accustomed to them that they become easy, and they cost them nothing, and one of them regards the evil deed as gain. It is like a person who recounts his adventures abroad, narrating his travels in Paris and London and the abominations he committed there, without realizing that he is recounting calamities into which he fell by his own choice.

Such a person does evil and is accustomed to it, so it becomes "kasb" for him. This is the opposite of another person upon whom a sin has fallen, who keeps weeping and weeping and weeping, and regrets, and may strike himself whenever he remembers the sin and regrets it (2). The first rejoices in his errors and sins and regards them as gain; they have become for him a habit, a training, and a familiarity.

Here the Exalted says:

﴿They swear to you that you may be pleased with them. But if you are pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiant people.﴾ (9:96)

1 Because Allah, glory be to Him, knows the past, the present, and the future, and what is in them and who is in them.
2 The sense of "ṣafḥ" (صفح, pardoning, overlooking) and forgiveness occurs in the Qur'an in the words of the Chieftain (al-'Azīz) to Yusuf: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this, and ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinners﴾ (12:29), that is: overlook, O Yusuf, what has happened and what the woman accused you of, and do not mention it to anyone.
3 Najis (نجس) means he was soiled by filth or dirt. It is literal in the physical sense and figurative in the moral sense; it is described with the verbal noun for emphasis, so the singular and other forms are alike in it. Allah says: ﴿The polytheists are only impure (najas)﴾ (9:28), and the impurity here is moral, namely disbelief and error.
4 Al-azlām (الأزلام): arrows without feathers, on some of which was written "do," and on others "do not." When a man wanted to travel or to marry, he would come to the keeper of the Ka'bah, who would say: "Bring out an arrow for me." If it came out with "do," he acted; if it was "do not," he did not act.
5 Al-ifti'āt (الإفتئات): fabrication and speaking falsehood.
6 Such people regard the evil deed as gain because it has become a habit for them.
7 It was narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The believer sees his sins as if he were sitting beneath a mountain, fearing that it will fall upon him, while the wicked person sees his sins as a fly that passed over his nose, so he waved it away with his hand." Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (6308), Ahmad in his Musnad (1/383), and al-Tirmidhi (2497). Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath (11/105): "This is the state of the Muslim: he is constantly fearful and watchful, he belittles his good deeds and fears the small evil deed."

Contentment (al-Rida) is the heart's tranquil acceptance of a matter in which there is benefit. When I say, "I am content with such-and-such a thing," the meaning is that the amount of benefit I receive from it suffices me. The stage of being satisfied differs from one person to another: you may be content with a certain benefit, while another person has something better yet is not content. The believer is distinguished by the fact that whatever befalls him not through his own earning must be accepted with contentment, because his Lord is Most Merciful. The mercy may concern a matter the believer does not know at present. For instance, Allah may withhold wealth from him, because if He gave him wealth he might squander it on his children, and wealth would become a means of their deviation(1). So the Truth (al-Haqq), glorified is He, gives him wealth only in proportion to what feeds his children, until his sons pass through the period of adolescence; then our Lord bestows wealth abundantly once the children have reached maturity. The Truth's withholding from the servant at times is itself the very giving, and for this reason it is said: "If you do not get what you want, then want what you get."

Why do the hypocrites swear (oaths)?(2) The answer comes from the Truth: ﴿That you may be pleased with them﴾. What does the contentment of the believers achieve for these hypocrites? Furthermore, does the believer have contentment that follows the contentment of the Messenger of Allah? And does the Messenger of Allah have contentment that follows the contentment of his Lord?

What delights is the contentment of one who possesses benefit. When you are pleased with them after they swear to you, and you are convinced by your human nature, and so you are pleased with them, then your contentment does not benefit them, nor does the Messenger of Allah have contentment beyond the contentment of his Lord. The true contentment here is the contentment of Allah. So beware lest they deceive you with smooth speech and deceptive methods, so that you may be pleased with them. Then the Truth says: ﴿But if you are pleased with them﴾, meaning: if this contentment is realised from you toward them, it is a contentment far from the contentment of Allah and His Messenger, and not from the inner core of the Messenger of Allah, nor from the inner core of the contentment of Allah. Therefore the Truth concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not pleased with the wicked people﴾. If Allah is not pleased, your contentment will not benefit you, and their seeking your contentment is foolishness on their part. Your contentment with them will neither advance nor delay anything, except if it stems from the inner core of the contentment of Allah and His Messenger.

Here there is a point: are they wicked (fasiqun) or disbelievers (kafirun)? We say: the Truth, glorified is He, has made clear to us: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire... (245)﴾ (al-Nisa'). That is, the place of the hypocrite in the Fire is the place of the disbeliever. And how can the hypocrite be a wicked person when the believer may himself be wicked? The believer may commit wickedness by perpetrating one of the major sins, and He, glorified is He, says: ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, as a deterrent from Allah... (2)﴾ (al-Ma'idah). So the believer may steal, and may also commit adultery. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer... (2)﴾ (al-Nur).

Since He, glorified is He, has forbidden the act and prescribed a punishment for it, it is possible for the believer to commit it. But we must distinguish between the fasiq (wicked) and the 'asi (disobedient): whoever commits major sins is a fasiq, and whoever commits minor sins is an 'asi. So how does Allah describe the hypocrites as fasiq?(3) Let us recall what we always say: disbelief is only disbelief in Muhammad and in Islam. Wickedness that comes with disbelief is not the wickedness of committing sin while a person is upon the religion of Islam; rather, it is departure from obedience, even within the religions that any people follow. All religions include a measure of values, and their adherents are held accountable for the values in their religions, yet they also transgress against them.

(1) The Shaykh said: Withholding from Allah is itself giving, and giving may be a calamity.
(2) Al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir (4/3156): "'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy swore that he would not stay behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after that, and asked that he be pleased with him."
(3) Wickedness when it concerns creed is disbelief; every act of it is transgression, i.e., departure from the command of Allah and His purpose. The wickedness of a believer is a temporary fall of the soul for which there is repentance. The Truth says: ﴿Repentance is only incumbent upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance (17)﴾ (al-Nisa').

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says after that: ﴿The Bedouins are the most severe in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

The Truth has already spoken about the hypocrites other than the Bedouins, namely the Arabs (al-'Arab) for whom and for all people the method of Allah was sent down. Here He, glorified is He, speaks about the Bedouins (al-A'rab). So what is the difference between the Arabs and the A'rab?

The Arabs (al-'Arab) are the inhabitants of villages who settle in fixed places, from which or in which they go about their affairs, and to which they return. Its outward sign is fixed houses and a settled way of life. But the A'rab are the inhabitants of the desert (al-badw), who have no settlement and no familiarity with any fixed station or place.

This means that each of them has no general political order governing him in that desert, and each one of them, as it is said, has his voice from his own brain, or from the brain of the tribal chief. As long as they are in this condition, without settlement, which implies companionship that requires gentleness of manner and good dealing, it is said of each one of them "mustawhish" (wild, unsociable), meaning that he has no familiarity with a place, neighbours, or a general law.

As for the one who lives in the village and settles in it, he has neighbours, he has a law that governs him, he has familiarity with the place and familiarity with its people, he cooperates with others, takes on the character of the villagers, and becomes familiar with them and they with him. With familiarity and harmony comes gentleness in dealing. This is the opposite of one who lives in the desert, who is filled with harshness, roughness and ferocity, because his environment has grown upon him and solitude has isolated him.

So when you hear "a'rab" (A'rab), know that they are the inhabitants of the desert, famous for coarseness, because there is no gathering among them that would inspire gentleness of conduct and courtesy of dealing. The word "A'rab" has the singular "A'rabi." There are things where the difference between singular and plural is the ta' marbuta, such as "inab" (grapes) and "inaba" (a grape) being the singular, and the difference between plural and singular may be made by the ya' of nisba, such as "Rum" and the singular "Rumi."

So "A'rab" is then the plural of "A'rabi" and not the plural of "Arab." These people are divided into two kinds: one kind has familiarity with the settled areas, because every settled people may have a desert to which they resort, that is, when the A'rabi goes to the desert he comes down as a guest among them, and they are called "al-ma'arif" (acquaintances). And each person in the desert may have a person in the settled area, so that when he is forced to go to the city or the village he stays with him.

And there is another kind that has neither desert nor settled area.

After the Truth spoke about the Arabs and their hypocrisy, here He speaks about the A'rab, saying:

﴿The Bedouins are the most severe in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

Why are they more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy? Because they are far from the places of knowledge and preaching, and they have harshness and coarseness. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger﴾ means: they are more deserving of not knowing the limits of what Allah has sent down, because recognition of the limits of what Allah has sent down, of commands and prohibitions, and of the lawful and the unlawful, comes through contact with knowledge, and this is not attained by moving from place to place. Rather, settlement is necessary, and knowledge, as we know, is that no matter of the affairs of the universe escapes the scholar; each of us knows according to the measure of his experience and his encounter with life, and according to the measure of his sitting with scholars. But Allah alone knows the knowledge of all.

Knowledge among humans may be put to use or not, and many people have knowledge but do not put it to use, and whoever does not put his knowledge to use, his knowledge becomes a proof against him. As for one who puts his knowledge to use, and places the matter in its place, and the prohibition in its place, and the lawful in its place, and the unlawful in its place, and gives a suitable ruling for the doubtful, he is described as wise, because he has placed everything in its place. So when Allah legislates a command, He, glorified is He, has legislated out of "knowledge" and "wisdom," and since He has legislated, we must not oppose Him, because every legislation that Allah sends down to His Messenger is only to organize the movement of life, since He, glorified is He, is the One who created life and created all creatures. Beware lest you study with your own nose and legislate what angers the Truth, because the corruption of the whole universe has come from those who wanted to make laws for creation, although they did not create them. We say to them: leave the legislating for creation to the One who created creation, for He is the Maker who knows the limits of what He made, and who set down laws to preserve what He created, and He, glorified is He, is the One who can repair it if it suffers damage or corruption.

And among these Bedouins, who are more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger, are another people about whom the Truth says:

﴿And among the Bedouins are those who take what they spend as a loss, and they await misfortunes to befall you. Upon them is the misfortune of evil. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

(1) Among examples of their harshness: Abu Hurayrah said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kissed al-Hasan ibn 'Ali while al-Aqra' ibn Habis al-Tamimi was sitting with him. Al-Aqra' said: "I have ten children and I have never kissed any of them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at him and then said: "Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy." Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (5997) and Muslim in his Sahih also (2318).

(2) Someone may say: How is this, when we cite their poetry and their languages, and the scholars of language such as al-Asma'i and others travelled through the tribes of the A'rab to learn their languages? Abu Yahya al-Ansari says in Fath al-Rahman, p. 172: "Their description with ignorance is only regarding the rulings of the Qur'an, not regarding its words. We do not cite their language in explaining the rulings, but in explaining the meanings of words, because the Qur'an and the Sunnah came in their language."

(3) Among the amusing reports on this from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i: a Bedouin sat with Zayd ibn Sawhan while he was narrating to his companions, and his hand had been injured on the day of Nahawand. The Bedouin said: "By Allah, your speech pleases me, but your hand troubles me." Zayd said: "What troubles you about my hand? It is the left one." The Bedouin said: "By Allah, I do not know whether they cut off the right or the left." Zayd ibn Sawhan wept and said: "Allah and His Messenger have spoken truly: ﴿The Bedouins are the most severe in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger﴾ (al-Tawbah: 97)."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 98:

For example: if a preacher (da'iyah) goes to them and tells them an idea about Islam, then one of these Bedouins outwardly claims that he follows Islam. And if he knows that Islam has zakat, he gives the zakat collector the prescribed portion (nisab) due from him, but he considers what he has paid to be a "maghram," that is, a fine, because he gave the portion while he was unwilling. As long as you are unwilling, you do not believe in its wisdom, and you think that what you have paid has been taken from you. You say, "They have taken my sweat," and "They have taken the product of my effort," and they have given it to someone who has not sweated and has not exerted himself in life, forgetting that this taking is a securing of your own life. For when you become incapable, you will find someone who gives to you. Islam takes from you while you are able, and gives to you when you are unable, and denying this is a security for your life.

You know that things are accidents (a'rad) in the cosmos: strength is an accident, sickness is an accident, health is an accident, and incapacity is an accident. You are subject to change: if you are capable, you may become incapable, and if your body is sound, you are liable to fall ill. So when the Lawgiver reassures you that your brother, when he becomes incapable, is given from what we took from you when you were able, you face life with a strong store of faith and courage. The truth shows you that you do not live alone, but live in a solidary society; if some incapacity befalls you, the capacity of the remainder is your refuge.

Each of these Bedouins used to pay the zakat portion while unwilling, considering it a maghram, and some of them wished that a calamity would befall the Muslims so that they would not take zakat from them. Thus each of them would wait for misfortune to turn against the Muslims (yatarabbasu bikum al-dawa'ir), confirming the saying of the Truth: ﴿ويتربص بكم الدوائر﴾ (And they wait for misfortunes to befall you). That is, he wishes and awaits that a calamity befall the Muslims, so that they will not take from him the zakat, which he considered a maghram.

Why did the Truth say ﴿al-dawa'ir﴾ (the misfortunes)? We know that when a severe affair befalls a person or a people, and it is dreadful and strong, it is said: "The circles (dawa'ir) have turned upon them." That is, the calamity has encompassed them, so that there is no exit for them to come out through. Some of the Bedouins were waiting for the circles to turn against the Muslims, because they were unwilling to pay zakat and thought of it as a fine, and they did not grasp that zakat is recorded in the balance, that it is a purification and growth of wealth, and that it is a bearing of the incapacity of the incapable; if one of them becomes incapable, he will find someone to bear him.

As for the one who waits for the circles to turn against you, and does not perceive the wisdom of taking from him, the circle of evil comes upon him, confirming the saying of the Truth: ﴿عليهم دائرة السوء والله سميع عليم﴾ (Upon them is a circle of evil, and Allah is Hearing and Knowing). Because none of them perceived or became aware of the value of existence in the faith-based society which gives him zakat if he becomes incapable. So if the circle waits for the one who takes from you, and you do not realise that the one who takes from you may take from others for your sake, then the circle will come upon you.

The saying of the Truth ﴿عليهم دائرة السوء﴾ appears like a supplication (du'a'), and who supplicates? It is Allah, and there is a difference between one who supplicates without ability and one who supplicates with ability. Our Lord is the one who says ﴿عليهم دائرة السوء﴾, so the circle of evil is surely coming upon them.

The Truth concludes the verse with ﴿والله سميع عليم﴾ (And Allah is Hearing and Knowing). He hears their words when the zakat collector comes to take the zakat portion, and how they receive him with what they dislike; they may hide their dislike within themselves and not speak, but if they speak, Allah is Hearing, and if they do not speak and conceal the dislike in their hearts, Allah is Knowing. Thus, they are encompassed by Allah's knowledge and hearing.

And among the desert Arabs are those who believe in God and the Last Day, and take what they spend as means of nearness to God and as (a means to) the prayers of the Messenger. Indeed, it is a means of nearness for them. God will admit them into His mercy. Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful.

Then, after that, the Exalted turns to the second category, namely those who have little familiarity (with the Prophet's community). If one is from the desert, he has people from the settled areas, or if he is from the settled areas, he has people from the desert. So He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And among the desert Arabs are those who believe in God and the Last Day, and take what they spend as means of nearness to God and as (a means to) the prayers of the Messenger. Indeed, it is a means of nearness for them. God will admit them into His mercy. Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

Among these are those who believe in God and believe in the Last Day, and what they spend in zakat or charity, they take as a means of nearness (qurba) to God in whom they believe, and as a treasure for them on the Last Day. "Qurbā" means: something that brings one near to God, which he stores up for himself on the Last Day. His words, the Exalted: ﴿and the prayers of the Messenger﴾ mean: they make what they spend a means of nearness to God, and likewise seeking the supplication of the Messenger, because "ṣalāh" (prayer) originally means supplication. Thus, when the charity of the Muslim poor, which he regards as a means of nearness, reaches the Messenger of God ﷺ, he supplicates for him.

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "O God, forgive the family of Abu Awfa, and bless them."

He prayed this when the charity that the family of Abu Awfa gave was brought to him. The supplication of the Messenger is answered, except what God has said, that He, glory be to Him, does not answer it, for a wisdom (1).

One may say: Does the one who presents zakat and charity as a means of nearness not know that He, glory be to Him, does not benefit from this deed? Does he not know that it is a means of nearness to Him personally? We know that he knows, and knows that God rewards him for a matter from which the poor benefit. This points to the fact that every obligation from God returns its benefit to the one obligated, not to the One who obligates. And since the benefit returns to the one obligated, God calls you for the good of your own self and for your own good.

As for the one who regards it as a means of nearness to God, for him is the true word: ﴿Indeed, it is a means of nearness for them. God will admit them into His mercy.﴾ He said this to the desert Arabs who spent as a means of nearness to God and in hope of the supplications of the Messenger ﷺ. So God made clear to them that it is a means of nearness for them, because they are the ones who benefit from it, and that He will admit them into His mercy. The mercy of God is an enduring bliss, lasting and abiding through the permanence of God, which has no limit; whereas Paradise is lasting and eternal through God's keeping it so. Therefore: your entry into the mercy of God is higher than your entry into His Garden.

So when it is said "he entered into mercy," the meaning is that mercy will shade him endlessly. When any desert Arab hears the word of the Truth: ﴿And among the desert Arabs are those who believe in God and the Last Day, and take what they spend as means of nearness to God and as (a means to) the prayers of the Messenger. Indeed, it is a means of nearness for them. God will admit them into His mercy.﴾; when the desert Arab heard this verse, he sat speaking to himself about the divine gifts, restraining the rush of evil thoughts in his soul, and his slips and lapses that he may utter. The desert Arab may say to himself: "I fear that God will not forgive the passing thoughts, the evil deeds and the lapses," and so the verse comes to reassure him, so long as he committed the evil through heedlessness or forgetfulness. He must know that God is Forgiving, Merciful, and there is no need for him to trouble himself with the thought that he will not enter the mercy of God (2).

Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ Perhaps one of those who hear this will think that reward, nearness, and entry into God's mercy are reserved for one who never sinned at all, so the word clarifies to him: Be reassured. If a lapse or heedlessness has occurred from you, know that God is Forgiving, Merciful, and let not your sin spoil your faith that you will enter the mercy of God.

(1) Such as His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them—even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, God will not forgive them﴾ (al-Tawba: 80).

(2) On the authority of Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: God the Exalted says: "I am according to My servant's assumption of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; and if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than theirs; if he draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; if he draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; and if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running." Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (7405) and Muslim (2675).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 9, verse 100:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in excellence—Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement.﴾ (9:100)

The "sābiq" (foremost) is the one who performed the act before others in whatever matter he is engaged in. All of us, praise be to Allah, are believers, and those who believed first and those who believed after them are all believers. But there are people who preceded others to faith, so was their precedence a precedence in time (sabq al-zamān) or a precedence in following (sabq ittibā')? The precedence in time is confined to those who were contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If someone supposes that the intended meaning of "the foremost" is those who preceded us in time, one of us might say: "And what is our fault, since we came after their time?"

Therefore we say: precedence is considered among contemporaries, that is, there were people with them besides them, and they preceded them. Hence the phrase "of the Emigrants" came, and we know that those who emigrated with the Messenger were not all the Muslims of Makkah. The phrase "of the Emigrants and the Helpers" came, and likewise not all the Helpers from the people of Madinah were among the foremost.

The meaning is confined to those who preceded to faith in Makkah and preceded to support in Madinah; these are "the foremost." In Surat al-Waqi'ah the Truth says: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost. Those are the ones brought near, in gardens of bliss﴾ (56:10–12). Then comes after them in rank: ﴿And the companions of the right—what are the companions of the right?﴾ (56:27). Then the Truth specifies these, saying: ﴿A multitude of the earlier ones, and a few of the later ones﴾ (56:13–14). Therefore, when someone says that no one from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who came after the era of Muhammad (ﷺ) can attain the rank of the Companions, because Allah said ﴿and the foremost﴾, it is said to him: No, rather reflect on the rest of His words: ﴿A multitude of the earlier ones and a few of the later ones﴾. This is evidence that some of those who came after the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will attain the lofty rank. Thus the Truth has not precluded that someone from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) until the Hour is established may reach the rank of the Companions.

The Prophet (ﷺ) reassured the people who did not attain his time when he said:

"I wish I had met my brothers." The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Are we not your brothers?" He said: "You are my companions, but my brothers are those who believed in me without having seen me." (1)

This is a true statement from the Chosen One (ﷺ), for among us are those whose wish is limited to performing Hajj and visiting the Noble Grave. He (ﷺ) further describes his beloved ones:

"The deed of one of them is like fifty [of yours]." They said: "From them, O Messenger of Allah, or from us?" He said: "Rather, from you; for you find helpers in good, while they do not find helpers in good."

And this is what actually happens in our time.

But who are the intended foremost in the verse we are discussing?

﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants﴾. We know that the foremost among the Emigrants are the people of Badr, who entered the first battle in Islam. Although they went out from Madinah not to witness war, but to intercept a caravan carrying goods and to return with spoils, nevertheless they entered the battle—not with the caravan that included the merchandise, the guards and the herders (2), but they entered the battle with the army of mobilization (al-nafīr), those who came out and mobilized from Makkah, and they were the nobles of Quraysh (3). Thus the rank of the people of Badr was that they were those who preceded to jihad in the first battle of Islam.

Therefore, when Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah informed the Messenger of Allah's enemies in Makkah, the Prophet (ﷺ) brought him and said: "What prompted you to this?" The Prophet (ﷺ) had wished to conquer Makkah without anyone knowing, so that the Muslims approaching would not fight some believers present in Makkah whom no one had identified. Therefore he (ﷺ) wanted the element of surprise in the conquest, so that the Kufr fierceness would subside. But Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah wrote a letter to some of the people of Quraysh, and Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ), so the Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and those with him: "Go to a place called Rawdat Khakh on the road between Makkah and Madinah; you will find a woman traveling (ẓa'īnah) with a letter from the people of Makkah, which she has hidden in her braid (4)."

When he, may Allah be pleased with him, and those with him went searching for the woman at the place the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had mentioned to them, they found the woman, but she denied that she had a letter, so they threatened her; then she took it out from her braid. It was from Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah to some polytheists of Quraysh. He returned with it to the Prophet (ﷺ), who summoned Hatib and said: "What prompted you to this, O Hatib?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am a stranger (laṣīq) (5) among Quraysh; I have family and property there, and I have no tribal strength there. I wanted to make a favor (yadan) (6) with Quraysh that they would recognize for me, so that they would protect my family and my property. I knew that this would not harm you at all, and that Allah is your helper. What I did benefits me and does not harm you." He said: "You have spoken the truth, you have spoken the truth." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wanted to strike him with his sword, but the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He has witnessed Badr. What would make you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do what you will, for I have forgiven you." (7)

The people of Badr entered the battle without equipment and without preparation, yet they held their souls cheap; it was as if Allah said: You have done what is incumbent upon you, and I have forgiven you what sins you commit.

So the foremost among the Emigrants are the people of Badr and the people of Hudaybiyyah, who are the people of the Pledge of Ridwan, who turned back with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the 'umrah, after which the Prophet (ﷺ) concluded the treaty with the Qurashis.

And the foremost among the Helpers are those who came to the Prophet in Makkah, gave him their support and gave him their protection and covenant; they were twelve at the First Pledge of 'Aqabah and seventy-five at the Second 'Aqabah (8). These are the foremost. Then the Truth added to them: ﴿and those who followed them in excellence﴾, that is, whoever comes after them.

Sayyiduna 'Umar had a pause regarding this verse: he used to recite it thus: "And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers," meaning he conjoined the word "the Helpers" to "the foremost," and it had been revealed as: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾. Sayyiduna 'Umar would continue after "and the Helpers" with "those who followed them in excellence," meaning that he made "those who followed them" a description of the Helpers.

Zayd ibn Thabit came and said to Sayyiduna 'Umar: "We recited it in a different way, O son of al-Khattab." He said: "Why?" He said: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers and those who followed them.﴾

'Umar said: "Send for Ubayy ibn Ka'b," and Ibn Ka'b was an authority in the Qur'an (9). Ubayy said: "So I heard it—as Zayd said—from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while you were selling tanning leaves (qarẓ) in al-Baqi'." That is, Ubayy ibn Ka'b was constantly with the Prophet (ﷺ) while 'Umar was selling tanning leaves. 'Umar laughed and said: "If you had said, you and we both witnessed it..." and 'Umar recited it afterward as it had been revealed (11).

﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers and those who followed them in excellence﴾. Especially since Sayyiduna Ubayy, the expert in the Qur'an, brought more than one proof from outside this verse, for the Truth said:

﴿And [others] among them who have not yet joined them... (62:3)﴾

And His saying in Surat al-Hashr:

﴿And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith... (59:10)﴾, which is likewise conjoined (12).

And here in the verse we are discussing the Truth says:

﴿Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement.﴾ (9:100)

In this statement is reassurance for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). He has not only informed us of the evil group of hypocrites among the Arabs, the hypocrites among the Bedouins, but He has also clarified for us that there are people who conveyed to us the beauty of this faith.

Then the Almighty says:

﴿And among those around you of the Bedouin are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice; then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾ (9:101)

He, glory be to Him, makes clear: Prepare yourselves to accept that among those around you of the Bedouin and among the people of Madinah there are hypocrites. This preparation gives the immunity of vigilance, so that no hypocrite may slip in among the heedless, good-hearted believers, and so that the Truth may alert them: "Be watchful, for you live in a society surrounded by hypocrites." Vaccination against the diseases that afflict nations is a means of confronting the enemy, and we do this physically when we hear of the spread of an epidemic nearby: we take the protective serum against it, even though it is a disease, because it gives us immunity against the illness.

Thus the Truth cultivates immunity, so that the believers cannot be attacked while heedless. He says: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouin are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy﴾. "Marada" (yamrudu) means to train and drill oneself, and the matter remains for him a craft, as if each of them had perfected hypocrisy to a complete degree. All of this is so that immunity may exist within the Islamic community, so that the believer has insight in facing anything; if he sees any conduct that contains hypocrisy, he detects it immediately. Vigilance repels harm from you, and does not prevent good from reaching you.

Suppose someone told you: "This road is dangerous; do not walk along it alone at night." Then another came and said: "It is a safe road, and we walked it and nothing happened." If you took precaution and carried with you a weapon or a companion, you have prepared yourself against evil in order to guard against it. Suppose nothing happens: what have you lost? You will lose nothing. This is a logical, philosophical argument with which he responds to those who cast doubt on the religion of God, such as the astrologers and those who claim philosophy and assert that there is no reckoning, no gathering, and no Last Day. The poet says:

"The astrologer and the physician both claim
that bodies will not be resurrected. I say to you both:
If your words are true, I am not the loser;
but if my words are true, the loser is you both."

That is: if your statement is correct, that there is no resurrection—God forbid—I will lose nothing, for I perform good deeds. And if there is a resurrection—which is true—I will receive my reward in Paradise; thus I have not lost, rather I have gained. But suppose you committed all evil and then the resurrection came: you are the losers. The logical philosophical proposition here is: if I do not gain, I will not lose; and if you do not lose, you will not gain.

In this verse the Almighty says: ﴿Among those around you of the Bedouin are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy...﴾ The phrase ﴿among those around you﴾ indicates that you are besieged, not only by those around you but also by some of those present among you in Madinah, who have trained themselves in hypocrisy until it has become familiar to them.

These verses, as we know, were revealed describing the state of the hypocrites. Hypocrisy involves a conflict between the faculties of the human soul, in that there exists a disbelieving faculty in the heart while a faith-faculty is found on the tongue, so the tongue does not agree with the heart. The believers' words agree with what is in their hearts, while the disbelievers' hearts agree with their tongues.

As for the third category: those who utter faith with their tongues but whose hearts do not believe. These are the hypocrites (munafiqun). The word is derived from "nafiqa'" of the spring (nafiqa' al-yarbu'), a desert animal resembling a mouse, which deceives whoever wants to hunt it. It makes its burrow or lair with several openings; when an animal or a human pursues it, it enters through one opening, so the hunter imagines it will come out from there, and remains waiting for its exit, while the jerboa comes out from another opening. It is as if it has deceived the hunter, who thinks the burrow has only one door, when in fact the burrow has more than one entrance and exit. Hypocrisy in this form has two aspects: a diseased aspect in the hypocrite and a healthy aspect in the hypocrite. For this reason hypocrisy did not arise in Makkah, but arose in Madinah.

It is remarkable that hypocrisy should arise in Madinah, the city that sheltered Islam and from which it spread and extended throughout the world, and did not appear in Makkah, whose leaders and champions fought the call and wanted to obliterate Islam.

Therefore we must take from hypocrisy two aspects. The first is the diseased aspect, where the Truth says: ﴿In their hearts is a disease, so God increased their disease...﴾ (2:10).

The second aspect is the healthy one: Islam had become strong in Madinah, unlike at the beginning of the call in Makkah. Hypocrisy is directed only at the strong, because the hypocrite wants to benefit from the strength of the strong, just as the hypocrite knows he cannot confront the strong or take an openly hostile stance toward them.

Therefore hypocrisy, when it appears, appears in areas of strength, not in areas of weakness: no one flatters a weak man, while people flatter a strong man. Hypocrisy is thus a diseased phenomenon with respect to the hypocrite, and a healthy phenomenon in the hypocrite [i.e., in the sense of revealing his nature].

The Almighty wished to reveal to the believers the matter of the hypocrites who spy upon them, that is, they adopt the way of thieves: they confront only in darkness, try to enter by entrances from which no one sees them, seek out those hidden entrances, and conceal what they show.

Confronting the disbeliever is a clear and open matter: he declares what he conceals and confronts you with hostility. You are confronted with all your strength and all your thinking, because his movements are clear. But the hypocrite who displays faith while disbelief is in his heart spies upon you; you must guard his entrances, for he waits for the moment when he stabs you from behind.

The Truth warns us of the necessity of caution, and that believers should possess discernment, insight, and sound judgment about things, and not be deceived by the outward appearances of things. He revealed to us all aspects of hypocrisy: He revealed the hypocrites of Madinah, among whom there are both hypocrites and non-hypocrites, and the hypocrites among the Bedouin, among whom there are both hypocrites and non-hypocrites, and the Truth taught believers how to recognize hypocrites through the signs that reveal what is in their breasts.

He, glory be to Him, says of the hypocrites: ﴿Had We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have known them by their marks; and you will surely know them by the tone of their speech...﴾ (47:30).

But there is a kind of hypocrisy, a subtle artful hypocrisy, which escapes the perception of the perceptive and his shrewdness. Therefore He makes clear to us: I do not leave you to your own perception to know the hypocrites; rather I know them and you do not know them, because they have excelled in hypocrisy: ﴿You do not know them; We know them.﴾ Despite the perception and shrewdness of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the Truth made clear to him that their matter would be hidden from him, because they had taken precautions with the artistry of hypocrisy so that it would not appear.

The Qur'an expressed this with precision, saying: ﴿Marada ʿala al-nifaq﴾ ("they have become adept at hypocrisy"). The root itself in the word ﴿marada﴾ is from m-r-d: marada, yamrudu, muruwwan, mariduan, and mariduan; this root describes a thing that is smooth and polished, with no protrusions on it. From it comes the "amrad" youth, meaning one on whose skin no hair has yet grown. Thus the whole root indicates steadfastness in something and the absence of anything in it that scratches this steadfastness.

He, glory be to Him, makes clear: Take heed! Among those around you of the Bedouin are hypocrites. His saying ﴿among those around you﴾ suggests that they are surrounded by hypocrisy. And why are they surrounded by hypocrisy? Because the calls to faith do not appear unless corruption has pervaded their environment.

We know that the Truth has placed in the soul things that repel falsehood; and even if falsehood presses upon the soul for a period, the soul becomes alert to it and expels it. [Footnote 2] These are the ones who repent: they commit a sin, then their faithful souls return to them and restrain them. Thus restraint is either intrinsic within the soul, or it comes from society for the soul that does not receive restraint from within itself. Such a soul is "commanding to evil" (ammarah bi-l-su'), and it does not command evil once and then stop; rather it is characterized by it, that is, it has made commanding evil a craft, because the form "fa''al" indicates habitual practice and repeated engagement.

If immunity is within the soul, this is an easy matter that comes from the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah), and society surrounding a person may restrain the soul if it weakens in something. Thus immunity exists in society. But if corruption pervades society as well, then the soul has no intrinsic guardian and society has no deterrent; here heaven must intervene, and the call of the Truth comes with its signs, its clear proofs, and the miracle of the Messenger.

Here those whose souls are commanding to evil take a stance by which they flatter the new emerging power, while their souls remain commanding to evil; thus the phenomenon of hypocrisy appears.

The Almighty says: ﴿Among those around you of the Bedouin are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah﴾, meaning that you are encircled in yourselves and by those around you; hypocrisy is in the very place where you dwell, and also in what surrounds you. What a person most fears is that harm exists both around him and within him; for if harm existed only in the place, one could still manage, but if he is besieged by harm from those around him and from the place in which he lives, where then can he go?

The Almighty wishes to alert the believers that the phenomenon of hypocrisy is widespread: some of it you, O believers, can recognize by knowing the movements and stillnesses of the hypocrites, the tone of their speech and their conduct [Footnote 3]; and some of it is subtle and hidden, which you do not know, but He knows it. Because you are not self-sufficient, and you have a Lord who teaches you what you do not know, be reassured: He will expose them to you. The consequence of this knowledge is that you will see punishments inflicted upon them; thus the true word comes: ﴿We will punish them twice [Footnote 4], then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾

They will therefore be punished twice in this world, and then returned to the punishment of the Hereafter. The first punishment for one who conceals his hypocrisy is the exposure, and therefore the Messenger of God (ﷺ) addressed the people and said: "Stand up, so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite; stand up, so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite; stand up, so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite" [Footnote 5]; or worldly calamities come upon him. One might ask: Are calamities a punishment for the hypocrite? Calamities also befall the believer.

We reply: Calamities come to the believer for his benefit, but they come to the hypocrite for his destruction. When a believer is afflicted, either God expiates a sin through it, or raises him a degree because of it [Footnote 6]. But when calamities befall the hypocrite, they are only a loss, because the hypocrite does not hope for the Hereafter. Therefore it is said:

"Affliction is not the one who suffers what he loves; rather affliction is what deprives one of reward."

If the believer receives calamity with contentment, and knows that He who ordained it is wise, and that nothing befalls him except what contains good even if he does not know it, then he earns reward for patience and recompense for contentment, and thus he exits the circle of severe pain. But the non-believer rebels against destiny, and by his lack of faith he is deprived of reward.

Or the punishment twice may be, apart from the exposure of their hypocrisy, that they try to appear in the appearance of faith and Islam, so one of them spends from his wealth, and wealth is dear to the soul; therefore he pays zakat unwillingly, feeling he has lost money because he does not believe in a god, so his affliction is great. And the hypocrite may send his son to war while knowing he has no reward in it; this is another kind of punishment.

This punishment is confirmed by the Truth's saying: ﴿Let not their wealth and their children impress you; God only wants to punish them thereby in this world...﴾ (9:85).

Or the punishment in this world may be what they see when the soul rattles in the throat, at the moment the spirit reaches the windpipe, and the one dying sees the angels, in confirmation of His saying: ﴿If you could see when those who disbelieved are taken, the angels striking their faces and their backs, [saying]: "Taste the punishment of the burning"﴾ (8:50).

All these forms of punishment are in this world. A person, as we know, faces time in three states: a time that is his life in this world, a time that is the moment of his death, and a time that is his Hereafter. When the believer is afflicted in the first time—the time of his life—the last time, which is his Hereafter, consoles him in his affliction.

[Footnote 1] Because it reveals the nature of his soul: this soul flatters the powerful to secure benefit, and there is no hypocrisy toward the poor or weak, since they are not sources of benefit, so no one flatters them.

[Footnote 2] He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, those who fear God, when an impulse from Satan touches them, remember, and then they are seeing clearly﴾ (7:201), i.e., they become upright and sober from what they were in. Said by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (2/279).

[Footnote 3] From Abu Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him), who said: "Indeed the hypocrites have signs by which they are recognized: their greeting is a curse, their food is plunder, their booty is theft; they do not approach the mosques except briefly, and they do not come to prayer except late, arrogant, not befriending nor being befriended, [they are like] a stick at night and noise by day." Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (2/293) and al-Bazzar (85, Kashf al-Astar). Al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (1/102): "In its chain is ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Qudamah al-Jahhami; Ibn Ma'in and others deemed him trustworthy, while al-Daraqutni and others weakened him."

[Footnote 4] One in this world and the other in the grave, by way of what is punished with in the Hereafter.

[Footnote 5] From Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) addressed us in a sermon; he praised God and extolled Him, then said: "Indeed among you are hypocrites; whoever I name, let him stand. Then he said: Stand, so-and-so; stand, so-and-so; stand, so-and-so, until he had named thirty-six men..." Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (5/273) and al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah (6/286). Al-Haythami said in al-Majma' (1/112): "In it is 'Iyad ibn 'Iyad from his father, and I have not seen anyone who has biographed the two of them."

[Footnote 6] From ʿAʾishah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No thorn or anything beyond it befalls a believer except that God raises him a degree by it or removes a sin from him by it." Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih (2572), Ahmad in his Musnad (6/42), and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (965), who said: a hasan sahih hadith.

God then says:
