Abraham's seeking forgiveness for his father is mentioned in the Qur'an twice: {Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the Day the account is established} (Ibrahim 41), and ﴿And forgive my father; indeed, he is of the misguided﴾ (Ash-Shuʿara 86). But this was before it became clear that his father was an enemy of Allah.
2 ʿIshq here is the highest level of love.
3 Allah has gathered the mention of these astonished people in His saying in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah and ʿĀd and Thamūd, and those after them, whom none knows but Allah? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they put their hands over their mouths and said, "Indeed, we have disbelieved in that with which you were sent, and indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about that to which you invite us." Their messengers said, "Is there doubt about Allah, Creator of the heavens and the earth? He invites you that He may forgive you of your sins and delay you until a specified term." They said, "You are not but human beings like us. You want to avert us from what our fathers used to worship, so bring us a clear authority."﴾ (Ibrahim 9–10).
4 Among the meanings of "awwāh" is also one who supplicates and humbles himself to Allah much, certain of being answered. See Lisan al-ʿArab (root: awwāh).
5 Yusalli: removes your distress.
6 Yajtabīka: chooses you and selects you for prophethood. Ta'wīl al-aḥādīth: is the interpretation of dreams and visions.
7 They mean the brother of Joseph from his mother Rachel, whose name was Benjamin.
8 Al-jubb: the well; and its depth (ghayābah): that is, its bottom, in the lowest part of it.
9 Joseph (peace be upon him) refused to leave prison to meet the king until his innocence of what was attributed to him concerning the wife of the Chief was made clear. Therefore he said to the king's messenger: ﴿Return to your lord and ask him about the case of the women who cut their hands. Indeed, my Lord is Knowing of their plotting﴾ (Yusuf 50). And it was accomplished for him as he wanted. The women said: ﴿Allah forbid! We know of him no evil.﴾ And the wife of the Chief said: ﴿Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed he is of the truthful﴾ (Yusuf 51).
10 Murāwadah: consultation and requesting permission from him gently.
11 That is because they said to their father: ﴿O our father, what more could we desire? This is our merchandise returned to us. We will provide for our family, protect our brother, and gain an extra camel's load﴾ (Yusuf 65). Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (2/484): "That is because Joseph (peace be upon him) used to give a man a camel's load."
12 Al-mīrah: is food that a person procures, that is, brings in.
13 Al-siqāyah: is a silver vessel with which they measured food, and perhaps drank from it. It is also called al-ṣiwāʿ.
14 Al-ʿīr: the caravan; and al-ʿīr is the people with their beasts and loads of food. Allah said: ﴿O caravan, indeed you are thieves﴾ (Yusuf 70), meaning: O people who are departing.
15 Zaʿīm: guarantor.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 115:

﴿And Allah would never leave a people astray after He had guided them until He makes clear to them what they should fear. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

Here, the guidance meant is the guidance of indication (hidayat al-dalalah), until He makes clear to them what they should fear. ﴿And Allah would never leave a people astray﴾ means: Allah would never decree the misguidance of a people until He makes clear to them what they should fear.

Taqwa (God-consciousness, i.e., safeguarding oneself against displeasing Allah) is the adherence to Allah's command and prohibition. So when they comply with the clarification, He guides them with the guidance of assistance (hidayat ma'unah); and when they do not comply, they are misguided. Allah decreed the misguidance of the uncle of Ibrahim, and He decreed his misguidance only after He had explained to him the method of guidance.

Ibrahim explained to his uncle the method of guidance, but he was not guided. For this reason, Allah, glorified and exalted, commanded Ibrahim not to seek forgiveness for him.

And God says next: ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper.﴾ (116)

The root م.ل.ك (m-l-k) gives rise to "mālik," "malik," and "mulk," and from it also "malakūt" (dominion). Al-mulk is what you possess within your own sphere: if there is someone who possesses you and those with you, and possesses others besides you, then that is mulk (dominion). But when the scope of human capability widens, meaning that which falls within his governance and management, it is called malk (kingship). Thus the tribal chief has mulk, the head of a village has mulk, and the ruler of a nation has malk, and it occurs in outward matters... As for malakūt, it is what belongs to God in His creation of hidden secrets.

Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the malakūt of the heavens and the earth...﴾ (75) (al-An'am).

When you see the intensive ending "tā' al-mubālaghah" (the ta' of intensification) in words like "rahbūt" and "azamūt," you realize that it is a great awe.

So then: beware lest you understand that when God forbids you to seek forgiveness for your parents, and if you cut ties with them, that this impairs your existence in life; for they and those who support them are within God's dominion, and as long as God has the dominion of the heavens and the earth, no one or nothing can harm you, and nothing that escapes you can escape from God; and as long as Allah, glorified is He, exists, everything is easy for whoever takes its causes with faith in Him.

And the True One, glorified is He, makes clear to us that He alone holds the dominion. So He said: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty from whom You will, You endow with honour whom You will and You humble whom You will; in Your hand is all good...﴾ (26) (Al 'Imran).

In this noble statement there are four contrasting things: ﴿You give sovereignty﴾ and ﴿You take sovereignty﴾. Giving sovereignty is good by people's customs, and taking it away is bad by people's customs; honouring people is good, and humbling them is bad. God did not say "in His hand: the good and the evil," but He said in each case: ﴿in Your hand is all good﴾.

So then: when God gives a person sovereignty, we say: this is good, and you must use it for good. When God takes sovereignty from him, we say to him: you have transgressed, and God has lightened from you the tyranny of oppression; so God has taken it from you, and this is good for you. If God honours you, He may test you truly; and if God humbles them, the purpose is that they not transgress or act arrogantly. So then, all of it is good.

﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty from whom You will, You endow with honour whom You will and You humble whom You will; in Your hand is all good...﴾ (26) (Al 'Imran).

When you find a "biting" rule (mulk ʿaḍūḍ)(1), beware of thinking that this biting rule took its dominion against the will of God. No, it is a gift from God. And if the subject were mindful of God in all his affairs, the heart of his master would be softened toward him. That is why He tells us in the sacred hadith: "I am God, King of kings; the hearts of kings and their forelocks are in My hand. If the servants obey Me, I make their rulers a mercy upon them, and if they disobey Me, I make them a punishment upon them. So do not occupy yourselves with cursing the kings, but obey Me and I will incline them toward you."

Since this is the case, we must know that every occurrence has a wisdom(2) in existence. If you see someone who has taken power while he is unjust(3), know that God brought him so as to train the subjects through him, for He, exalted is He, does not train the wicked through the good, because the good do not know how to discipline(4); their hearts are filled with mercy. That is why He teaches us, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others...﴾ (129) (al-An'am). The good does not enter the battle but watches the conflict from afar, and everything proceeds by God's knowledge, for He, exalted is He, is the Owner of the heavens and the earth, and He is the One who gives life and causes death. So beware of being tempted in other than your Creator, ever; for creation, however great its power and tyranny, cannot protect itself from the changes of God in His dominion. Therefore the believer should take from God a protector and a helper.

After He said, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, He brings us the matter in which the effect of power appears, and in which no other shares with Him: ﴿He gives life and causes death.﴾ Some scholars said regarding His saying ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ that He, glorified is He, "gives life to the inanimate" and "causes death to the animate," because they thought life is sensation and movement that we see before us: motion, speech, going and coming; and they forgot that life is what God has deposited in every atom of the universe, by which it performs its task. In a grain of sand there is life, the mountain has life, and everything has life, by the text of the Qur'an where He says:

﴿That whoever perishes might perish upon clear evidence, and whoever lives might live upon clear evidence...﴾ (42) (al-Anfal).

So then: everything, before it becomes perished, was alive. Thus we know that life is not the apparent sensation and movement; and after the immense scientific advance in powerful microscopes, the movement and sensation of creatures we did not see were revealed to us. If man has, through the instruments he invented, come to perceive many kinds of life in what he believed had no life, then everything in existence has a life suited to it. If you bring, for example, a metal and leave it, you will find it oxidized, meaning some reaction with other materials has occurred... this is a life.

1 Mulk ʿaḍūḍ (the "biting" kingship): a harsh rule full of injustice and oppression. It is of the intensive forms. ʿaḍūḍ is the plural of ʿaḍḍ, meaning the wicked and fierce one. This rule was called "biting" as if it bites people.
2 Ḥikmah (wisdom): correctness, soundness, truth, knowledge, justice, forbearance, prophethood, the Qur'an and the Gospel. God says: ﴿And teach them the Book and the wisdom (129)﴾ (al-Baqarah).
3 On the authority of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "... God, Mighty and Majestic is He, gives this world to whom He loves and to whom He does not love, but He gives the religion only to whom He loves." A portion of a hadith narrated by Aḥmad in his Musnad (1/387) and al-Ḥākim in his Mustadrak (1/33) (2/447) (4/165), who authenticated it and al-Dhahabi agreed; al-Haythami attributed it in Majmaʿ al-Zawāʾid (10/228) to Aḥmad and said: its narrators are trustworthy, though some differ.
4 Tarbiyah in the sense of discipline and rebuke. This is a very subtle point: God knows that the hearts of believers contain mercy, compassion, pardon and forgiveness. That is why, in applying the hadd for fornication, for example, He said: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress, flog each one of them with a hundred lashes, and let not compassion for them detain you in the religion of God, if you believe in God and the Last Day; and let a group of the believers witness their punishment (2)﴾ (al-Nur).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 117:

After that, the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿Indeed, Allah turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet, the Emigrants, and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a group of them had nearly inclined to deviate. Then He turned to them in forgiveness. Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them.﴾ (9:117)

We have said that repentance (tawbah) has stages. There is repentance that Allah has legislated, and the very legislation of repentance is a mercy to creation, and it is also a mercy to the sinner. For if the Truth, glory be to Him, had not legislated repentance, a person would have spread into sins merely by deviating once, and if a person spreads into sins, the whole society suffers from it. So the legislation of repentance itself is a mercy to the one who commits the sin and to the one against whom the sin is committed, and the acceptance of repentance is another mercy to the one who did the sin. When you hear the words of the Truth, glory be to Him:

﴿Then He turned to them so that they might repent...﴾ (9:118)

understand that the legislation of repentance came so that the servants would actually repent, and after they repent, Allah accepts the repentance.

Here the Truth says: ﴿Indeed, Allah turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet﴾, "toward" being governed by ('atf) the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, ﴿the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾. So what did the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, do that Allah should say: ﴿Indeed, Allah turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet﴾? We say: Did not the Truth, glory be to Him, say to him: ﴿Allah pardon you. Why did you give them permission...﴾ (9:43)?

When some of the hypocrites came and asked the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, for permission to stay behind from the expedition, he granted them permission, although Allah, glory be to Him, had said: ﴿If they had gone out with you, they would not have increased you except in corruption...﴾ (9:47)

So the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, had, by sound natural disposition, taken the correct decision, but the Truth, glory be to Him, does not want them to follow only their natural disposition; rather He wanted to establish a specific legislation.

Allah willed to inform us that He had presented pardon to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, because he gave permission to those hypocrites who asked him not to go out to fighting. There are things that Allah holds against His servant, because the servant has done them against his own good. An example of this from our lives, and Allah has the highest similitude: if you see your son studying twenty hours a day, you enter his room to take the book from him or to turn off the room's lamp, and you say to him, "Get up and sleep." In this state you are only reprimanding him because you love him, not because he opposed a method, but because he went to excess in a method and manner of work that wears him out.

When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, granted a people permission to stay behind, did he do that against the interest of the war or in its interest? Indeed, if they had joined the war, their reward would have been greater even if they guarded the baggage or did any other work. So his granting them permission to stay behind was making the matter harder on himself.

For this reason we find that the reproach directed at the Prophet of Allah was in fact a reproach for his benefit, not against him. He, glory be to Him, says to him:

﴿Why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you...﴾ (66:1)

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not make lawful what Allah had forbidden; rather he forbade to himself what Allah had made lawful for him, and this is against his own interest, and the Truth was questioning him: Why do you burden yourself? So this reproach was for the benefit of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Likewise, when the blind Ibn Umm Maktum came asking the Messenger of Allah about a matter of religion, and that was in the presence of the chiefs of Quraysh, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, turned toward the chiefs, who were disbelievers, wishing to soften their hearts, and left Ibn Umm Maktum; so there came down the Truth's words:

﴿He frowned and turned away, that the blind man came to him﴾ (80:1-2)

Ibn Umm Maktum came to inquire about a matter of faith, and he would not argue as the chiefs of Quraysh argued, so why would the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, choose the difficult matter that requires greater effort to do? So the reproach here was for the benefit of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. And when the Truth says to him: ﴿Allah pardon you. Why did you give them permission...﴾ (9:43)

Then in this verse He mentioned the Emigrants and the Helpers coupled with the Messenger of Allah, so that none of the Emigrants or Helpers would feel embarrassed that Allah had turned in forgiveness toward him; rather the repentance includes him and includes the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, himself, so there is no embarrassment.

These matters that occurred had their justifications. The Truth said: ﴿after the hearts of a group of them had nearly inclined﴾, and "yazigh" means: to incline, i.e., to leave the battlefield entirely, because it was a battle in the hour of hardship (al-'usrah), and "'usrah" means severe constriction. The matter was long, the soldiers they would face were the soldiers of Rome, the weather was hot, and they did not have enough mounts; every ten of them had one camel, which one of them would ride for an hour and then dismount so the second would ride, then the third, and so on. They found no food except dates, in which worms had multiplied.

The hardship reached the point that one of them would take a date and suck it with his mouth to draw out a little juice, then take it out of his mouth to give it to another to suck a little, and so on until it became only a pit. The barley had been attacked by weevils, and the weevil had so spread that it rotted, and one who witnessed the battle said: "Even when one of us took a handful of barley to eat, he would hold his nose so as not to be harmed by the smell of the barley." All these difficulties made some of the Companions desire to return and not complete the journey to the expedition.

So the repentance was for the nearness of the inclining of the hearts of a group of them. The Truth, by His decree, mentioned the circumstance of hardship, and therefore He foretold the thoughts that were in their intentions, and among them were some who resolved not to go, then their souls spoke to them to go, like Abu Khaythamah, who remained behind after the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, had departed for the expedition, and ten days passed. The man entered his orchard and found the two arbors (al-'arishayn), and at each arbor was a beautiful wife of his, each of whom had prepared food. Thus Abu Khaythamah saw the cool shade and the hanging fruit, and a breath of clarity of soul touched him, so he said: "The Messenger of Allah is in the scorching heat and the wind, and the cold and the chill, and I am here in cool shade, with cooked food, and two beautiful women, and a soft arbor. By Allah, that is not fair to you, O Messenger of Allah." He took the reins of his mount and rode it, and the two women called after him, but he did not turn to either of them and went to catch up with the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah said: "O Messenger of Allah, we see the figure of a man approaching." The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, looked and said: "Be Abu Khaythamah!" and he was Abu Khaythamah. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a group of them had nearly inclined to deviate. Then He turned to them in forgiveness. Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them.﴾ (9:117)

And in the incident of the Companions whose souls tempted them to turn back, Allah also turned in forgiveness toward others who admitted their sins, so the Truth turned to them when He said: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins; they had mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad. Perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (9:102)

And the Truth deferred the matter of others concerning whom He said: ﴿And [there are] others deferred until the command of Allah...﴾ (9:106)

Since Allah said ﴿deferred until the command of Allah﴾, meaning: Allah, glory be to Him, has not decided their matter with anything; so there must be waiting until the command of Allah comes, and we must not confront them until the word of Allah comes. And He also turned in forgiveness toward the three who stayed behind, in His words, glory be to Him:

﴿And [He turned in forgiveness to] the three who were left behind, until when the earth closed in on them despite its vastness, and their souls confined them, and they were certain that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned to them so they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ (9:118)

1 Al-'atf is associating two or more things in one ruling.
2 This is the Expedition of Tabuk, the last expedition the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, undertook. It was in the month of Rajab in the ninth year after the Hijrah, and it was in severe heat, drought and hardship, while Medina had its shade and trees, and its fruits were good; therefore it was a difficult trial that shook hearts, and reactions varied regarding responding to the self according to the faith that dwelt in the hearts.
3 Khabalan: the meaning: they would have caused you corruption, weakness, disorder, and lack of steadfastness before the enemies.
4 From Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, entered the mosque and a rope was stretched between two pillars. He said: "What is this?" They said: "It is for Zaynab; she prays, and when she becomes lax or weary she holds on to it." He said: "Untie it. Let each of you pray with his vigor; when he becomes lax or weary, let him sit." Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (1150) and Muslim in his Sahih (784).
5 The well-known name is Abdullah, and it is said 'Amr. As for his mother Umm Kulthum, she is 'Atikah bint Abdullah. He embraced Islam early in Mecca and was among the first Emigrants. The Messenger of Allah appointed him as deputy over Medina 13 times during his expeditions. (al-Isabah fi Tamyiz al-Sahabah 4/285).
6 The chiefs of Quraysh: their great ones and the nobility among them. Here they are: Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, al-Hakam ibn Hisham (Abu Jahl), and al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and he hoped for their Islam. Ibn Umm Maktum came to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and began to say: "Guide me," and with the Messenger of Allah were great men of the polytheists. The Prophet kept turning away from him and turning to the other, saying: "Do you see any harm in what I say?" He would say: "No." It was concerning this that there was revealed: ﴿He frowned and turned away, that the blind man came to him﴾ (80:1-2). Related by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (3331), who said: a gharib hadith. Ibn Hibban (1769, Mawarid al-Dhaman).
7 Some scholars said: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is mentioned in the repentance because, since he was the cause of their repentance, he was mentioned with them. Quoted by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (4/3204).
8 Rawahil: plural of rahilah, which is every camel capable of the hardships of travel, whether male or female.
9 He is Abdullah ibn Khaythamah al-Ansari al-Salimi; he witnessed Uhud and lived until the caliphate of Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah. See al-Isabah (7/53), see (4/63).
10 Al-'arish: something resembling a tent inside the orchard, shaded with palm fronds.
11 Wathir: soft. It means the cushions and carpets that were spread inside the arbor. Al-nisfah: fairness, justice. Zimam al-rahilah: the rope by which the camel is led.
12 The story of Abu Khaythamah is related in full in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham from Ibn Ishaq (4/520), and Ibn Hisham mentioned verses of Abu Khaythamah on this:
When I saw the people had become hypocrites in religion, I came to her who was more chaste and more noble,
And I pledged allegiance with my right hand to Muhammad, so I earned no sin and did not cheat one who was sacred...
I left behind a dyed-handed woman in the arbor and a cluster of palms, and two women who had gathered their dates while still unripe...
And when the hypocrite doubted, I surrendered my soul to the religion, half of it, when it had proceeded...
Khadiba: a woman who has dyed her hands with henna. Sirmah: a group of palm trees. Safaya: laden with dates. Bisruha: the dates before they ripen. Tahammama: meaning it began to ripen, and turned black.
The saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, "Be Abu Khaythamah," occurs in the hadith of the repentance of Ka'b ibn Malik in Muslim's Sahih (2769).
13 Hardship: in terms of provision, mounts, food and water.
14 The three are: Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah, and Murarah ibn Rabi'ah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 118:

It may be thought that (khullifū, "were left behind") here indicates that someone told them, "Sit back from going out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and that no one said this to those who were not left behind. Rather, (khullifū) means: the command of the Lawgiver did not become manifest concerning them as it did concerning others; rather, the Truth (al-Haqq) spoke about them beforehand: ﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command﴾, and since the ruling was delayed concerning them, there must be waiting.

{And [He also turned in forgiveness to] the three who were left behind, until, when the earth closed in on them despite its vastness, and their souls confined them, and they thought that there was no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned to them so that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.} (9:118) (At-Tawbah).

We know that when a person is preoccupied with a worry, he speaks to himself about leaving the place where he sits, which causes him constriction, and perhaps the constriction will be released (1). But these three faced constriction in every place they went, until the earth closed in on them despite its breadth, so that none of them found a place to go. This means that the distress surrounding them had become general. A person may find the earth closing in on him despite its vastness, yet his soul contains him.

The Truth says about them: ﴿and their souls confined them﴾, meaning: the earth closed in on them despite its vastness, and their souls also closed in on them. The three had stayed behind from the expedition without any excuse except mere laziness and procrastination. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the Muslims to boycott them. Ka'b ibn Malik (2) would go out to the market and no one would speak to him; he would go to his relatives and no one would speak to him; he would climb over (yatasawwar (3)) their walls, hoping they would look at him, but they would not look at him. After that the matter escalated in isolating these men, until it extended to their wives, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded him that they should not approach their wives (4). Thus the isolation reached a severe and minute degree: first it was control over the society, then over relatives, then over the most private matter of residence, which is the woman. Hilal ibn Umayyah's wife came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Hilal ibn Umayyah is a sick man, and I ask your permission to do for him what would sustain him." He said to her: "But let him not approach you." She said: "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, he has no inclination toward anything, and by Allah, he has not stopped weeping since what happened to him until this day." Some Muslims went to Ka'b ibn Malik to inform him that the Messenger of Allah had permitted Hilal's wife to serve him, and they said to him: "Go to the Messenger of Allah and ask his permission for your wife to serve you."

He said: "Hilal is an old man, so what shall I say to the Messenger of Allah when I am a young man? By Allah, I will never go to him."

The three remained in a psychological and social siege for fifty days, until Allah brought repentance, and in this there was purification (tamhīs (6)) for them. Ka'b ibn Malik, for example, relates his condition before the expedition, saying: "I had never been stronger or more affluent than when I stayed behind from him in that expedition. By Allah, I had never gathered two riding camels before, until I gathered them in that expedition." That is, there was no excuse preventing him.

After that, the bearer of good tidings comes, and a man comes from the mountain of Sal' and says: "O Ka'b, rejoice in the best day that has passed over you. Allah has sent down concerning you a Qur'an, and that He has turned to you in forgiveness."

Ka'b said: "I found nothing with me to give him as a gift for his good tidings except my two garments, so I took them off and gave them to him. Then I borrowed two garments and went to the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

And he said: "O Messenger of Allah, part of the completion of my repentance is that I withdraw from my wealth, which caused me this punishment, as a charity to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) (7)."

Therefore, the delay of the ruling was intended for the purification of these men and for giving an example to others. When they see that the earth has closed in on them, though it may have been vast, and likewise their souls have confined them, they become certain of the Truth's words:

﴿And they thought that there was no refuge (8) from Allah except in Him...﴾ (9:118) (At-Tawbah). That is: no one grants protection except Allah, and He, glory be to Him, grants protection from Himself. How? You know that you are a commodity that no one protects you from except the one who pursues you. So know that there is no authority for anyone at all; therefore we say: you take refuge in Allah, not from His creation, but you take refuge (9) in Allah to protect you from Allah. He, glory be to Him, has attributes of majesty (jalāl) and attributes of beauty (jamāl). The attributes of majesty appear in that He is: the Subduer (Qahhār), the Compeller (Jabbār), the Avenger (Muntaqim), the Severe in seizing (Shadīd al-Baṭsh), and so on through those attributes. And among the attributes of beauty of the Truth, glory be to Him, are the Forgiving (Ghafūr), the Merciful (Raḥīm), and others. So when a person commits a sin, the domain in that case is that he be punished by the attributes of majesty, and nothing protects the servant from the attributes of majesty except the attributes of beauty.

We all know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supplicated to Allah saying: "I seek refuge in You from You" (10). That is: I seek refuge in the attributes of beauty in You from the attributes of Your majesty; nothing will protect me from the attributes of Your majesty except the attributes of Your beauty.

Therefore, when there came in the noble hadith concerning the last night of Ramadan his saying (ﷺ): "When it is the last night of Ramadan, the Compeller (al-Jabbār) manifests Himself with forgiveness."

Some people think this matter is illogical: how does the Compeller manifest Himself with forgiveness? Would it not have been more appropriate to say, "the Forgiver (al-Ghaffār) manifests Himself"? We say: No; for forgiveness requires a sin, and the station becomes that of the attribute of the Compeller. Thus the attribute of mercy takes its authority from the attribute of the Compeller, and it is as if we are saying: O Compeller, You alone are the Truth, but we intercede by Your attributes of beauty before Your attributes of majesty. This is the meaning of: "the Compeller manifests Himself with forgiveness."

It is also related that al-Aṣma'ī (11), while circumambulating, heard a Muslim at the door of al-Multazam saying: "O Allah, I am ashamed to ask You for forgiveness because I have disobeyed You, but I looked for it and found no one other than You to ask."

He said to him: "O man, indeed Allah forgives you for the goodness of your request (12)."

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Then He turned to them so that they might repent﴾. Repentance first, as we have known, is His legislating it; repentance comes with acceptance. His saying ﴿so that they might repent﴾ means that it becomes a repentance of return and coming back to what they were upon before the disobedience.

The Truth concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾, for there is no one who accepts repentance and no one who is merciful except Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

1 yanfakk: the person is freed from it. From it comes "fakk al-raqabah," meaning freeing him from bondage and slavery. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "Fakka fulan" means he was freed and relieved from the thing. (Lisan al-Arab, root f-k-k).
2 Ka'b ibn Malik used to mingle with people and go out seeking that people would speak to him; as for his two companions, Murarah ibn al-Rabi' and Hilal ibn Umayyah, they stayed in their houses. As for him, he says: "I would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and greet him, while he was in his assembly after the prayer, and I would say to myself: Did he move his lips to return the greeting or not? Then I would pray near him and steal glances at him; when I turned to my prayer he would look at me, and when I turned toward him he would turn away from me."
3 tasawwur: he climbed the wall until he rose over it. From it is the Qur'anic saying: ﴿And has the news of the adversaries reached you, when they climbed over the sanctuary wall? (21)﴾ (Sad).
4 Ka'b said regarding this: "Until, when forty of the fifty days had passed and revelation had withdrawn, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to me and said: The Messenger of Allah commands you to separate from your wife. I said: Shall I divorce her, or what shall I do? He said: No, rather separate from her and do not approach her."
5 This is called general isolation socially, domestically, and psychologically.
6 tamhīs: trial, testing, and purification from sins. The trial reached its extent for Ka'b such that the king of Ghassan sent him a letter saying: "It has reached us that [Muhammad] has abandoned you, and Allah has not made you a house of humiliation or loss; so join us, and we will console you." Ka'b threw it into the fire after reading it.
7 The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Keep some of your wealth, for it is better for you." Ka'b said: "Then I will keep my share at Khaybar." The full hadith is related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4418) and Muslim (2769).
8 mulja': the stronghold, refuge, and protector.
9 Seeking refuge is directed toward the attributes of beauty for protection from the attributes of majesty; here, seeking refuge is toward Allah to protect you from Allah.
10 A portion of a hadith related by Muslim (486) and Ahmad in his Musnad (6/58, 120), from the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I missed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night from the bed, so I searched for him, and my hand fell upon the soles of his feet while he was in the mosque, and they were upright, and he was saying: 'O Allah, I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, and in Your pardon from Your punishment, and I seek refuge in You from You. I cannot number the praises upon You; You are as You have praised Yourself.'"
11 al-Aṣma'ī: he is 'Abd al-Malik ibn Qurayb Abu Sa'id al-Asma'i, one of the imams of learning in language, poetry, and regions; his birth and death were in Basra at the age of 95, and he died in the year 216 (al-A'lam by al-Zirikli, 4/162).
12 Also related from al-Asma'i with this same meaning: that he heard a Bedouin supplicating to Allah, saying: "I have fled to You with myself, O refuge of those fleeing with the burdens of sins, carrying them on my back; I find no intercessor except my knowledge that You are the most generous to whom the distressed turn, and the hope of those who desire what is with You?" See al-Amali of Abu 'Ali al-Qali (1/32).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 9, verse 119:

The Truthful One (al-Haqq subhanahu) says after that:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful.﴾ (119)

When the Real (al-Haqq, ʿazza wa jall) calls out to the believing servants, He either calls them with a ruling connected to faith, or He calls them by faith and demands faith from them, like His saying:

﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger...﴾ (136) (an-Nisa)

The Real (subhanahu) makes clear to those who have believed in Him, before He addresses them, that a person may believe and then waver in his faith. So He demands from them "continuance of faith" (dawam al-iman). If Allah asks His servants for something that was already present in them at the moment of address, then what is demanded is its continuance. And if He asks them for a ruling connected to faith, then He directs them to listen to and apply what is asked of them. An example of this is the saying of the Real (subhanahu):

﴿Fear Allah...﴾ (119) (at-Tawba)

The word ﴿ittaqu﴾ (fear/guard) means: make between yourselves and Allah a shield (wiqaya). Someone may ask: does anyone ask a person to make a shield between himself and his Lord? The believing servant seeks to be in the company of Allah (maʿiyya). Here the necessity arises of understanding the attributes of beauty (jamal) and the attributes of majesty (jalal). His saying (subhanahu) ﴿Fear Allah﴾ means: make between yourselves and the attributes of majesty a shield, just as He said (subhanahu):

﴿Then fear the Fire...﴾ (24) (al-Baqara)

Because the Fire is among the soldiers of the attributes of majesty, so make between yourselves and Allah a shield from the attributes of majesty.

Here the Real says: ﴿Fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾. Some scholars explained His saying ﴿be with the truthful﴾ to mean "be among the truthful," meaning that "with" (maʿa) here carries the sense of "from" (min), and the intent is that this statement gives a general, comprehensive meaning. But I say: there is a difference between ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ and "be among the truthful." The saying of the Real ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ means: join yourselves to them, so that you will be in their company, and after you join them, those who come after you will find you with the truthful.

The matter here requires us to recall what we have previously said about the verbal relation (al-nisba al-kalamiyya) and the mental relation (al-nisba al-dhihniyya). Any proposition that passes through your mind before you say it is a mental relation, like your saying: "Muhammad visited me." Before you utter this phrase, it came to your mind to say it, and this is a "mental relation." The one who hears you does not know of it; since you are the speaker, you alone know it. When you utter it and the addressee hears it from you, he knows that a mental relation came into your mind and you translated it into speech as a verbal relation. When you said "Muhammad visited me yesterday," it came into your mind before you said it, and when the listener heard it, he understood that there were two relations: a relation he heard, and a relation in your mind.

When the listener scrutinizes this statement, he knows that there is in reality one person named Muhammad, and he learned from you that he visited you, and his experience with you is always that you are truthful. So: truthfulness (al-sidq) is that the verbal relation conforms to reality. But if you say: "Muhammad has travelled to America," and he has not travelled, then this means the verbal relation did not conform to the actual relation, and this is lying (al-kadhib). So there is a "mental relation," a "verbal relation," and an "actual relation." If the verbal relation conforms to the actual relation, that is truthfulness, and if it does not conform, it is lying.

Every relation you state may be true or false, and the decider in this matter is reality: does what you say conform to reality or not? But if I say to you "Visit so-and-so," this is a relation of instruction (inshaʾ), because reality comes after it, not before it.

Here the Real (subhanahu) says: ﴿Fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾, and truthfulness is the quality (khilla) that gathers all of faith. Let us see the application of this in the story of the Bedouin man who went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, there are three traits in me that I cannot ever abandon: the first is women, the second is wine, and the third is lying. I have come to you, O Messenger of Allah, so that you may choose for me one trait from the three and strengthen me upon it, and I will covenant our Lord upon it." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) chose for the Bedouin that he repent of lying and adorn himself with truthfulness, and he said to him: "Be truthful, and nothing is upon you." When the Bedouin desired to drink a cup of wine, he asked himself: "And what if the Prophet (ﷺ) asks me, 'Did you drink wine?'" and he refrained from wine so as not to lie to the Messenger. When he came to steal a glance at a woman, he said to himself: "And what if the Prophet (ﷺ) asks me, and how would I disgrace myself with a quality not befitting a Muslim?" so he refrained from looking at those who are forbidden to him. Thus truthfulness took control of the man and refined his conduct. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "Can a believer be a coward?" he said: "Yes." It was said to him: "Can a believer be stingy?" he said: "Yes." It was said to him: "Can a believer be a liar?" he said: "No."(5) Because the entrance to faith is affirmation (taslid) of the firm doctrinal proposition, and thus you find that truthfulness is "the head of the whole matter."

The saying of the Real ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ means: do not say words that reality does not correspond to; and beware also of saying words your deeds contradict. For this reason the Real (subhanahu) says:

﴿Why do you say what you do not do? Greatly hateful is it in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ (2-3) (as-Saff)

In surat al-Baqara the Real (subhanahu) says: ﴿Righteousness(6) is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets, and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveller, those who ask, and for freeing slaves, and establishes prayer and gives zakah...﴾ (177) (al-Baqara).

Let us pay attention to a subtle point in this verse. The Real says here: ﴿and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives...﴾ (177) (al-Baqara).

Then He mentions establishing prayer and giving zakah, so why then did He mention ﴿and gives wealth﴾? I say: the Real here mentions wealth that the believer spends without its being obligatory for him to pay, such as zakah. Zakah is obligatory, but giving wealth as charity is beyond what is obligatory.(7)

Then He (subhanahu) says: ﴿And those who fulfil their promise when they promise, and the patient in poverty(8) and hardship and during battle. Those are the ones who have been truthful, and it is those who are the righteous﴾ (177) (al-Baqara).

These are the qualities of those who were truthful, and they here, in the verse we are reflecting upon, have been truthful and God-fearing.

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾ (119) (at-Tawba). The Real has brought the attribute of "truthfulness" here, because the context is speaking of those who stayed behind from the expeditions and lied in the excuses they fabricated; therefore the heavenly directive comes: enter through the gate of truthfulness.(9)

1 Here the knower of Allah says: faith is demanded either by way of guidance (hidaya), or by way of indication (dalala), or by way of companionship (maʿiyya). The faith of guidance is perception through being affected by what is perceived, and the faith of companionship is by choice. So when the address is repeated, its demand is stations of faith, in confirmation of His (ta'ala) saying: ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts become fearful, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely﴾ (2) (al-Anfal).
2 When the verbal relation conforms to reality, that is truthfulness, and when the verbal relation contradicts reality, it is lying. This is what the scholars of rhetoric and logic have held.
3 Khilla: a quality and disposition; its plural is khilal.
4 Khisla: a quality and attribute; its plural is khisal and khislat.
5 Related by Imam Malik in his Muwatta' (p. 990) from the hadith of Safwan ibn Sulaym, as a mursal report.
6 Al-birr: goodness and beneficence; it is sincere faith and doing good deeds.
7 Zakah is an obligation; giving wealth as charity is a virtue; and goodness is for one who combines both.
8 Al-basa': that is, in a state of poverty. Al-darra': in a state of illness and sickness. Hin al-ba's: in a state of fighting and meeting enemies.
9 From Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hold to truthfulness, for truthfulness guides to righteousness, and righteousness guides to Paradise. A man continues to be truthful and seeks truthfulness until he is written with Allah as a truthful one (siddiq). Beware of lying, for lying guides to wickedness, and wickedness guides to the Fire. A man continues to lie and seek lies until he is written with Allah as a liar." Related by Muslim in his Sahih (2607) and al-Bukhari in his Sahih (6094).

Almighty Allah then says: "It was not fitting for the people of Medina and those of the Bedouins around them to hold back from the Messenger of Allah, nor to prefer their own selves over his self. That is because they will not suffer thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of Allah, nor tread on any ground that enrages the disbelievers, nor gain anything from an enemy, except that a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby. Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers" (9:120).

The discourse here returns to those who stayed behind from the expedition. We have known before that when you say "ma kana laka an taf'ala kadhā" (it was not for you to do such-and-such), you are negating the capacity to do the act; but if you say "ma yanbaghī" (it is not fitting), it means you have the capacity to do it, but it is not obligatory that you do it.

Here the Truth says: "It was not for the people of Medina and those of the Bedouins around them to hold back from the Messenger of Allah," and some of them had indeed held back from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the campaign.

Then He, glorified is He, says: "nor to prefer their own selves over his self." Here there is a discussion of two kinds of selves: the selves of those who stayed behind, and the self of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When you say "raghibtu" (I desired), it means you inclined with a heartfelt inclination. If you say "raghiba fī" (he desired in), the inclination of the heart is toward engaging in the act, and it carries the sense of penetration; but if you say "raghiba 'an" (he turned away from), it carries the sense of going beyond, meaning the inclination of the heart is aimed at distancing oneself from the act. Thus, the prepositional particle is what determines the nature of the inclination of the heart.

The Truth's saying: "nor to prefer their own selves over his self" means that they were indifferent to a matter that came from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and preferred the matter of their own selves over the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So the Truth makes clear to them that it was not for them to do that, because as long as you have believed in Allah, your faith is not complete until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is more beloved to you than your own selves.

That is why we find that our master 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), when he heard that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you truly believes until I am more beloved to him than his own self" (3), said: "O Messenger of Allah, I love you more than my family and my wealth, but not more than my own self." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No, [not until I am more beloved to him than his own self]." Then 'Umar said: "By Allah, now you are more beloved to me than my own self." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Now, O 'Umar." Such was the sincerity of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) repeated the saying: "None of you truly believes until I am more beloved to him than his own self." 'Umar knew that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was firm in this matter of faith, and he knew that the love required is not the love of emotion but the love of the intellect. There is a difference between the love of emotion and the love of the intellect: the love of emotion carries no obligation, but the love of the intellect brings with it obligation.

For example, you love your son with your emotion even if he is not intelligent, but with your intellect you love the son of your enemy if he is intelligent, trustworthy and successful. We gave this example earlier: a person may love a bitter medicine because in it is the cure; he does not love this medicine with his emotions, nor does he enjoy it while drinking it, but he loves it with his intellect, because this medicine may be the cause of his health. And if he cannot find it in the pharmacies, he becomes angry and complains, and he rejoices at whoever brings it to him from other lands.

So, those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whether from the people of Medina or from those around them, it was not for them to stay behind, because this contradicts their faith that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) should be more beloved to them than their own selves. It was obligatory for them to desire the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over their own selves; as for the matter being the reverse, that is not acceptable, because following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brings only good (4).

As for following their love of themselves, it is narrowness of insight; it will bring them evils, and even if its good comes to them, it is temporary and according to their capacities. But their love of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over themselves brings them the enduring, lasting good that is commensurate with the power of Allah, glorified is He.

Then He, glorified is He, says: "That is because they will not suffer..." — "That" refers to the grounds of the inclination by which they receive the good reward from the Truth, glorified is He, namely that they "will not suffer." We know that thirst afflicted them in the army of hardship (Jaysh al-'Usra), to the point that a fighter would slaughter a camel and filter the water in its stomach to moisten his mouth and the mouths of his companions.

"Nor fatigue" — al-nasab is weariness, and the campaign was in a hot, exhausting climate. "Nor hunger" — al-makhmasa is famine; they used to eat dates infested with worms and barley riddled with weevils. Even if they endured all of that, it is in the way of Allah, who is able to bestow on them every good as recompense for what they offer in support of His cause.

"Nor tread on any ground that enrages the disbelievers" — we know that the disbelievers had a tract of land where they were stationed; when the believers raid them and dislodge them from this place, and descend into the valleys and orchards owned by the disbelievers, this is a matter that enrages the people of disbelief. So when they tread on a ground, this enrages the disbelievers.

"Nor gain anything from an enemy" — that is, they take from an enemy a gain, and the meaning is that they overcome the enemy so that it retreats and feels loss; then they receive the good reward from Allah. Each of these events — thirst, fatigue, hunger, treading on ground that enrages the disbelievers, and gaining from their enemy — has a reward that the Truth determines: "except that a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby."

So, those who preferred their own selves over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and did not go out for the campaign have lost much, and they have lost the righteous deed that Allah, glorified is He, has recorded as recompense for every event that those who went out with the Messenger (ﷺ) encountered (5).

The Truth, glorified is He, concludes the verse: "Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers." Those who did good, Allah never wastes their reward.

1 Al-zama': thirst. Al-nasab: weariness. Al-makhmasa: famine. Yata'una: they trample.
2 From Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever has three qualities will find the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anything else; that he loves a person only for the sake of Allah; and that he hates to return to disbelief as he hates to be thrown into the Fire." Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (16) and Muslim (43).
3 Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (6632) and Ahmad in his Musnad (4/233). In the chain of Ahmad is Ibn Lahi'a, but he is followed by Haywa from Zuhra ibn Ma'bad. The rest of the hadith here is narrated in meaning.
4 On this, the Lord of Might says: "O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to what gives you life..." (8:24) — i.e., gives life to your religion and your hearts. Al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4647) related from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, who said: "I was praying in the mosque when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called me, but I did not answer him. Then I came and said: O Messenger of Allah, I was praying. He (ﷺ) said: 'Did not Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say: "Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to what gives you life"?' Then he (ﷺ) said: 'I will teach you the greatest surah in the Qur'an before I leave.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went to leave, and I reminded him, and he (ﷺ) said: 'It is "Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin," the seven oft-repeated (verses).'"
5 This verse necessitates the obligation of mobilization upon individual Muslims. Some scholars said it was abrogated by the following verse: "It is not for the believers to go forth all together..." (9:122). Qatada said: this was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ): when he went out to fight himself, no one might stay behind except with an excuse; as for other imams and rulers, whoever wished could stay behind among the Muslims if there was no need or necessity for him. Others said it is muhkam (not abrogated). Al-Qurtubi said: Qatada's view is good, based on the expedition of Tabuk. See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi (4/3217).

Then He mentions other kinds of events besides thirst, toil, and hunger, besides treading a path that enrages the disbelievers, and inflicting a blow upon the enemy of Allah, so He, glorified be He, says:

﴿And they do not spend an expenditure, small or large, and do not cross a valley, except that it is recorded for them, that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ (9:121)

So everything, then, is counted. Even those who spent, Allah, glorified be He, knows what they spent and will reward them for it. And those who traveled the long road and crossed the valleys to catch up with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his expeditions, Allah, glorified be He, records good for them. After that, the Muslims rushed to carry out the orders of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so much so that Madinah was almost emptied of Muslims, who went to join the detachments (sarayā) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out to spread the call.

Then came the word of the Truth:

﴿It was not for the believers to go forth all together. Why should not a group from every section of them go forth, that they might gain understanding in the religion and warn their people when they return to them, that they may beware?﴾ (9:122)

This verse came after the verses about those who stayed behind from the expedition with the Messenger of God, and after God had explained the virtues of the fighters (mujahidun) and the reward He gives them for this struggle. Before it, God said:

﴿That is because they suffer no thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of God, nor do they tread any path that angers the disbelievers, nor do they inflict any harm upon an enemy, but a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby. Indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers. And they spend no expenditure, small or large, nor do they cross any valley, but it is recorded for them, that God may reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾ (at-Tawbah)

These were the considerations that encouraged people to take part in jihad, an encouragement that drew them out of what they were accustomed to, namely living in their homelands among their families and their wealth; for the reward they receive in exchange for that jihad is a great reward. Then this verse came.

When the scholars received this verse, they said: it is a continuation of the verses on jihad. Since God had encouraged jihad with this kind of encouragement, people swore after it that they would not leave any military campaign (ghazwah) or detachment (sariyyah) without going out to it. As a result, Medina nearly became empty of people, leaving the Messenger of God (ﷺ) alone, while he was receiving the revelation of God.

Receiving the revelation of God requires the presence of listeners to convey it. So when people turned toward the matter of jihad, God wished to correct this wave of eagerness for jihad. He explained that Islam was sent down from God to His Messenger in order to convey it to the people, because the religion of God needs two things: a matter carried by people, and a matter that proves its truth among people. When people see a man sacrifice his life and enter battle, and another sacrifice his wealth, then people know that whoever does this must be fully certain of the creed for whose sake he gives both the precious and the cheap.

But there remains another matter, which is the necessity of the existence of those who carry knowledge of Islam. If the fighters who sacrifice their lives and the spenders who sacrifice their wealth are a proof of the sincerity of faith, this does not mean dispensing with those who must hear from the Messenger of God what God reveals.

So: there is a method from God, and there is reception of this method by the Messenger of God first, and by the listeners to the Messenger second, so that they may travel through the lands, a journey of informing about the religion of God in order to spread Islam. Thus remaining with the Messenger of God was the reception of that information; otherwise, what would they teach?

So: the Muslims must preserve two matters: the matter of continued reception from heaven, and the matter of informing (1) others of what they have received in the lands. If you have gone out to jihad in the way of God, you have accomplished one matter, but you have not accomplished the other, which is that you remain to receive from the Messenger of God. So God, glory be to Him, wished to divide the two matters between fighters who strive to inform, and those who remain with the Messenger of God to receive the transmission of heaven to this earth. So He said: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together.﴾

When you hear "kana" (was) negated, know that it is a denial of this matter, i.e., it is not proper for the Muslims to go forth all together, that is, entirely, without any of them remaining.

And ﴿kaffah﴾ (all together) is derived from kaff of a thing. You hear the tailor say, "I want to kaffif the cloth": this means that when the tailor cuts the fabric, some threads come out of it, so he kaffafha (gathers and secures them) so that the fabric's weave does not unravel. So the meaning of the word ﴿kaffah﴾ is: all together.

We may ask: why should the Muslims not all go forth to jihad? Is not jihad a means of informing about the method of God?

We say: yes, it is informing and journeying with the method of God on earth, but the one who journeys to inform about the method of God must have a stock of knowledge with which to inform, and this stock in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to come from the method of heaven when it descended upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

So: there must be people who hear the revelation of heaven, then learn from it and send it to the people of the earth (2) all together. Had all of these believers gone forth to jihad, the carrying of the call to Islam would not have been achieved. Therefore the Truth said: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together.﴾ In this there is a command implying capability (intiba'), that is, they have the ability to do it and can carry out what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asks of them.

We know that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) grew up among an Arab nation possessing eloquence and rhetoric, a nation of expression and strong delivery that enchants, and among this nation were many people who had the gift of poetry and speech. But the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was not known for this. Some of them tried to belittle the eloquence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), saying: it is an eloquence inferior to that of the one who gave speeches, inferior to the one who spoke, inferior to the one who wrote poetry. The response came from the Truth:

﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him...(69)﴾ (Ya-Sin). That is: he (ﷺ) was able to excel in that, but the Truth, glory be to Him, did not teach him poetry, because it is not befitting for him to learn it. Why? Because the Arabs know that the sweetest poetry is the most false, and since the sweetest is the most false, the Truth, glory be to Him, did not want people to think that Muhammad (ﷺ) was a practised master (muratid) (3) of the craft of eloquence and the methods of literature, and then surprise the world with supreme eloquence in the Qur'an, announcing (ﷺ) that this eloquence is not from himself.

The Messenger (ﷺ) lived among them for a long period and they never heard poetry from him. Everything he brought was a message from God, not attributed to Muhammad, but attributed to the Lord of Muhammad.

His words, the Truth: ﴿and it is not befitting for him﴾ mean: this matter is not proper, despite Muhammad's (ﷺ) readiness for it, and it would have been possible for his Lord to teach him poetry and the arts of speech. Therefore, when some people said the Qur'an is from Muhammad, the true word came addressing Muhammad: ﴿Indeed I have remained among you a lifetime before it. Will you not reason? (16)﴾ (Yunus). The Messenger (ﷺ) lived among them forty years and did not say a poem or an essay.

And who can delay his genius until forty? We know that the time when genius begins to appear is before twenty, that is, in the second decade of life, and no one delays the appearance of his genius.

So: when the Qur'an was sent down to the Messenger (ﷺ) encouraging jihad, Medina nearly became empty of Muslims; so the true word came:

﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together. Why should not a group from every division of them go forth, that they may gain understanding in the religion and warn their people when they return to them, that they may beware? (122)﴾ (at-Tawbah). In this noble statement there is a preservation of two matters: the matter of receiving the revelation of God, and the matter of informing about it. Thus jihad is diversified: one group receives, and another group teaches and sends out. For if they all left the Messenger (ﷺ), how would revelation reach the believers from the Messenger (ﷺ)? And if they all sat in Medina, who would travel through the earth teaching the people? As for when the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers remain with him in a period without fighting, that is a different matter, because it will be a period of reception only.

Likewise, if the Messenger of God (ﷺ) goes out to fight, the believers capable of fighting must accompany him, because the Messenger capable of receiving revelation from God is present with them, and the informing of the message is present too.

So: the problem was in the case of the absence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from those going out to jihad. If the fighters go out to jihad while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) remains in Medina, they must divide into two parts: a part remains with the Messenger of God to learn the method of God, and a part goes out to fight.

When the Messenger went out to fight, the undertaking was called a ghazwah (campaign), and when he did not go out but sent a group to fight, the operation was called a sariyyah (detachment) (4).

Only one operation departed from being named a sariyyah and was called a ghazwah, although the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not go out in it, and it should have been called a sariyyah, but it was called a ghazwah (5).

The fighting mission departed from the designation of sariyyah to the designation of ghazwah, although the Messenger did not attend it, because the battle involved things like those that happen in ghazwahs: it was a decisive battle in which a number of Muslims were killed; one carried the banner and fought and was martyred, another took it up and was killed, a third took it up, and the battle was fierce. So they said: we cannot call that battle a "sariyyah"; rather it is a ghazwah, because there was intense violence in it.

They overlooked one thing, namely that the designation ghazwah applied perfectly to Mu'tah, because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in Medina while the Muslims went out to the campaign, and he sent word to the forces: if so-and-so is killed in the fighting, then so-and-so succeeds him, and if so-and-so is killed, then so-and-so succeeds him (6). That is: he (ﷺ) arranged the affairs of the campaign before it began.

It is the only military expedition that went out with these instructions, among its counterparts of specified expeditions from which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not go out with the fighters, as if he (ﷺ) knew in advance who among those going out to fight would die.

Then the force reached its location, and the fighting took place, while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in Medina. The Companions turned and heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) speaking; he said: the banner was taken by so-and-so and he was killed; then it was taken by so-and-so and he was killed. Then he said: and it was taken after him by so-and-so. The Messenger (ﷺ) was narrating the battle while he was in Medina, and they said: he would not have said that except because he was a witness.

When the fighters returned, the Companions learned from them that the matter had unfolded just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had related it while sitting in Medina, and it had happened in complete agreement. They said: the Messenger of God witnessed it; and since the Messenger of God (ﷺ) witnessed it, it is a ghazwah.

We return to the verse in which the Truth says: ﴿Why should not a group from every division of them go forth...(122)﴾ (at-Tawbah).

When you hear the word "law-la" (why not / if not), know that in the language there are words close to one another: "law", "lawla", "lawma" and "hal-la" are, then, words found in the language. When you hear "law", this means there is a judgement of the impossibility of two things: one thing is impossible because of the impossibility of another thing, as in your saying: "Law kana 'indaka Zaydun laji'tuka" (if Zayd had been with you, I would have come to you), where your coming is made impossible by the impossibility of Zayd's coming. So "law" is a particle of impossibility due to impossibility. And you say: "Law ji'tani fi baytī la-akramtuka" (if you had come to me in my house, I would have honoured you). So I did not honour you because you did not come.

And you say: "Lawla Zaydun 'indaka lajitka" (were it not for Zayd with you, I would have come to you), meaning that my coming to you has been made impossible by the presence of Zayd. So "lawla" is a particle of impossibility due to existence. We note that in "lawla" here, what follows is a noun, "Zayd". But what if a verb follows it, as in your saying: "Lawla fa'alta kadhā" (why did you not do such-and-such)? Here the speech contains urging toward the action, like the Truth's saying: ﴿Why did they not, when you heard it, say...(12)﴾ (an-Nur) — ﴿Lawla idh sami'tumūhu zanna al-mu'minūna wal-mu'minatu bi-anfusihim khayran﴾.

Like His saying: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses for it...(13)﴾ (an-Nur).

Likewise "lawma", as in the Truth's saying: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are of the truthful? (7)﴾ (al-Hijr).

Also your saying: "hal-la". It too is an urging, as in our saying: "Hal-la dhakarta durūsaka?" (Why did you not study your lessons?). By this you are asking with hal, but you bring the lengthening so it becomes hal-la, to urge him to study. Or your saying: "Hal-la akramta Fulānan?" (Why did you not honour so-and-so?), and in this there is an urging that you honour so-and-so (8).

Here, the style of the verse we are reflecting upon gathers the believers and says to them: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together,﴾ then the urging to divide into two parts comes in His saying: ﴿Why should not a group from every division go forth,﴾ and one of the two parts goes off to inform and to fight, while the second part remains with the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

1 Because jihad in the way of God to meet the enemy is an obligation according to its motives and according to the condition of the call, whereas informational jihad is required until the Hour is established. It is a jihad that continues as long as there is falsehood opposing truth.

2 Religious informing is a jihad that has the quality of continuity, because it is a means of lasting persuasion to strengthen the values of heaven to organize the chaos of earth, and jihad by the sword is not carried out except after persuasion and persistence in falsehood to obliterate the features of truth. ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes (18)﴾ (al-Anbiya').

3 Muratid: that is, accustomed to composing poetry, for whom rhymes, metres, weights and language have been made pliable to compose whatever he wishes. This is not befitting for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for otherwise it would be a basis for attack upon the Qur'an.

4 The number of campaigns in which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out personally as a fighter was twenty-seven, and he personally fought in nine of them: Badr, Uhud, al-Muraysi', al-Khandaq, Qurayzah, Khaybar, the Conquest of Makkah, Hunayn and al-Ta'if. The number of his expeditions or detachments reached forty-seven; it is said: rather, nearly sixty.

5 It is the expedition of Mu'tah, a village in the land of al-Balqa' in al-Sham, among the districts of Damascus; it was also called "the army of the commanders".

6 Al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih (4261) from Abdullah ibn Umar who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) appointed Zayd ibn Harithah in the campaign of Mu'tah, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: if Zayd is killed, then Ja'far; and if Ja'far is killed, then Abdullah ibn Rawahah. Abdullah said: I was among them in that campaign, and we searched for Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and we found him among the slain, and we found in his body more than ninety wounds from stabbing and shooting."

7 From Anas ibn Malik who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave a sermon and said: the banner was taken by Zayd and he was struck down; then Ja'far took it and was struck down; then Abdullah ibn Rawahah took it and was struck down, and his eyes were shedding tears; then it was taken without command, and God granted victory through him. And I would not be pleased that they were with us, or he said: what would please them that they were with us. Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4262) and Ahmad in his Musnad (3/113).

8 The three tools (lawla, lawma, hal-la) are not followed except by the present-tense verb, apparent or implied. If they enter upon a past tense verb, its time is turned into the future, on condition that they convey urging. Among them is the verse we have here, and similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿My Lord, if only You would delay me to a near term...(10)﴾ (al-Munafiqun). See: an-Nahw by Abbas Hasan.

Then Allah, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿O you who have believed, fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers and let them find in you harshness. And know that Allah is with the righteous. (123)﴾

Here the Truth turns us once again to the discussion of jihad. And we may ask: why, then, does the discussion of nafr (going forth) and fiqh (jurisprudence) come as an interruption within a continuous discussion of jihad? I answer: it was the will of Allah, glorified is He, to teach us that every believer who goes forth in order to acquire fiqh, and to teach others, is in need of a stage of learning, and of knowing the reasons for which the Muslims fight and the grounds of jihad in the way of Allah.

The Truth, glorified is He, has divided the verses of jihad into two parts: a group that goes forth, and a portion of them that remains with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the matter is settled, one group fights and another group learns and teaches (1), and the two groups exchange faith-based and combat experience, so that the faculties of faith become mutually supportive rather than opposed, and after that they turn towards the disbelievers.

﴿O you who have believed, fight those adjacent to you﴾. This means that there are people near them who are still disbelievers, and there are people further away from them. And the Truth has said: ﴿Fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together... (36)﴾ (al-Tawbah).

So, there are priorities in fighting. Fighting the disbelievers who are near you secures the camp of faith; for this reason the command to fight the nearer came, because it is a fight that will not require mounts or the provision for a long journey. Also, the enemy near you, you know his condition better than you know the condition of the disbelievers far from you; therefore you know the places of their strength and their weakness, and how their fortifications are built. If the fight against the nearer enemy is made easy, that becomes a path to confronting the farther enemy, instead of facing the far enemy while the near enemy allies with him; then the two of them would form a "pincer" around you, in the language of war, so you must first protect your back from the evil of the nearer enemy.

So there is no contradiction between fighting the far enemy and fighting the near enemy. And there is no contradiction between His saying: ﴿Fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers﴾ and His, glorified is He: ﴿and fight the polytheists all together﴾; because the meaning of ﴿kaffah﴾ is "all together," but the group has priority. Take the one near you, so that you may join him to you; and when you join him to you, you reduce a land from your enemy and it becomes an addition to you. If the opponent has a sword and you have a sword, and then you enter the battle and knock the sword from his hand and take it, then you end up with two swords while he has none.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, makes clear to the disbelievers: consider, O disbelievers, for you do not see the land each day diminishing from beneath your feet (2), and what diminishes from the land of the disbelievers increases the land of faith. And since the Truth has come with the word "fighting," this word requires resolve, and boldness that emboldens one to fight, and patience in it. You may find in facing you someone stronger than you or braver than you; if he sees in you a courage that surpasses his courage, and senses in you a strength and perseverance that surpass his strength and perseverance, then this strips the hope of victory over you from his heart. For this reason the Truth says:

﴿and let them find in you harshness﴾. Ghilzah (harshness) is a quality, and it is said: ghilzah, ghilzah, and ghilzah (3), and what is well known is that it means severity. When you strike your enemy, strike him with strength, boldness, and courage.

And when your enemy tries to strike you, receive the blow with endurance. Thus we find that harshness is required in two states: in the state of giving from you, and in the state of receiving from him. It is not sufficient that you strike your enemy a strong blow, and when he returns the blow you falter and weaken. The Truth requires of you a harshness that bears down upon your enemy, and a harshness that you bear from your enemy.

For this reason we find, in the verse of Al Imran, the Truth says in it:

﴿Be patient... (200)﴾ (Al 'Imran)

But suppose your enemy also is patient; then the command comes from the Truth:

﴿and be more patient... (200)﴾ (Al 'Imran)

That is: try to overcome him in patience. And the Truth warned against laying down arms after the battle has ended, because the enemy may lull the believer into complacency (4); therefore the command came from the Truth:

﴿and stand guard... (200)﴾ (Al 'Imran). That is: settle, O believer, in the land, so that he knows that you are awaiting him should he attempt a return attack or should he be tempted to fight again. So harshness requires of you that you attack, and requires of you that you endure, and enduring requires patience, and bearing down requires courage. If your opponent has a stubborn courage, then you must outlast him in endurance, that is, be more patient than he is. The word is originally derived from "nafasa fulan fulanan," meaning he competed with him, that is, he sought to outdo him; and competition (munafasah) is from the soul (nafs), and the Truth says: ﴿And for that let the competitors compete (26)﴾ (al-Mutaffifin), that is, compete in goodness. We know that the composition of the human soul needs something once or twice a day, and needs another thing five or six times a day, and needs a third thing constantly. In eating you take three meals, and in drinking you need two or four liters of water or more. As for breathing, you cannot endure being cut off from it, and it is the most essential necessity for human life.

We have said in the past: among the mercy of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is that a person may possess another person's food, and a person can endure being without food for weeks, but a person cannot endure cut-off water except for days ranging from three to ten, depending on the amount of water in his body; therefore the Truth, glorified is He, did not make water owned as He made food owned. As for air, you cannot endure its loss for even moments; for this reason Allah has never made air owned by anyone at all. It is as if He, glorified is He, knew that His servants are not safe from one another, and for this reason the inhaling and exhaling of air is called tanaffus (breathing), and it is from nafs, and it is the cause of the existence of the soul (nafs), which is a blend of matter and spirit; and the foundation is the very air that guarantees the continuation of the soul in life.

And if you compete with the enemy, you are hunting the precious thing, which is the elevation of Allah's method. And when you are patient against the people of falsehood, each one of the people of falsehood may be patient out of obstinacy (5) for a short period and then retreat, because falsehood is bound to vanish. Here He, glorified is He, says: ﴿and let them find in you harshness﴾, that is: harshness against the enemy, and harshness that you bear from the enemy, and that you be patient, and persevere, and stand guard.
